manifest:title: Corpus
organs:structures/brain/location: Inside the cranium, above and behind the eyes.
organs:structures/brain/summary: The control centre of the nervous system: about 1.4 kg of neurons and support cells that process the senses, control movement and generate thought, memory and emotion.
organs:structures/brain/functions/0: Interprets the senses and controls movement
organs:structures/brain/functions/1: Regulates breathing, heart rate and hormones through the brainstem and hypothalamus
organs:structures/brain/issues/0/note: Sudden face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech. Call emergency services immediately (think FAST).
organs:structures/brain/issues/1/note: A throbbing, often one-sided headache with nausea and sensitivity to light, sometimes after a visual aura.
organs:structures/brain/issues/2/note: Headache, confusion or dizziness after a head injury. Vomiting, a worsening headache or drowsiness needs urgent care.
organs:structures/brain/issues/3/note: Fever, severe headache, stiff neck, light sensitivity or a rash that doesn’t fade under a glass. It is an emergency.
organs:structures/pituitary/location: At the base of the brain behind the bridge of the nose, sitting in a saddle-shaped hollow of the sphenoid bone (the sella turcica).
organs:structures/pituitary/summary: A pea-sized gland hanging from the hypothalamus on a thin stalk. Often called the master gland, its hormones drive the thyroid, the adrenal glands, the ovaries and testes, growth and milk production.
organs:structures/pituitary/members/0/no: Makes growth hormone and prolactin, and the hormones that drive the thyroid (TSH), the adrenal glands (ACTH) and the ovaries or testes (FSH and LH).
organs:structures/pituitary/members/1/no: Releases two hormones made in the hypothalamus: antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which controls water balance, and oxytocin, for birth and breastfeeding.
organs:structures/pituitary/functions/0: Controls the thyroid, the adrenal glands and the ovaries or testes
organs:structures/pituitary/functions/1: Growth hormone drives growth in childhood and tissue repair throughout life
organs:structures/pituitary/functions/2: ADH tells the kidneys how much water to keep
organs:structures/pituitary/issues/0/not: A usually benign growth. It can cause headaches, loss of side vision, or symptoms from too much or too little of a hormone.
organs:structures/pituitary/issues/1/not: Passing large amounts of dilute urine with constant thirst, from too little ADH. It is not related to sugar diabetes.
organs:structures/eye/location: In the orbit, a bony socket in the skull, cushioned by fat and turned by six small muscles.
organs:structures/eye/summary: A fluid-filled ball about 24 mm across. The cornea and lens focus light onto the retina, which turns it into nerve signals that the optic nerve carries to the brain.
organs:structures/eye/members/0/note: The clear front window, which does most of the focusing.
organs:structures/eye/members/1/note: The coloured ring, which widens or narrows the pupil to let in more or less light.
organs:structures/eye/members/2/note: Changes shape to focus on near or distant things.
organs:structures/eye/members/3/note: The light-sensitive lining at the back. Its centre, the macula, gives sharp detail and colour.
organs:structures/eye/members/4/note: Six small muscles that turn the eye, worked by the oculomotor, trochlear and abducens nerves.
organs:structures/eye/functions/0: Focuses light and turns it into nerve signals
organs:structures/eye/functions/1: Adjusts to bright and dim light
organs:structures/eye/functions/2: Tears keep the surface clean and moist
organs:structures/eye/issues/0/note: A red, gritty or sticky eye from an infection or allergy. It usually settles by itself.
organs:structures/eye/issues/1/note: A painful red eye, sudden loss or blurring of vision, new flashes and floaters, or a shadow spreading over the vision needs urgent same-day care.
organs:structures/eye/issues/2/note: Cloudy or dim vision and glare from lights as the lens clouds with age. Treatable with surgery.
organs:structures/eye/issues/3/note: Raised pressure slowly damages the optic nerve, often without symptoms at first. Regular eye tests catch it.
organs:structures/ear/location: On each side of the head. The outer ear leads through the ear canal to the eardrum; the middle and inner ear lie inside the temporal bone.
organs:structures/ear/summary: The organ of hearing and balance. The outer ear gathers sound, three tiny bones in the middle ear amplify it and the cochlea turns it into nerve signals, while the semicircular canals sense movement of the head.
organs:structures/ear/members/0/note: The visible auricle and the ear canal, ending at the eardrum.
organs:structures/ear/members/1/note: An air-filled space with the three ossicles (malleus, incus and stapes), joined to the throat by the Eustachian tube.
organs:structures/ear/members/2/note: The cochlea for hearing, and the semicircular canals and vestibule for balance.
organs:structures/ear/functions/1: Balance, and sensing movement of the head
organs:structures/ear/functions/2: The Eustachian tube evens out pressure on the eardrum
organs:structures/ear/issues/0/note: Earache, often with a cold and especially in children. It usually settles within a few days.
organs:structures/ear/issues/1/note: An itchy, painful ear canal, often after swimming.
organs:structures/ear/issues/2/note: Muffled hearing and a full feeling. Avoid cotton buds; ear drops can soften it.
organs:structures/ear/issues/3/note: Sudden hearing loss in one ear needs same-day assessment. Vertigo with weakness, slurred speech or double vision is an emergency.
organs:structures/skin/listOnly: Not drawn on the map: it covers the whole body, so a drawing of it would hide everything underneath.
organs:structures/skin/location: Covers the whole body, about 1.5–2 m² in an adult. Thickest on the soles and palms, thinnest on the eyelids.
organs:structures/skin/summary: The body’s largest organ, at about 4 kg. It is a waterproof barrier against germs, sun and injury, helps control temperature, and is packed with receptors for touch, pain, heat and cold.
organs:structures/skin/members/0/note: The thin outer layer, renewed about every month. It makes melanin, and vitamin D in sunlight.
organs:structures/skin/members/1/note: The tough inner layer with blood vessels, nerve endings, hair roots and sweat and oil glands.
organs:structures/skin/functions/0: A barrier against germs, water loss and ultraviolet light
organs:structures/skin/functions/1: Controls temperature by sweating and changing blood flow
organs:structures/skin/functions/2: Senses touch, pain, heat and cold
organs:structures/skin/issues/0/note: Dry, itchy, inflamed patches, often in skin creases. Moisturisers help.
organs:structures/skin/issues/1/note: Spreading red, hot, swollen and painful skin, often with fever. It needs a doctor promptly.
organs:structures/skin/issues/2/note: A mole that changes size, shape or colour, bleeds or itches, or a sore that doesn’t heal needs checking.
organs:structures/skin/issues/3/note: A painful band of blistering rash on one side of the body, along one nerve.
organs:structures/pineal-gland/location: Deep in the middle of the brain, between its two halves, behind the third ventricle.
organs:structures/pineal-gland/summary: A tiny pine-cone-shaped gland that releases melatonin in the dark, helping to set the body’s sleep–wake rhythm.
organs:structures/pineal-gland/functions: Releases melatonin at night, which helps bring on sleep
Keeps the body clock in step with day and night
organs:structures/pineal-gland/issues/0/: Common, small and usually harmless, often found by chance on a brain scan.
organs:structures/pineal-gland/issues/1/: It gathers calcium with age. This shows up on scans and is normal.
organs:structures/thyroid/location: Front of the neck, wrapped around the windpipe below the Adam’s apple.
organs:structures/thyroid/summary: A butterfly-shaped gland whose hormones set the pace of the body’s metabolism.
organs:structures/thyroid/functions/1: Sets metabolic rate, heart rate and body temperature
organs:structures/thyroid/functions/2: Makes calcitonin, which helps regulate calcium
organs:structures/thyroid/issues/0/note: Tiredness, weight gain, feeling cold, constipation, dry skin.
organs:structures/thyroid/issues/1/note: Weight loss, a racing heart, tremor, heat intolerance, anxiety.
organs:structures/thyroid/issues/2/note: A swelling or lump at the front of the neck that moves when you swallow. Get it checked.
organs:structures/parathyroid/location: On the back of the thyroid gland, usually two behind each lobe.
organs:structures/parathyroid/summary: Usually four rice-grain-sized glands that keep the level of calcium in the blood steady with parathyroid hormone (PTH).
organs:structures/parathyroid/functions/: Raise blood calcium when it falls, drawing on the bones
Tell the kidneys to keep calcium and to activate vitamin D
Steady calcium keeps nerves and muscles working normally
organs:structures/parathyroid/issues/0/n: Too much calcium: thirst, kidney stones, thinning bones, tummy pain, low mood and tiredness. Often found on a routine blood test.
organs:structures/parathyroid/issues/1/n: Tingling around the mouth or in the fingers, or muscle cramps, after thyroid surgery needs prompt medical advice.
organs:structures/adrenal-gland/location: On top of each kidney, high at the back of the abdomen beside the spine (about T12).
organs:structures/adrenal-gland/summary: A small gland of about 5 g with two layers that work as separate glands: the outer cortex makes steroid hormones and the inner medulla releases adrenaline.
organs:structures/adrenal-gland/sideNote: The right adrenal is a small pyramid capping the top of the kidney, tucked behind the liver and the inferior vena cava.
The left adrenal is a crescent along the upper inner edge of the kidney, behind the stomach and pancreas.
organs:structures/adrenal-gland/members/: Makes cortisol (stress and blood sugar), aldosterone (salt and blood pressure) and small amounts of sex hormones.
Releases adrenaline and noradrenaline for the “fight or flight” response.
organs:structures/adrenal-gland/function: Cortisol helps the body handle stress, keeps blood sugar up and damps down inflammation
Aldosterone balances salt, water and blood pressure
Adrenaline readies the body for action: a faster heart and more blood to the muscles
organs:structures/adrenal-gland/issues/0: Tiredness, weight loss, dizziness on standing, salt craving and darker skin. Vomiting, confusion or collapse is an emergency (adrenal crisis).
organs:structures/adrenal-gland/issues/1: Too much cortisol, most often from steroid medicines: weight gain on the trunk and face, thin skin, easy bruising and high blood pressure.
organs:structures/adrenal-gland/issues/2: Usually benign and found by chance on a scan. Rarely one releases bursts of adrenaline, with pounding headaches, sweating and a racing heart.
organs:structures/pharynx/location: Behind the nose, mouth and larynx, from the base of the skull down to the sixth cervical vertebra, where it becomes the oesophagus.
organs:structures/pharynx/summary: A muscular funnel about 12–14 cm long, shared by air and food. It carries air on to the larynx and, when you swallow, squeezes food down into the oesophagus.
organs:structures/pharynx/members/0/note: Behind the nose. Holds the adenoids and the openings of the Eustachian tubes to the middle ears.
organs:structures/pharynx/members/1/note: Behind the mouth, with the palatine tonsils and the back of the tongue.
organs:structures/pharynx/members/2/note: Behind the larynx, down to the start of the oesophagus.
organs:structures/pharynx/functions/0: Carries air from the nose and mouth to the larynx
organs:structures/pharynx/functions/1: Swallowing: its muscles push food down while the airway is sealed off
organs:structures/pharynx/functions/2: Tonsils and adenoids in its walls guard against infection
organs:structures/pharynx/functions/3: Shapes the sound of the voice
organs:structures/pharynx/issues/0/note: Usually viral and better within a week. A severe sore throat with fever, or one side much worse than the other, needs a doctor.
organs:structures/pharynx/issues/1/note: Drooling, being unable to swallow saliva, or noisy breathing with a sore throat is an emergency.
organs:structures/pharynx/issues/2/note: Common and usually harmless when food goes down normally. Get it checked if it lasts, or if swallowing becomes difficult or painful.
organs:structures/nose/location: The middle of the face, from between the eyes to the nostrils. The nasal cavity behind opens into the nasopharynx.
organs:structures/nose/summary: The entrance to the airway. It warms, moistens and filters the air, and a small patch in its roof holds the smell receptors.
organs:structures/nose/members/0/note: Divides the nose into left and right halves: bone at the back, cartilage at the front.
organs:structures/nose/members/1/note: Three curled shelves on each side wall that warm and moisten the air.
organs:structures/nose/members/2/note: Air spaces in the frontal, maxillary, ethmoid and sphenoid bones that drain into the nose.
organs:structures/nose/members/3/note: A small patch in the roof of the nasal cavity with the smell receptors.
organs:structures/nose/functions/0: Warms, moistens and filters the air
organs:structures/nose/issues/0/note: Facial pain and pressure, a blocked nose and thick discharge after a cold, usually settling within 2–3 weeks.
organs:structures/nose/issues/1/note: Lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for 10–15 minutes. Bleeding for more than 20 minutes, or after a head injury, needs urgent care.
organs:structures/nose/issues/2/note: Sneezing, an itchy runny nose and itchy eyes at certain times of year.
organs:structures/nose/issues/3/note: Common after colds. If it lasts more than a few weeks, see a doctor.
organs:structures/tongue/location: Floor of the mouth, anchored to the hyoid bone and the jaw. Its back third faces the throat.
organs:structures/tongue/summary: A muscular organ that moves food while chewing, starts each swallow, shapes speech and carries most of the taste buds.
organs:structures/tongue/functions/0: Taste: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami
organs:structures/tongue/functions/1: Moves food around and pushes it back to swallow
organs:structures/tongue/issues/0/note: Small painful sores that heal within 2 weeks. An ulcer or patch lasting more than 3 weeks needs checking.
organs:structures/tongue/issues/1/note: White patches that wipe off and leave soreness, common after antibiotics or with steroid inhalers.
organs:structures/tongue/issues/2/name: Swelling of the tongue or lips
organs:structures/tongue/issues/2/note: With difficulty breathing or swallowing, it is an emergency (anaphylaxis).
organs:structures/salivary-glands/locati: In front of each ear (parotid), under the jaw (submandibular) and under the tongue (sublingual).
organs:structures/salivary-glands/summar: Three pairs of major glands, plus hundreds of tiny ones in the lining of the mouth, that make 0.5–1.5 litres of saliva a day.
organs:structures/salivary-glands/member: The largest, in front of the ear over the angle of the jaw. Its duct opens inside the cheek beside the upper second molar.
Under the jaw. Its duct opens under the tongue.
The smallest, under the tongue (not drawn).
organs:structures/salivary-glands/functi: Saliva moistens food and starts digesting starch
Protects the teeth and fights germs
Helps taste, chewing, swallowing and speech
organs:structures/salivary-glands/issues: Painful swelling of the parotid glands with fever. Vaccination prevents it.
Pain and swelling under the jaw or in front of the ear at mealtimes.
Common with many medicines, dehydration and some conditions.
organs:structures/larynx/location: Front of the neck, between the hyoid bone and the trachea (about C3–C6). The Adam’s apple is the ridge of its thyroid cartilage.
organs:structures/larynx/summary: The voice box: a framework of cartilages, muscles and vocal folds that guards the entrance to the airway and makes the sound of the voice.
organs:structures/larynx/members/0/note: The shield at the front. Its ridge is the Adam’s apple.
organs:structures/larynx/members/1/note: The only complete ring of cartilage in the airway, just below the thyroid cartilage.
organs:structures/larynx/members/2/note: A leaf-shaped flap that tips back over the airway when you swallow.
organs:structures/larynx/members/3/note: Two bands that vibrate in the outgoing air to make the voice.
organs:structures/larynx/functions/0: Closes the airway when you swallow
organs:structures/larynx/functions/2: Sets off coughing to clear the airway
organs:structures/larynx/issues/0/note: A hoarse or lost voice after a cold or overuse, usually better within 2 weeks.
organs:structures/larynx/issues/1/note: Hoarseness for more than 3 weeks, especially in smokers, needs checking by a doctor.
organs:structures/larynx/issues/2/note: A barking cough and noisy breathing in a young child, usually after a cold. Struggling to breathe needs urgent care.
organs:structures/trachea/location: From the front of the neck to the middle of the chest, where it splits into the left and right main bronchi.
organs:structures/trachea/summary: The windpipe: a tube about 10–12 cm long, held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage, that carries air from the larynx to the lungs.
organs:structures/trachea/functions/0: Carries air to and from the lungs
organs:structures/trachea/functions/1: Mucus and tiny hairs (cilia) sweep trapped particles upward
organs:structures/trachea/functions/2: Coughing clears and protects the airway
organs:structures/trachea/issues/0/note: A chesty cough and soreness behind the breastbone after a cold.
organs:structures/trachea/issues/1/note: Unable to speak, cough or breathe. Act immediately with back blows and abdominal thrusts, and call emergency services.
organs:structures/trachea/issues/2/note: Small objects usually lodge in the right main bronchus, which is wider and more vertical.
organs:structures/esophagus/location: Behind the trachea and heart, passing through the diaphragm to the stomach.
organs:structures/esophagus/summary: A muscular tube about 25 cm long that pushes swallowed food down to the stomach in waves (peristalsis).
organs:structures/esophagus/functions/0: Moves food and drink to the stomach
organs:structures/esophagus/functions/1: A lower sphincter stops stomach acid flowing back up
organs:structures/esophagus/issues/0/not: Heartburn and an acid taste, worse lying down or after large meals.
organs:structures/esophagus/issues/1/not: Food sticking on the way down, especially if it is getting worse or comes with weight loss, needs prompt assessment.
organs:structures/lung/location: Either side of the heart inside the rib cage, from just above the collarbone down to the diaphragm.
organs:structures/lung/summary: Spongy organs where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves, across hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs (alveoli).
organs:structures/lung/sideNotes/right: The right lung has three lobes (upper, middle and lower) and is shorter and wider, because the liver sits below it.
organs:structures/lung/sideNotes/left: The left lung has two lobes (upper and lower) and a notch where the heart sits.
organs:structures/lung/functions/0: Gas exchange: oxygen in, carbon dioxide out
organs:structures/lung/functions/1: Helps control the acidity of the blood
organs:structures/lung/functions/2: Filters small clots out of the circulation
organs:structures/lung/issues/0/note: Fever, cough with phlegm, breathlessness, and sharp chest pain when breathing in.
organs:structures/lung/issues/1/note: Wheezing, coughing and breathlessness from narrowed airways.
organs:structures/lung/issues/2/note: Sudden one-sided chest pain and breathlessness. It is urgent.
organs:structures/lung/issues/3/note: Sudden breathlessness, chest pain or coughing blood, often with a swollen calf. It is an emergency.
organs:structures/heart/location: Middle of the chest behind the sternum, tilted to the left. Its tip (apex) lies near the fifth rib space.
organs:structures/heart/summary: A fist-sized, four-chambered muscular pump. The right side sends blood through the lungs and the left side pumps it around the body, about 100,000 beats a day.
organs:structures/heart/functions/0: Pumps about 5 litres of blood a minute at rest
organs:structures/heart/functions/1: Its own electrical system sets the rhythm
organs:structures/heart/functions/2: Four valves keep blood flowing one way
organs:structures/heart/issues/0/note: Crushing or tight chest pain, possibly spreading to the arm, jaw or back, with sweating or breathlessness. Call emergency services.
organs:structures/heart/issues/1/note: Chest tightness on exertion that eases with rest. It needs medical assessment.
organs:structures/heart/issues/2/note: Palpitations, fluttering, or a racing or irregular pulse. With fainting or chest pain, get urgent care.
organs:structures/liver/location: Upper right abdomen under the right ribs, reaching across the midline.
organs:structures/liver/summary: The largest internal organ (about 1.5 kg). It processes everything absorbed from the gut, makes bile and many proteins, stores energy and clears toxins.
organs:structures/liver/issues/0/note: Often silent, and linked to weight, diabetes and alcohol.
organs:structures/liver/issues/1/note: Inflammation from viruses, alcohol or drugs: tiredness, yellow skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine.
organs:structures/liver/issues/2/note: Long-term scarring: a swollen belly, easy bruising, confusion.
organs:structures/gallbladder/location: Under the lower edge of the liver, where the right costal margin meets the midclavicular line.
organs:structures/gallbladder/summary: A small pear-shaped pouch that stores and concentrates bile, squeezing it into the duodenum after fatty meals.
organs:structures/gallbladder/functions/: Releases bile to help digest fats
organs:structures/gallbladder/issues/0/n: Severe pain under the right ribs or in the upper middle, often after fatty food, lasting minutes to hours. It can spread to the right shoulder blade.
organs:structures/gallbladder/issues/1/n: Persistent pain under the right ribs with fever. It needs medical care.
organs:structures/gallbladder/issues/2/n: Yellow skin or eyes with pale stools and dark urine may mean a stone is blocking the bile duct.
organs:structures/stomach/location: Upper left and central abdomen, just under the diaphragm.
organs:structures/stomach/summary: A stretchy, J-shaped bag that stores food, churns it and starts protein digestion with acid and enzymes.
organs:structures/stomach/functions/2: Releases food gradually into the small intestine
organs:structures/stomach/issues/0/note: Burning pain in the upper abdomen, bloating, nausea.
organs:structures/stomach/issues/1/note: Gnawing upper-abdominal pain, sometimes eased or worsened by food. Black stools or vomiting blood is an emergency.
organs:structures/stomach/issues/2/note: Vomiting and diarrhoea, usually viral. Watch for dehydration.
organs:structures/duodenum/location: Curves in a C around the head of the pancreas, from the stomach (about L1, right of the midline) to just left of the midline, behind the transverse colon.
organs:structures/duodenum/summary: The first 25 cm or so of the small intestine. It receives food from the stomach and mixes it with bile and pancreatic juice, which enter through a small opening in its wall (the major duodenal papilla).
organs:structures/duodenum/members/0/not: Starts at the pylorus. Its first, widened stretch (the duodenal cap) is where most duodenal ulcers form.
organs:structures/duodenum/members/1/not: Runs down beside the head of the pancreas. The bile and pancreatic ducts open into it.
organs:structures/duodenum/members/2/not: Crosses the midline in front of the aorta and the inferior vena cava.
organs:structures/duodenum/members/3/not: Rises to the duodenojejunal flexure, where the jejunum begins.
organs:structures/duodenum/functions/2: Releases hormones (secretin and cholecystokinin) that pace digestion
organs:structures/duodenum/issues/0/note: A burning or gnawing pain in the upper middle abdomen, often eased by eating and worse at night. Black stools or vomiting blood is an emergency.
organs:structures/duodenum/issues/1/note: Gluten damages the lining here first, so a small sample (biopsy) from the duodenum confirms it.
organs:structures/spleen/location: Upper left abdomen behind the stomach, sheltered by ribs 9–11.
organs:structures/spleen/summary: A fist-sized organ that filters the blood, removes old red cells and stores immune cells that fight infection.
organs:structures/spleen/functions/0: Filters blood and recycles old red blood cells
organs:structures/spleen/issues/0/note: After a blow to the left side: left upper pain, sometimes pain at the tip of the left shoulder, and dizziness. It is an emergency.
organs:structures/spleen/issues/1/note: From infections such as glandular fever (avoid contact sports while it is enlarged), or from liver or blood conditions.
organs:structures/pancreas/location: Deep in the upper abdomen behind the stomach, its head tucked into the curve of the duodenum.
organs:structures/pancreas/summary: A long gland with two jobs: it releases digestive enzymes into the gut, and hormones (insulin and glucagon) into the blood.
organs:structures/pancreas/members/0/not: Tucked into the curve of the duodenum.
organs:structures/pancreas/members/1/not: Crosses the spine behind the stomach.
organs:structures/pancreas/members/3/not: About a million clusters of hormone cells (islets of Langerhans), only 1–2% of the gland, that release insulin and glucagon into the blood.
organs:structures/pancreas/functions/0: Digestive enzymes for fats, proteins and carbohydrates
organs:structures/pancreas/functions/1: Insulin and glucagon control blood sugar
organs:structures/pancreas/issues/0/note: Severe upper-abdominal pain boring through to the back, with vomiting. Often from gallstones or alcohol, and urgent.
organs:structures/pancreas/issues/1/note: Thirst, passing a lot of urine, weight loss and tiredness.
organs:structures/pancreas/issues/2/note: Painless jaundice, back pain and weight loss. See a doctor promptly.
organs:structures/kidney/location: High at the back of the abdomen either side of the spine (about T12–L3), partly behind the lowest ribs. The right one sits a little lower.
organs:structures/kidney/summary: Bean-shaped filters that process about 180 litres of blood plasma a day into 1–2 litres of urine, balancing water, salts and blood pressure.
organs:structures/kidney/functions/0: Filters waste from the blood into urine
organs:structures/kidney/functions/2: Makes hormones for blood pressure (renin) and red-cell production (EPO)
organs:structures/kidney/issues/0/note: Waves of severe pain in the flank spreading to the groin, sometimes with blood in the urine.
organs:structures/kidney/issues/1/note: Flank pain, fever, shivering and urinary symptoms. See a doctor the same day.
organs:structures/kidney/issues/2/note: Usually silent, and found with blood and urine tests. Worth checking with diabetes or high blood pressure.
organs:structures/ureter/location: From each kidney down the back wall of the abdomen, over the brim of the pelvis, to the back of the bladder.
organs:structures/ureter/summary: A muscular tube about 25–30 cm long that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder in waves (peristalsis).
organs:structures/ureter/functions/0: Carries urine from the kidney to the bladder
organs:structures/ureter/functions/1: Squeezes it along in waves, several times a minute
organs:structures/ureter/functions/2: Enters the bladder at a slant, which stops urine flowing back up
organs:structures/ureter/issues/0/name: Kidney stone in the ureter (renal colic)
organs:structures/ureter/issues/0/note: Waves of severe pain from the flank to the groin as a stone moves down, often with nausea. With fever or shivering, get urgent care.
organs:structures/ureter/issues/1/note: A stone or a narrowing can back urine up and swell the kidney (hydronephrosis), which a scan shows.
organs:structures/small-intestine/locati: Coiled in the centre of the abdomen, framed by the large intestine.
organs:structures/small-intestine/summar: About 6 metres of coiled tube where most digestion and nutrient absorption happen, across millions of finger-like villi. It runs from the duodenum (shown separately) through the jejunum to the ileum.
organs:structures/small-intestine/functi: Digests food with enzymes and bile
Hosts a large part of the immune system
organs:structures/small-intestine/issues: Gluten triggers inflammation: bloating, diarrhoea, weight loss, anaemia.
Colicky pain, a swollen belly, vomiting and no wind or stools. It is an emergency.
Inflammation causing pain, diarrhoea and weight loss, often at the end of the ileum in the lower right.
organs:structures/large-intestine/locati: Frames the abdomen: up the right side, across under the stomach, then down the left side into the pelvis, where it becomes the rectum.
organs:structures/large-intestine/summar: About 1.5 m long (caecum and colon), ending in the rectum. It absorbs water and salts, hosts trillions of gut bacteria and forms stool.
organs:structures/large-intestine/functi: Gut bacteria ferment fibre and make vitamins
Forms stool and moves it on to the rectum
organs:structures/large-intestine/issues: Cramping, bloating and a change in bowel habit. Very common.
Pain in the lower left abdomen with fever, mostly in older adults.
Blood in the stool, a lasting change in bowel habit, unexplained weight loss or anaemia. See a doctor.
organs:structures/appendix/location: Lower right abdomen, hanging from the caecum.
organs:structures/appendix/summary: A finger-sized pouch off the start of the large intestine. It holds lymphoid tissue and may act as a reservoir for helpful gut bacteria.
organs:structures/appendix/functions/1: A possible reservoir of gut bacteria
organs:structures/appendix/issues/0/note: Pain that starts around the navel and moves to the lower right, worse with movement or coughing, with loss of appetite, nausea and fever. It is urgent.
organs:structures/rectum/location: At the back of the pelvis, following the curve of the sacrum and coccyx, from the end of the sigmoid colon (about S3) down to the anus.
organs:structures/rectum/summary: The last 12 cm or so of the large intestine. It holds stool until it is convenient to pass, and stretch sensors in its wall create the urge to go.
organs:structures/rectum/members/0/note: The wide lower part where stool waits.
organs:structures/rectum/members/1/note: The last 3–4 cm, ringed by the internal (automatic) and external (voluntary) anal sphincters.
organs:structures/rectum/functions/0: Holds stool until you pass it
organs:structures/rectum/functions/1: Senses fullness and triggers the urge to go
organs:structures/rectum/functions/2: The sphincters and pelvic floor keep it closed
organs:structures/rectum/issues/0/note: Bright red blood on the paper, itching or a soft lump at the anus. Common, and usually manageable at home.
organs:structures/rectum/issues/1/note: Sharp pain while passing stool, then a burning ache, with a little bright red blood.
organs:structures/rectum/issues/2/note: Dark or mixed-in blood, a lasting change in bowel habit or weight loss needs a doctor. Heavy bleeding needs urgent care.
organs:structures/bladder/location: Low in the pelvis, behind the pubic bones.
organs:structures/bladder/summary: A muscular, stretchy reservoir that holds urine from the kidneys (around 400–500 ml) until it is convenient to empty.
organs:structures/bladder/functions/1: Empties under control of sphincters and the pelvic floor
organs:structures/bladder/issues/0/note: Burning, urgency, passing urine often, and low central pain.
organs:structures/bladder/issues/1/note: Unable to pass urine, with a painful, full lower belly. It is urgent.
organs:structures/bladder/issues/2/note: Leaking when coughing (stress) or with a sudden urge. Common and treatable.
organs:structures/ovary/location: Low in the pelvis on each side of the uterus, against the side wall, about the size and shape of an almond.
organs:structures/ovary/summary: The female gonads. From puberty to the menopause they ripen an egg about once a month and make the hormones oestrogen and progesterone, which run the menstrual cycle.
organs:structures/ovary/functions/0: Ripens and releases an egg each cycle (ovulation)
organs:structures/ovary/issues/0/note: Fluid-filled sacs are common and usually harmless, coming and going with the cycle. A large one can ache or cause one-sided pain.
organs:structures/ovary/issues/1/note: Sudden, severe one-sided low pain, often with vomiting, when the ovary twists on its stalk. It is an emergency.
organs:structures/ovary/issues/2/note: Irregular or absent periods, extra hair growth, acne and difficulty getting pregnant. See a doctor.
organs:structures/ovary/issues/3/note: Bloating that doesn’t go away, feeling full quickly, pelvic or belly pain and needing to pass urine more often, especially over 50. See a doctor if it lasts three weeks or more.
organs:structures/uterine-tube/location: From each upper corner of the uterus out to the ovary, about 10 cm long.
organs:structures/uterine-tube/summary: A narrow tube whose fringed end catches the egg released by the ovary. Egg and sperm usually meet here, and the tube carries the early embryo to the uterus over a few days.
organs:structures/uterine-tube/functions: Catches the egg from the ovary
Moves the fertilised egg to the uterus
organs:structures/uterine-tube/members/0: The funnel-shaped end beside the ovary, fringed with finger-like fimbriae.
organs:structures/uterine-tube/members/1: The wide middle part, where fertilisation usually happens.
organs:structures/uterine-tube/members/2: The narrow part next to the uterus.
organs:structures/uterine-tube/issues/0/: A pregnancy that implants in the tube: one-sided low pain, vaginal bleeding, pain at the tip of the shoulder or fainting, usually 4–12 weeks into pregnancy. It is an emergency.
organs:structures/uterine-tube/issues/1/: Infection spreading up from the cervix, often a sexually transmitted infection: low pain, fever, unusual discharge, pain during sex. It can scar the tubes, so see a doctor promptly.
organs:structures/uterus/location: In the middle of the pelvis, between the bladder in front and the rectum behind, usually tipped forward over the bladder.
organs:structures/uterus/summary: A hollow, pear-sized muscular organ. Its lining thickens each cycle and is shed as a period if no pregnancy starts. In pregnancy it grows to hold the baby, and in labour its muscle pushes the baby out.
organs:structures/uterus/functions/0: Builds and sheds its lining in the menstrual cycle
organs:structures/uterus/functions/2: Contracts to deliver the baby in labour
organs:structures/uterus/members/0/note: The domed top, above where the tubes enter.
organs:structures/uterus/members/1/note: The main hollow, lined by the endometrium.
organs:structures/uterus/members/2/note: The narrow neck that opens into the vagina. Cervical screening checks it for changes that could turn into cancer.
organs:structures/uterus/issues/0/note: Cramping low central pain around periods. Simple painkillers and heat help. Pain bad enough to stop daily life is worth checking.
organs:structures/uterus/issues/1/note: Soaking through pads or tampons every hour or two, passing large clots, or feeling tired and breathless from anaemia. Common and treatable: see a doctor.
organs:structures/uterus/issues/2/note: Non-cancerous growths of the womb muscle: heavy or long periods, pressure in the pelvis, needing to pass urine often.
organs:structures/uterus/issues/3/note: Tissue like the womb lining growing outside the uterus: severe period pain, pain during sex and long-lasting pelvic pain. It often takes years to diagnose, so keep raising pain that doesn’t settle.
organs:structures/uterus/issues/4/note: Bleeding and cramping in early pregnancy. Get care the same day; heavy bleeding or fainting is an emergency.
organs:structures/uterus/issues/5/note: Bleeding after sex, between periods or after the menopause needs a doctor. Regular cervical screening finds early changes.
organs:structures/vagina/location: A muscular tube from the cervix down and forward to the vulva, with the bladder and urethra in front and the rectum behind.
organs:structures/vagina/summary: A stretchy, muscular passage that lets out menstrual blood, receives the penis in sex and becomes the birth canal in childbirth. Its natural bacteria keep it slightly acidic, which protects against infection.
organs:structures/vagina/functions/2: Stretches to become the birth canal
organs:structures/vagina/issues/0/note: Itching, soreness and a thick white discharge. Very common; a pharmacy treatment works for most.
organs:structures/vagina/issues/1/note: A thin grey or white discharge with a fishy smell. It is treated with antibiotics.
organs:structures/vagina/issues/2/note: Common after the menopause and while breastfeeding: soreness and pain during sex. Moisturisers and treatment help.
organs:structures/vulva/location: The external genitals, between the thighs below the pubic bone.
organs:structures/vulva/summary: The outer folds of the labia protect the openings of the urethra and the vagina. The clitoris, with as many nerve endings as the tip of the penis, is the centre of sexual pleasure.
organs:structures/vulva/functions/0: Protects the openings of the urethra and vagina
organs:structures/vulva/members/0/note: The outer folds of skin and fat, with hair from puberty.
organs:structures/vulva/members/1/note: The thin inner folds around the vestibule.
organs:structures/vulva/members/2/note: Erectile tissue whose small visible tip extends deep along each side of the vestibule.
organs:structures/vulva/members/3/note: The space between the labia minora, with the openings of the urethra and vagina and of Bartholin’s glands.
organs:structures/vulva/issues/0/note: A swelling at one side of the vaginal opening. A painful, hot one may be an abscess and needs a doctor.
organs:structures/vulva/issues/1/note: Burning or soreness lasting months with no visible cause. It is real and treatable: see a doctor.
organs:structures/vulva/issues/2/note: Itchy white patches of skin. See a doctor: it is treated with creams and needs follow-up.
organs:structures/vulva/issues/3/note: Painful blisters and sores, or small painless lumps. A sexual health clinic can test and treat confidentially.
organs:structures/breast#female/location: On the front of the chest over the pectoralis major, from about the 2nd to the 6th rib, with a tail of tissue toward the armpit.
organs:structures/breast#female/summary: Glandular and fatty tissue that develops at puberty. After childbirth its milk glands make breast milk, which flows through ducts to the nipple. Most of its lymph drains to the armpit nodes.
organs:structures/breast#female/function: Makes and releases milk after childbirth
organs:structures/breast#female/members/: 15–20 lobes of milk glands, each with a duct to the nipple.
The milk ducts open on the nipple; small glands in the areola keep it supple.
A strip of breast tissue reaching up into the armpit.
organs:structures/breast#female/issues/0: Most lumps are harmless cysts or fibroadenomas, but any new lump, change in shape, puckered skin, nipple change or discharge needs a doctor.
organs:structures/breast#female/issues/1: A painful, hot, red area, usually while breastfeeding, sometimes with fever. Keep feeding or expressing, and see a doctor if it isn’t better within a day.
organs:structures/breast#female/issues/2: Often comes and goes with periods. Pain alone is rarely cancer, but get it checked if it persists.
organs:structures/breast#female/issues/3: The most common cancer in women. Know what is normal for you, and go to screening when invited.
organs:structures/testis/location: In the scrotum, below the penis. The left usually hangs a little lower.
organs:structures/testis/summary: The male gonads, each about the size of a small plum. From puberty they make sperm and the hormone testosterone. They hang outside the body because sperm develop best a few degrees below body temperature.
organs:structures/testis/issues/0/note: Sudden, severe pain in one testicle, often with swelling, belly pain and vomiting, most often in teenagers. It is an emergency: surgery within hours saves the testicle.
organs:structures/testis/issues/1/note: A painless lump or swelling, or a heavy feeling in the scrotum. Most common between 15 and 49 and very treatable. See a doctor.
organs:structures/testis/issues/2/note: A soft, painless swelling of fluid (hydrocele) or of veins that feels like a bag of worms (varicocele). Usually harmless, but have any swelling checked.
organs:structures/epididymis/location: A coiled tube along the top and back of each testis.
organs:structures/epididymis/summary: About six metres of tightly coiled tube in which sperm mature and are stored before ejaculation.
organs:structures/epididymis/issues/0/no: Pain and swelling at the back of the testicle building up over a day or two, sometimes with fever or burning when passing urine. Usually an infection: see a doctor the same day.
organs:structures/epididymis/issues/1/no: A smooth, painless lump above and behind the testicle. Common and harmless, but get any new lump checked.
organs:structures/vas-deferens/location: From the epididymis up in the spermatic cord through the groin (the inguinal canal), then over and behind the bladder to the prostate.
organs:structures/vas-deferens/summary: A muscular tube about 45 cm long that carries sperm from the epididymis to the urethra. Cutting it (vasectomy) is a permanent form of contraception.
organs:structures/vas-deferens/issues/0/: Bruising and an ache for a week or two are common. A growing, painful swelling or fever needs a doctor.
organs:structures/seminal-vesicle/locati: Behind the bladder, above the prostate.
organs:structures/seminal-vesicle/summar: A coiled gland that makes most of the fluid of semen, rich in sugar (fructose) that fuels the sperm. Its duct joins the vas deferens inside the prostate.
organs:structures/seminal-vesicle/functi: Makes most of the fluid in semen
organs:structures/seminal-vesicle/issues: Usually harmless and settles by itself. See a doctor if it keeps happening, or if you are over 40.
organs:structures/prostate/location: Just below the bladder, wrapped around the start of the urethra, in front of the rectum.
organs:structures/prostate/summary: A walnut-sized gland that adds a thin, milky fluid to semen. It grows with age, and because the urethra runs through it, an enlarged prostate can make passing urine harder.
organs:structures/prostate/functions/1: Helps close off the bladder during ejaculation
organs:structures/prostate/issues/0/note: A weak stream, needing to go often or at night, and not emptying fully. Common after 50 and treatable.
organs:structures/prostate/issues/1/note: Pain between the scrotum and the anus, in the lower back, or when passing urine or ejaculating, sometimes with fever. See a doctor.
organs:structures/prostate/issues/2/note: Often causes no symptoms early on. Talk to a doctor about testing, especially over 50, or over 45 with a family history or of Black ethnicity.
organs:structures/penis/location: In front of the scrotum, its root attached to the pubic bones.
organs:structures/penis/summary: Carries the urethra, through which both urine and semen leave the body. Its spongy tissue fills with blood to make it stiff in an erection.
organs:structures/penis/functions/0: Carries urine and semen out of the body
organs:structures/penis/members/0/note: Two columns of spongy tissue that fill with blood in an erection.
organs:structures/penis/members/1/note: Surrounds the urethra and widens into the glans.
organs:structures/penis/members/2/note: The sensitive tip, covered by the foreskin unless circumcised.
organs:structures/penis/issues/0/note: Common, and often linked to blood-vessel health, diabetes, stress or medicines. Worth seeing a doctor, as it can be an early sign of heart disease.
organs:structures/penis/issues/1/note: Soreness, redness and discharge under the foreskin. Gentle washing helps; see a doctor if it persists.
organs:structures/penis/issues/2/note: An erection lasting more than four hours without arousal is an emergency.
organs:structures/scrotum/location: A pouch of skin and thin muscle below the penis, holding the testes.
organs:structures/scrotum/summary: Keeps the testes about 2–3 °C cooler than the rest of the body: its muscle draws them up in the cold and lets them hang lower in the heat.
organs:structures/scrotum/functions/0: Holds the testes and keeps them cool
organs:structures/scrotum/issues/0/note: A painless swelling is often a hydrocele or a hernia. A sudden, painful swelling is an emergency.
organs:structures/scrotum/issues/1/note: A bulge that comes down into the scrotum when standing or straining. A tender, hard swelling that won’t go back is urgent.
organs:structures/breast#male/location: On the front of the chest over the pectoralis major, behind the nipple.
organs:structures/breast#male/summary: A small disc of breast tissue behind the nipple, which doesn’t develop at puberty the way it does in women. Its lymph drains to the armpit nodes.
organs:structures/breast#male/issues/0/n: Swelling of the breast tissue, common in teenage boys and older men and with some medicines or weight gain. Usually harmless, but see a doctor about a firm or one-sided lump.
organs:structures/breast#male/issues/1/n: Rare in men, but a painless lump, a turned-in nipple or discharge needs a doctor.
organs:groups/reproductive-female/summar: The ovaries make eggs and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone; the uterine tubes carry the egg to the uterus, which holds a pregnancy; the vagina and vulva are the birth canal and the external genitals. The breasts make milk after childbirth.
organs:groups/reproductive-male/summary: The testes make sperm and testosterone; the epididymis stores the sperm, and the vas deferens carries them to the urethra, where the seminal vesicles and prostate add the fluid of semen. The penis carries urine and semen out of the body.
skeleton:structures/frontal/summary: Forms the forehead, the roofs of the eye sockets and the front of the skull vault. The frontal sinuses sit just above the brows.
skeleton:structures/frontal/issues/0/not: Pressure or pain over the forehead and brows, worse when bending forward, often after a cold.
skeleton:structures/frontal/issues/1/not: Usually from a direct blow. A dent, swelling or clear fluid from the nose needs urgent care.
skeleton:structures/parietal/summary: The two parietal bones form the roof and upper sides of the skull, meeting each other at the sagittal suture along the top of the head.
skeleton:structures/parietal/issues/0/no: A common site of fracture after head injury. The middle meningeal artery runs beneath the nearby temple region, so worsening headache, vomiting or drowsiness after a blow is an emergency.
skeleton:structures/temporal/summary: Forms the lower side of the skull around the ear. It houses the ear canal, the hearing and balance organs and the mastoid air cells, and provides the socket of the jaw joint.
skeleton:structures/temporal/issues/0/no: The inner ear lives inside this bone, so vertigo, hearing loss and tinnitus often start here.
skeleton:structures/temporal/issues/1/no: Infection spreading from the middle ear: pain, redness and swelling behind the ear with fever.
skeleton:structures/occipital/summary: Forms the back and base of the skull. The spinal cord passes through its large opening (foramen magnum), and its condyles rest on the atlas.
skeleton:structures/occipital/issues/0/n: Muscles and nerves around the base of the skull often cause pain at the back of the head, sometimes spreading over the scalp.
skeleton:structures/sphenoid/summary: A butterfly-shaped bone at the centre of the skull base, visible at the temples and at the back of the eye sockets. It cradles the pituitary gland in a pocket called the sella turcica.
skeleton:structures/sphenoid/issues/0/no: A deep headache behind the eyes or at the top of the head that is hard to pin down.
skeleton:structures/sphenoid/issues/1/no: Grows in the sella turcica and can press on the optic nerves, narrowing side vision.
skeleton:structures/ethmoid/summary: A light, honeycombed bone between the eye sockets. It forms the upper nasal septum, the inner walls of the orbits and the roof of the nose, where its sieve-like plate lets the nerves of smell through to the brain.
skeleton:structures/ethmoid/issues/0/not: Pain and pressure between the eyes and across the bridge of the nose.
skeleton:structures/ethmoid/issues/1/nam: Loss of smell after head injury
skeleton:structures/ethmoid/issues/1/not: The thin cribriform plate can fracture and tear the olfactory nerves.
skeleton:structures/nasal/summary: Two small oblong bones forming the bony bridge of the nose. The lower part of the nose is cartilage.
skeleton:structures/nasal/issues/0/note: The most commonly fractured facial bone: swelling, bruising, a crooked bridge, nosebleed.
skeleton:structures/maxilla/summary: The two maxillae form the upper jaw and hold the upper teeth. They also form the floor of the eye sockets, the sides of the nose and most of the hard palate. Each contains a large maxillary sinus.
skeleton:structures/maxilla/issues/0/not: Cheek pain and pressure, sometimes felt as an upper toothache.
skeleton:structures/maxilla/issues/1/not: Infection at a tooth root: throbbing pain and cheek swelling. Spreading swelling or fever needs prompt care.
skeleton:structures/zygomatic/summary: The cheekbone. It forms the prominence of the cheek and the outer rim of the eye socket, and joins the temporal bone through the zygomatic arch.
skeleton:structures/zygomatic/issues/0/n: After a punch or fall: a flattened cheek, numbness of the cheek or upper lip, double vision.
skeleton:structures/lacrimal/summary: The smallest facial bone, on the inner wall of each eye socket. It holds the tear sac and begins the tear duct that drains into the nose.
skeleton:structures/lacrimal/issues/0/no: A constantly watery eye or sticky discharge; common in babies.
skeleton:structures/palatine/summary: L-shaped bones at the back of the nasal cavity that form the rear of the hard palate.
skeleton:structures/palatine/issues/0/no: If the palate does not fuse before birth, a gap is left in the roof of the mouth.
skeleton:structures/inferior-concha/summ: A scroll-shaped bone on the side wall of each nasal cavity. It warms, humidifies and filters the air you breathe in.
skeleton:structures/inferior-concha/issu: The lining over these bones swells with allergies or colds, causing a blocked nose.
skeleton:structures/vomer/summary: A thin, plough-shaped bone forming the lower back part of the nasal septum.
skeleton:structures/vomer/issues/0/note: A bent septum narrows one nostril, causing blockage, snoring or nosebleeds.
skeleton:structures/mandible/summary: The lower jaw: the largest and strongest facial bone and the only skull bone that moves. It holds the lower teeth and hinges at the two jaw joints.
skeleton:structures/mandible/issues/0/no: Often breaks in two places: pain, a misaligned bite, a numb lower lip.
skeleton:structures/mandible/issues/1/no: Clicking, aching or locking when chewing. See the temporomandibular joint.
skeleton:structures/ossicles/summary: Three tiny bones in each middle ear that pass sound vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear, amplifying them on the way.
skeleton:structures/ossicles/members/1/n: The “anvil”, the middle link of the chain.
skeleton:structures/ossicles/members/2/n: The “stirrup” and the smallest bone in the body. Its footplate sits in the oval window of the inner ear.
skeleton:structures/ossicles/issues/0/no: Abnormal bone growth fixes the stapes in place, causing slowly worsening hearing loss.
skeleton:structures/ossicles/issues/1/no: Fluid around the ossicles muffles hearing and causes ear pain, especially in children.
skeleton:structures/hyoid/summary: A U-shaped bone in the front of the neck, just above the larynx. It anchors the tongue and the muscles of swallowing.
skeleton:structures/hyoid/noJoints: The hyoid is the only bone in the body that doesn’t articulate with any other bone. Instead it hangs in a sling of muscles from the jaw, skull, sternum and shoulder blade (listed below), which raise and lower it every time you swallow.
skeleton:structures/hyoid/issues/0/note: Rare. It can follow strangulation or severe neck trauma and is always an emergency.
skeleton:structures/c1/summary: The ring-shaped first vertebra, which has no body. It carries the skull on its two lateral masses, and the nodding “yes” joint sits between them.
skeleton:structures/c1/issues/0/note: A burst fracture from a heavy blow to the top of the head, such as diving into shallow water. It is an emergency.
skeleton:structures/c2/summary: The second vertebra. A tooth-like peg (the dens) projects up into the atlas and acts as the pivot for turning the head (“no”).
skeleton:structures/c2/issues/0/note: A common neck fracture in older adults after a fall. Neck pain after any fall in an older person should be checked.
skeleton:structures/c3/summary: A typical cervical vertebra: a small body and transverse processes pierced by holes for the vertebral arteries.
skeleton:structures/c4/summary: A typical cervical vertebra. Nerve roots from C3–C5 form the phrenic nerve that drives the diaphragm (“C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive”).
skeleton:structures/c5/summary: A typical cervical vertebra. C5–C6 is the most common level for disc wear and pinched nerves in the neck.
skeleton:structures/c6/summary: Its transverse process has a prominent front bump (the carotid tubercle) beside the carotid artery. The larynx becomes the trachea at about this level.
skeleton:structures/c7/summary: It has the longest spinous process of the neck: the bump you can feel at the base of your neck when you bend your head forward.
skeleton:structures/t1/summary: The first thoracic vertebra. It carries the first pair of ribs.
skeleton:structures/t2/summary: A thoracic vertebra. The notch at the top of the sternum lines up with T2.
skeleton:structures/t3/summary: A thoracic vertebra. Each rib attaches to the side of the vertebral body and to the transverse process, so the spine and rib cage move together.
skeleton:structures/t4/summary: The sternal angle, and the split of the trachea into the two main bronchi, lie at about the level of T4–T5.
skeleton:structures/t5/summary: A thoracic vertebra. Each rib attaches to the side of the vertebral body and to the transverse process, so the spine and rib cage move together.
skeleton:structures/t6/summary: A typical thoracic vertebra: a heart-shaped body with facets for the ribs, and a long spinous process angled steeply down.
skeleton:structures/t7/summary: A thoracic vertebra. Each rib attaches to the side of the vertebral body and to the transverse process, so the spine and rib cage move together.
skeleton:structures/t8/summary: A thoracic vertebra. The inferior vena cava passes through the diaphragm at about this level.
skeleton:structures/t9/summary: A thoracic vertebra. Each rib attaches to the side of the vertebral body and to the transverse process, so the spine and rib cage move together.
skeleton:structures/t10/summary: A thoracic vertebra. The esophagus passes through the diaphragm at about this level.
skeleton:structures/t11/summary: Carries the 11th ribs, the first of the two floating pairs.
skeleton:structures/t12/summary: The last rib-bearing vertebra. The junction with the lumbar spine (T12–L1) is the most common site of spinal compression fractures.
skeleton:structures/l1/summary: The spinal cord itself ends at about L1–L2. Below this, nerve roots continue down as the cauda equina (“horse’s tail”).
skeleton:structures/l2/summary: A lumbar vertebra with a large, kidney-shaped body built to carry the weight of the upper body.
skeleton:structures/l3/summary: Usually the most mobile lumbar level, with the longest transverse processes. The navel lies at about L3–L4.
skeleton:structures/l4/summary: The tops of the iliac crests line up with L4, the landmark doctors use for a lumbar puncture.
skeleton:structures/l5/summary: The largest vertebra, wedge-shaped where it sits on the sacrum. The L4–L5 and L5–S1 discs carry the most load and are the most common sites of disc herniation.
skeleton:structures/l5/issues/0/note: L5 can slip forward on the sacrum, causing low back pain and tight hamstrings. It is common in young gymnasts and fast bowlers.
skeleton:structures/sacrum/summary: Five vertebrae fused into a triangular wedge that locks the spine into the pelvis between the two hip bones. Nerve roots leave through its four pairs of holes (foramina).
skeleton:structures/sacrum/issues/0/note: Low-back or buttock pain, often on one side. See the sacroiliac joint.
skeleton:structures/sacrum/issues/1/note: Deep low-back or buttock pain on weight-bearing in runners and in people with osteoporosis.
skeleton:structures/sacrum/sexNotes/0/te: In women the sacrum is shorter, wider and less curved, tilted back to widen the pelvic outlet.
skeleton:structures/sacrum/sexNotes/1/te: In men the sacrum is longer, narrower and more curved.
skeleton:structures/coccyx/summary: The tailbone: 3–5 small fused vertebrae at the bottom of the spine, which anchor pelvic-floor muscles and ligaments.
skeleton:structures/coccyx/issues/0/note: Pain when sitting, often after a fall onto the bottom or after childbirth.
skeleton:structures/sternum/summary: The breastbone. The collarbones and the first seven pairs of ribs attach to it, and it shields the heart.
skeleton:structures/sternum/members/0/no: The top part. The clavicles and first ribs attach here, and the jugular notch sits above it.
skeleton:structures/sternum/members/1/no: The long middle part, which carries ribs 2–7. Its joint with the manubrium forms the sternal angle.
skeleton:structures/sternum/members/2/no: The small tip at the bottom, cartilage in youth and slowly turning to bone.
skeleton:structures/sternum/issues/0/not: Usually from a seat-belt or steering-wheel impact. The heart underneath can be bruised too.
skeleton:structures/sternum/issues/1/not: Tender spots along the edges of the sternum where the rib cartilages attach.
skeleton:structures/rib-1/summary: The shortest, broadest and most curved rib, tucked under the collarbone. The subclavian artery and the nerves to the arm cross over it.
skeleton:structures/rib-2/summary: Joins the sternum at the sternal angle, the bump used as the starting point for counting ribs.
skeleton:structures/rib-3/summary: A true rib: its costal cartilage joins the sternum directly.
skeleton:structures/rib-4/summary: A true rib. The nipple usually lies near the space below this rib.
skeleton:structures/rib-5/summary: A true rib. The tip (apex) of the heart lies behind the space just below it, on the left.
skeleton:structures/rib-6/summary: A true rib. The lower edge of the lungs crosses this rib at the front.
skeleton:structures/rib-7/summary: The last true rib. Its long cartilage reaches the sternum beside the xiphoid process.
skeleton:structures/rib-8/summary: A false rib: its cartilage joins the cartilage of the rib above instead of the sternum, helping form the costal margin.
skeleton:structures/rib-9/summary: A false rib, joined to the cartilage of rib 8. Its cartilage marks the usual position of the gallbladder fundus on the right.
skeleton:structures/rib-10/summary: The last false rib, forming the lowest point of the costal margin at the side.
skeleton:structures/rib-11/summary: A floating rib: it ends free in the muscles of the flank with no attachment at the front.
skeleton:structures/rib-12/summary: The shortest rib and a floating rib. The upper pole of the kidney lies behind it.
skeleton:structures/clavicle/summary: The collarbone: an S-shaped strut that holds the shoulder out from the chest. It is the only bony link between the arm and the trunk.
skeleton:structures/clavicle/issues/0/no: One of the most common fractures, usually from a fall onto the shoulder or an outstretched hand: a bump and pain over the bone.
skeleton:structures/scapula/summary: The shoulder blade: a triangular plate that glides over the back of the rib cage. Its shallow socket (the glenoid) holds the head of the humerus, and 17 muscles attach to it.
skeleton:structures/scapula/issues/0/not: The cuff muscles start on the scapula: shoulder pain when lifting the arm, and pain at night.
skeleton:structures/scapula/issues/1/not: The shoulder blade sticks out when you push, usually from a nerve problem affecting serratus anterior.
skeleton:structures/humerus/summary: The upper arm bone. Its ball-shaped head fits the shoulder socket, and at the elbow it widens into the trochlea and capitulum. The ulnar nerve runs behind its inner knob, the “funny bone”.
skeleton:structures/humerus/issues/0/not: Common in older adults after a fall: shoulder pain and bruising that spreads down the arm.
skeleton:structures/humerus/issues/1/not: Just above the elbow, typical in children. It can injure nearby vessels and nerves and is urgent.
skeleton:structures/humerus/issues/2/not: Can injure the radial nerve, causing wrist drop.
skeleton:structures/radius/summary: The forearm bone on the thumb side. It rotates around the ulna to turn the palm up and down, and carries most of the load at the wrist.
skeleton:structures/radius/issues/0/note: The most common fracture in adults, from a fall on an outstretched hand: wrist pain, swelling and a “dinner-fork” bend.
skeleton:structures/radius/issues/1/note: In toddlers, a sudden pull on the arm can slip the radial head out of its ligament ring.
skeleton:structures/ulna/summary: The forearm bone on the little-finger side. Its hooked upper end (the olecranon) forms the point of the elbow and grips the humerus like a wrench.
skeleton:structures/ulna/issues/0/note: From a fall directly onto the point of the elbow.
skeleton:structures/ulna/issues/1/note: A soft swelling over the point of the elbow after pressure or a minor knock. A red, hot one may be infected.
skeleton:structures/carpals/summary: Eight small bones in two rows that form the flexible wrist. Their arch makes the floor of the carpal tunnel, which carries the median nerve and the finger tendons.
skeleton:structures/carpals/members/0/no: Boat-shaped and on the thumb side, bridging both rows. The most commonly broken carpal bone.
skeleton:structures/carpals/members/1/no: Crescent-shaped, in the centre of the first row. The carpal most often dislocated.
skeleton:structures/carpals/members/3/no: A pea-sized sesamoid bone within a tendon, sitting in front of the triquetrum.
skeleton:structures/carpals/members/4/no: Forms the saddle joint at the base of the thumb.
skeleton:structures/carpals/members/5/no: A small wedge at the base of the index finger.
skeleton:structures/carpals/members/6/no: The largest carpal bone, at the centre of the wrist.
skeleton:structures/carpals/members/7/no: Has a hook that helps form Guyon’s canal for the ulnar nerve.
skeleton:structures/carpals/issues/0/not: After a fall on an outstretched hand: pain in the hollow at the base of the thumb (the “anatomical snuffbox”). Easy to miss on X-ray and slow to heal, so get it checked.
skeleton:structures/carpals/issues/1/not: Pressure on the median nerve: tingling and numbness in the thumb, index and middle fingers, often worse at night.
skeleton:structures/carpals/issues/2/not: Wrist pain and clicking after a fall. Left untreated it can lead to arthritis.
skeleton:structures/metacarpals/summary: Five long bones forming the palm, numbered I (thumb) to V (little finger). Their heads are the knuckles.
skeleton:structures/metacarpals/members/: The thumb: short, thick and very mobile.
The index finger, the longest metacarpal.
The middle finger, with a small styloid process at its base.
The little finger. Its neck breaks in a “boxer’s fracture”.
skeleton:structures/metacarpals/issues/0: Fracture of the fifth metacarpal neck from punching a hard object.
skeleton:structures/metacarpals/issues/1: A fracture at the base of the thumb metacarpal that runs into the joint.
skeleton:structures/hand-phalanges/summa: The finger bones: three in each finger (proximal, middle and distal) and two in the thumb, 14 per hand.
skeleton:structures/hand-phalanges/membe: The longest, next to the knuckles.
The fingertips, each with a rough tuft under the nail bed.
skeleton:structures/hand-phalanges/issue: Common in ball sports. A finger that looks rotated or crooked needs assessment.
The fingertip droops and can’t straighten after a blow to its tip, because the extensor tendon has torn.
skeleton:structures/hip-bone/summary: Each hip bone is three bones (ilium, ischium and pubis) fused at the hip socket, the acetabulum. With the sacrum they form the pelvic ring that carries the weight of the trunk to the legs.
skeleton:structures/hip-bone/members/0/n: The broad wing. Its crest is the “hip” you rest your hands on.
skeleton:structures/hip-bone/members/1/n: The lower back part. You sit on its tuberosity, the “sitting bone”.
skeleton:structures/hip-bone/members/2/n: The front part, joined to its partner at the pubic symphysis.
skeleton:structures/hip-bone/issues/0/no: High-energy injuries such as road accidents can bleed heavily and are an emergency. In older people, a pubic ramus fracture after a minor fall causes groin pain.
skeleton:structures/hip-bone/issues/1/no: A bruise of the iliac crest from a direct blow in sport.
skeleton:structures/hip-bone/issues/2/no: In teenage athletes, a strong muscle pull can tear off a fragment of bone at the front of the pelvis or at the sitting bone.
skeleton:structures/hip-bone/sexNotes/0/: The female pelvis is wider and shallower, with a round, roomy inlet, a wider pubic arch (more than 90°) and hip sockets set further apart, making room for childbirth.
skeleton:structures/hip-bone/sexNotes/1/: The male pelvis is narrower and deeper, with a heart-shaped inlet, a narrow pubic arch (about 60°) and heavier bones with stronger muscle markings.
skeleton:structures/femur/summary: The longest and strongest bone in the body, about a quarter of your height. Its ball-shaped head sits in the hip socket, and at the knee it ends in two rounded condyles.
skeleton:structures/femur/issues/0/note: A common, serious injury in older people after a fall: hip or groin pain, unable to bear weight, the leg shortened and turned out. It needs emergency care.
skeleton:structures/femur/issues/1/note: Takes great force and can cause major blood loss.
skeleton:structures/femur/issues/2/note: Loss of blood supply to the femoral head (for example with long-term steroids or heavy alcohol use): deep groin pain.
skeleton:structures/patella/summary: The kneecap: the body’s largest sesamoid bone, embedded in the quadriceps tendon. It increases the leverage of the thigh muscles and shields the front of the knee.
skeleton:structures/patella/issues/0/not: An ache around or behind the kneecap on stairs, when squatting or after sitting. Common in runners and teenagers.
skeleton:structures/patella/issues/1/not: The kneecap slips out sideways during a twist. It usually pops back but can damage cartilage.
skeleton:structures/patella/issues/2/not: From a fall straight onto the knee: you can’t straighten the leg.
skeleton:structures/tibia/summary: The shinbone, which carries nearly all of the body’s weight from the knee to the ankle. Its flat top (the tibial plateau) forms the knee, and its lower inner end is the bump of the inner ankle, the medial malleolus.
skeleton:structures/tibia/issues/0/note: A diffuse pain along the inner shin with running. A very focused, worsening sore spot may be a stress fracture.
skeleton:structures/tibia/issues/1/note: The most common long-bone fracture. If bone breaks through the skin, it is an emergency.
skeleton:structures/tibia/issues/2/note: A painful bump below the kneecap in active adolescents.
skeleton:structures/fibula/summary: The slender bone on the outer side of the leg. It carries little weight but anchors muscles and forms the bump of the outer ankle (lateral malleolus), which steadies the ankle.
skeleton:structures/fibula/issues/0/note: Often from rolling the ankle: the bony bump is tender and it is hard to put weight on the foot.
skeleton:structures/fibula/issues/1/note: The nerve wraps around the neck of the fibula, and a blow there can cause foot drop.
skeleton:structures/tarsals/summary: Seven bones forming the ankle and the back half of the foot. The talus links the leg to the foot, and the calcaneus forms the heel.
skeleton:structures/tarsals/members/0/no: Sits in the ankle socket between the tibia and fibula and passes body weight to the foot. No muscles attach to it.
skeleton:structures/tarsals/members/1/no: The heel bone, the largest tarsal. The Achilles tendon attaches to it.
skeleton:structures/tarsals/members/2/no: Boat-shaped, on the inner side of the midfoot.
skeleton:structures/tarsals/members/3/no: On the outer side of the midfoot.
skeleton:structures/tarsals/members/4/no: The largest cuneiform, at the base of the big toe.
skeleton:structures/tarsals/members/6/no: Together the three cuneiforms form the transverse arch of the foot.
skeleton:structures/tarsals/issues/0/not: Stabbing heel pain with the first steps in the morning, where the plantar fascia attaches to the calcaneus.
skeleton:structures/tarsals/issues/1/not: From a fall from height onto the heels. The spine should be checked too.
skeleton:structures/tarsals/issues/2/not: A deep ankle ache that doesn’t settle after a sprain.
skeleton:structures/metatarsals/summary: Five long bones of the forefoot, numbered from the big toe (I) to the little toe (V). Their heads form the ball of the foot.
skeleton:structures/metatarsals/members/: Short and thick; carries the most weight when you push off.
The longest, and the most common site of stress fractures.
Has a bump at its base (tuberosity) that can break when the ankle rolls.
skeleton:structures/metatarsals/issues/0: Gradual forefoot pain when walking or running more than usual, usually in the second or third metatarsal.
skeleton:structures/metatarsals/issues/1: Pain on the outer edge of the foot after rolling the ankle.
skeleton:structures/metatarsals/issues/2: Burning pain in the ball of the foot. A neuroma between the third and fourth toes can cause numbness.
skeleton:structures/foot-phalanges/summa: The toe bones: two in the big toe and three in each of the others, 14 per foot.
skeleton:structures/foot-phalanges/issue: Very common. Most heal with buddy-taping, but a deformed big toe needs checking.
A toe bent at its middle joint, often from tight shoes.
skeleton:joints/cranial-sutures/summary: Interlocking fibrous seams that bind the skull bones: coronal (frontal–parietal), sagittal (between the parietals), lambdoid (parietal–occipital) and squamous (parietal–temporal). In babies they are flexible and leave soft spots (fontanelles). They fuse gradually through adult life.
skeleton:joints/cranial-sutures/issues/0: A suture closes too early in infancy, giving an unusual head shape.
skeleton:joints/cranial-sutures/issues/1: A sunken soft spot can signal dehydration. A tense, bulging one in an unwell baby needs urgent care.
skeleton:joints/facial-sutures/summary: Fixed fibrous joints that knit the 14 facial bones to each other and to the cranium. Examples are the zygomatic arch (zygomatic to temporal) and the midline seam between the two maxillae.
skeleton:joints/facial-sutures/issues/0/: Breaks often run along suture lines after high-energy impacts (the Le Fort patterns).
skeleton:joints/tmj/subtype: Modified hinge with a gliding disc
skeleton:joints/tmj/summary: Where the condyle of the jaw meets the temporal bone, just in front of each ear. A cartilage disc lets it both hinge and slide. Put a finger in front of your ear and open your mouth to feel it move.
skeleton:joints/tmj/issues/0/note: Jaw pain, clicking, headaches or limited opening, linked to clenching, grinding and stress.
skeleton:joints/tmj/issues/1/note: The jaw gets stuck open after a big yawn or a blow and needs prompt reduction.
skeleton:joints/ossicular/subtype: Tiny synovial joints, with the stapes footplate held in a ligament ring
skeleton:joints/ossicular/movements/0: Rocking that passes sound along the chain
skeleton:joints/ossicular/summary: The three ear ossicles hinge on each other through tiny synovial joints. The footplate of the stapes is held in the oval window of the temporal bone, delivering sound into the inner ear.
skeleton:joints/ossicular/issues/0/note: Bone growth fixes the stapes footplate, causing conductive hearing loss.
skeleton:joints/atlanto-occipital/summar: The “yes” joint: the occipital condyles rock in the cupped upper surfaces of the atlas.
skeleton:joints/atlanto-occipital/issues: Severe neck trauma can disrupt this joint. Neck pain with any tingling, weakness or numbness after an injury is an emergency.
skeleton:joints/atlanto-axial/summary: The “no” joint: the atlas swivels around the dens of the axis. About half of all head rotation happens here.
skeleton:joints/atlanto-axial/issues/0/n: Loose ligaments (for example in rheumatoid arthritis or Down syndrome) let the dens shift and press on the spinal cord.
skeleton:joints/intervertebral/subtype: Symphysis (discs) with paired synovial facet joints
skeleton:joints/intervertebral/movements: A little movement at each level, adding up to bending, arching, side-bending and twisting
skeleton:joints/intervertebral/summary: Between each pair of vertebrae from C2 down to the sacrum sits an intervertebral disc: a tough fibrous ring around a gel-like core that absorbs shock. Two small facet joints sit behind it. The 23 discs make up about a quarter of the spine’s length.
skeleton:joints/intervertebral/issues/0/: The core bulges through the ring and can press on a nerve root: arm or leg pain with tingling or weakness.
skeleton:joints/intervertebral/issues/1/: Discs lose water and height with age, causing stiffness and back pain.
skeleton:joints/intervertebral/issues/2/: Back or neck pain that is worse when you lean backwards.
skeleton:joints/sacrococcygeal/movements: Slight backward bending, for example in childbirth
skeleton:joints/sacrococcygeal/summary: A small cartilaginous joint between the sacrum and the tailbone.
skeleton:joints/sacrococcygeal/issues/0/: A fall onto the bottom can bruise, sprain or break the joint.
skeleton:joints/sacroiliac/subtype: Plane, braced by very strong ligaments
skeleton:joints/sacroiliac/movements/0: A few degrees of nodding and gliding
skeleton:joints/sacroiliac/summary: Links the spine to the pelvis on each side, passing the weight of the upper body into the legs. It is built for stability rather than movement.
skeleton:joints/sacroiliac/issues/0/note: Low-back and buttock pain on one side, worse standing on one leg, on stairs or rolling over in bed. Common in pregnancy.
skeleton:joints/sacroiliac/issues/1/note: Inflammation, for example in ankylosing spondylitis: low-back stiffness in young adults that is worst in the morning and improves with exercise.
skeleton:joints/pubic-symphysis/summary: A disc of fibrocartilage joining the two pubic bones at the front of the pelvis. It loosens during pregnancy to help with childbirth.
skeleton:joints/pubic-symphysis/issues/0: Pain at the front of the pelvis, worse when walking, on stairs or when parting the legs.
skeleton:joints/pubic-symphysis/issues/1: Groin pain in athletes who kick and run a lot, from overload.
skeleton:joints/sternoclavicular/summary: The only joint that connects the arm to the trunk. A disc inside makes it surprisingly mobile but very stable.
skeleton:joints/sternoclavicular/issues/: Rare. A backward dislocation can press on the large vessels and the windpipe and is an emergency.
A swollen, tender bump at the inner end of the collarbone.
skeleton:joints/acromioclavicular/moveme: Gliding and rotation as the shoulder blade moves
skeleton:joints/acromioclavicular/summar: A small joint at the top of the shoulder, where the collarbone meets the acromion of the shoulder blade.
skeleton:joints/acromioclavicular/issues: After a fall onto the point of the shoulder: pain and a step or bump at the top of the shoulder.
Pain at the top of the shoulder when reaching across the body.
skeleton:joints/shoulder/summary: The most mobile joint in the body: a large humeral head on a shallow socket, held in place mainly by the rotator cuff muscles. Its mobility comes at the cost of stability.
skeleton:joints/shoulder/issues/0/note: Usually forward, after a fall or tackle. The shoulder looks squared off and needs prompt reduction.
skeleton:joints/shoulder/issues/1/note: Pain when lifting the arm sideways or overhead, and pain at night lying on that side.
skeleton:joints/shoulder/issues/2/note: Gradual, painful stiffening in every direction, most often between 40 and 60 or with diabetes.
skeleton:joints/sternocostal/subtype: Plane (the first is a fixed cartilaginous joint)
skeleton:joints/sternocostal/movements/0: Small gliding movements that let the chest expand
skeleton:joints/sternocostal/summary: Where the costal cartilages of ribs 1–7 meet the sternum. The first is fixed. The others are small gliding joints that move with each breath.
skeleton:joints/sternocostal/issues/0/no: Tender chest wall where the ribs meet the breastbone, worse on pressing or deep breathing. Always get chest pain checked to rule out heart problems.
skeleton:joints/sternocostal/issues/1/no: Like costochondritis but with visible swelling, usually at the second or third rib.
skeleton:joints/interchondral/summary: Joins the costal cartilages of the false ribs (8–10) to the cartilage above, forming the curved lower border of the rib cage, the costal margin.
skeleton:joints/interchondral/issues/0/n: A loose lower-rib cartilage clicks and causes sharp pain in the upper abdomen or lower chest.
skeleton:joints/costovertebral/summary: At the back, each rib attaches to the vertebral bodies and, for ribs 1–10, to the transverse processes too. They work like bucket handles, so the chest widens when you breathe in.
skeleton:joints/costovertebral/issues/0/: Sharp pain beside the spine when breathing or twisting, often after awkward lifting.
skeleton:joints/costovertebral/issues/1/: Inflammation can stiffen these joints and limit how far the chest can expand.
skeleton:joints/elbow/summary: A hinge formed by the humerus with the ulna (at the trochlea) and the radius (at the capitulum). It shares a capsule with the proximal radioulnar joint.
skeleton:joints/elbow/issues/0/note: Pain on the outer elbow with gripping and lifting (lateral epicondylitis).
skeleton:joints/elbow/issues/1/note: Pain on the inner elbow with gripping (medial epicondylitis).
skeleton:joints/elbow/issues/2/note: After a fall on an outstretched hand: deformity, unable to move the elbow. It is urgent.
skeleton:joints/proximal-radioulnar/summ: The head of the radius spins inside a ligament ring on the ulna, letting you turn your palm up and down.
skeleton:joints/proximal-radioulnar/issu: A toddler suddenly won’t use the arm after being pulled by the hand.
Pain on the outer elbow, worse when turning the forearm, after a fall.
