skeleton:joints/distal-radioulnar/summar: At the wrist, the radius rotates around the head of the ulna. A cartilage cushion, the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC), steadies it.
skeleton:joints/distal-radioulnar/issues: Pain on the little-finger side of the wrist and clicking when you rotate it, for example turning a key.
skeleton:joints/wrist/summary: The end of the radius cradles the scaphoid and lunate. The ulna doesn’t touch the carpals directly: a cartilage disc sits between them.
skeleton:joints/wrist/issues/0/note: A ligament injury after a fall. A “sprain” that doesn’t settle may hide a scaphoid fracture.
skeleton:joints/wrist/issues/1/note: A smooth, often painless lump on the back of the wrist.
skeleton:joints/wrist/issues/2/note: Pain on the thumb side of the wrist when gripping, common in new parents.
skeleton:joints/intercarpal/movements/0: Gliding that adds range to wrist movement
skeleton:joints/intercarpal/summary: Gliding joints between the eight carpal bones, held together by a dense web of ligaments.
skeleton:joints/intercarpal/issues/0/not: Torn ligaments (for example scapholunate) cause pain, clicking and weakness.
skeleton:joints/carpometacarpal/summary: Join the carpals to the metacarpals. The thumb’s saddle joint (trapezium to first metacarpal) allows opposition, touching the thumb to the fingertips, which makes a precise grip possible.
skeleton:joints/carpometacarpal/issues/0: Aching at the base of the thumb when pinching, opening jars or turning keys. Very common after 50.
skeleton:joints/metacarpophalangeal/summ: The knuckles, where the heads of the metacarpals meet the proximal phalanges.
skeleton:joints/metacarpophalangeal/issu: Swelling and stiffness of the knuckles on both hands, worse in the morning. See a doctor early.
A finger catches or locks when bending, from a thickened tendon sheath at the base of the finger.
A torn ligament on the inner side of the thumb knuckle after a fall onto the thumb.
skeleton:joints/hand-interphalangeal/sum: Hinge joints between the phalanges: two in each finger (PIP and DIP) and one in the thumb.
skeleton:joints/hand-interphalangeal/iss: Bony swellings at the end and middle joints of the fingers (Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes).
A sprain of the middle finger joint in ball sports. A joint that stays swollen or bent needs checking.
skeleton:joints/hip/summary: A deep ball-and-socket joint: the head of the femur sits in the acetabulum, deepened by a cartilage rim (the labrum). Built for stability and weight-bearing.
skeleton:joints/hip/issues/0/note: Groin or thigh pain and stiffness, worse with walking; trouble putting on socks.
skeleton:joints/hip/issues/1/note: After a fall in an older person: unable to bear weight. It is an emergency.
skeleton:joints/hip/issues/2/note: Deep groin pain and catching in active young adults.
skeleton:joints/hip/issues/3/note: Hip or knee pain or a limp in a child needs assessment, urgently if there is fever.
skeleton:joints/knee/summary: The largest joint in the body. The femoral condyles roll and glide on the tibial plateau, cushioned by two crescent-shaped menisci and held by four main ligaments (ACL, PCL, MCL and LCL). The kneecap glides in a groove at the front.
skeleton:joints/knee/issues/0/note: A pop during a twist or landing, rapid swelling, and a knee that feels unstable.
skeleton:joints/knee/issues/1/note: Pain along the joint line, catching or locking, and swelling the next day.
skeleton:joints/knee/issues/2/note: Pain and stiffness, worse with activity, and creaking. Common in older adults.
skeleton:joints/knee/issues/3/note: A red, hot, swollen joint with fever may be infected. It is urgent.
skeleton:joints/proximal-tibiofibular/mo: Slight gliding as the ankle moves
skeleton:joints/proximal-tibiofibular/su: A small gliding joint just below the outer knee, between the head of the fibula and the tibia.
skeleton:joints/proximal-tibiofibular/is: Rare: pain and clicking on the outer knee after a twisting injury.
skeleton:joints/distal-tibiofibular/move: Slight give as the ankle flexes
skeleton:joints/distal-tibiofibular/summ: Strong ligaments bind the lower ends of the tibia and fibula into a socket (the mortise) that grips the talus.
skeleton:joints/distal-tibiofibular/issu: Pain above the ankle after the foot is twisted outward. It heals more slowly than a common sprain.
skeleton:joints/ankle/summary: The talus sits in a socket formed by the tibia and fibula. Tilting the foot side to side happens just below, at the subtalar joint.
skeleton:joints/ankle/issues/0/note: Rolling the foot inward tears the outer ligaments: swelling and bruising. Not being able to take four steps, or tenderness on the bone, suggests a fracture.
skeleton:joints/ankle/issues/1/note: Pain on the ankle bumps (malleoli) and unable to bear weight.
skeleton:joints/ankle/issues/2/note: Feels like being kicked in the back of the heel, and you can’t push off. It is urgent.
skeleton:joints/subtalar-midfoot/summary: Joints among the tarsal bones, chiefly the subtalar joint under the talus, that let the foot tilt and adapt to uneven ground.
skeleton:joints/subtalar-midfoot/issues/: A collapsed arch, usually painless. A newly flattening, painful foot needs checking for a tibialis posterior tendon problem.
Aching on top of the midfoot with walking.
skeleton:joints/tarsometatarsal/movement: Slight gliding that stiffens the arch
skeleton:joints/tarsometatarsal/summary: Where the tarsals meet the metatarsals across the midfoot. They are a keystone of the foot’s arch.
skeleton:joints/tarsometatarsal/issues/0: Midfoot pain, and bruising on the sole, after a twist or crush. Easily missed and serious.
skeleton:joints/metatarsophalangeal/summ: The joints at the ball of the foot. The big-toe joint bends with every step as you push off.
skeleton:joints/metatarsophalangeal/issu: Sudden, severe pain with redness and swelling of the big-toe joint, often at night.
The big toe angles toward the others, with a bony bump on the inner side.
A stiff, painful big toe from arthritis.
skeleton:joints/foot-interphalangeal/sum: Small hinge joints between the toe bones: one in the big toe and two in each of the other toes.
skeleton:joints/foot-interphalangeal/iss: Fixed bends at these joints that rub on shoes and cause corns.
skeleton:groups/axial/summary: The central axis of the body: skull, spine, ribs and sternum. It protects the brain, spinal cord and the organs of the chest.
skeleton:groups/skull/summary: 22 bones that protect the brain and form the face, plus the six tiny ear ossicles and the hyoid in the neck.
skeleton:groups/cranium/summary: Eight bones forming the vault and base of the skull that enclose the brain.
skeleton:groups/face/summary: Fourteen bones forming the face, the eye sockets, the nose and the jaws.
skeleton:groups/spine/summary: 26 bones stacked from skull to tailbone: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic and 5 lumbar vertebrae, plus the sacrum and coccyx. It carries the body’s weight and shelters the spinal cord.
skeleton:groups/cervical/summary: The seven small, mobile vertebrae of the neck. Holes in their transverse processes carry the vertebral arteries to the brain.
skeleton:groups/cervical/issues/0/note: Pain and stiffness after a sudden jolt or awkward posture; usually improves over a few weeks.
skeleton:groups/cervical/issues/1/note: Neck pain radiating into the arm with tingling, numbness or weakness, from a disc or bone spur pressing on a nerve root.
skeleton:groups/cervical/issues/2/note: Age-related wear of the discs and facet joints: stiffness, grinding, sometimes headaches at the back of the head.
skeleton:groups/thoracic/summary: Twelve vertebrae that carry the ribs. Linked to the rib cage, this is the stiffest part of the spine.
skeleton:groups/thoracic/issues/0/note: An ache between the shoulder blades from long periods of sitting or slouching.
skeleton:groups/thoracic/issues/1/note: Sudden mid-back pain, sometimes after only minor strain, in people with thin bones; height loss and rounding (kyphosis) can follow.
skeleton:groups/thoracic/issues/2/note: A sideways curve of the spine, most often noticed in adolescence as uneven shoulders or hips.
skeleton:groups/lumbar/summary: The five largest vertebrae, in the lower back. They carry the weight of the upper body and allow bending and arching.
skeleton:groups/lumbar/issues/0/note: Very common and usually from muscles, ligaments and joints. It normally settles within weeks, and staying gently active helps.
skeleton:groups/lumbar/issues/1/note: Disc material presses on a nerve root, causing pain shooting down the leg, sometimes with numbness or weakness.
skeleton:groups/lumbar/issues/2/note: Narrowing of the spinal canal in older adults: leg pain or heaviness when walking, eased by sitting or bending forward.
skeleton:groups/sacral/summary: Fused vertebrae at the base of the spine that lock it into the pelvis.
skeleton:groups/thorax/summary: The sternum, 12 pairs of ribs and the thoracic vertebrae: a flexible cage that protects the heart and lungs and expands with every breath.
skeleton:groups/ribs/summary: 12 pairs. Ribs 1–7 are “true” ribs, each joining the sternum through its own cartilage. Ribs 8–10 are “false” ribs, joining the cartilage above. Ribs 11–12 are “floating” ribs that end free in the flank.
skeleton:groups/ribs/issues/0/note: Sharp pain on breathing, coughing or twisting after a fall or blow. Breathlessness or coughing blood needs urgent care.
skeleton:groups/ribs/issues/1/note: Inflammation where the ribs meet their cartilage: the chest wall is tender to press. Chest pain should always be checked to rule out heart causes.
skeleton:groups/ribs/issues/2/note: Pain between the ribs after coughing fits, lifting or twisting sports.
skeleton:groups/appendicular/summary: The limbs and the girdles that attach them to the trunk: 126 bones built for movement.
skeleton:groups/shoulder-girdle/summary: The clavicle and scapula on each side. Together they hang the arm from the trunk.
skeleton:groups/upper-limb/summary: Arm, forearm and hand: 30 bones on each side.
skeleton:groups/hand/summary: 27 bones per hand: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals and 14 phalanges.
skeleton:groups/pelvic-girdle/summary: The two hip bones. Joined to the sacrum at the back and to each other at the front, they form the pelvic ring.
skeleton:groups/lower-limb/summary: Thigh, knee, leg and foot: 30 bones on each side.
skeleton:groups/foot/summary: 26 bones per foot: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals and 14 phalanges.
ligaments:structures/acl/summary: Runs inside the knee from the front of the top of the tibia up and back to the inner side of the outer femoral condyle. It stops the shin sliding forward under the thigh and controls twisting, so it takes the strain when you land, cut or pivot.
ligaments:structures/acl/issues/0/note: A pop during a twist or awkward landing, rapid swelling within hours, and a knee that gives way. See a doctor or physiotherapist. Many people do well with focused rehabilitation, and some need reconstruction.
ligaments:structures/pcl/summary: The stronger of the two cruciates. It runs from the back of the top of the tibia up and forward to the inner femoral condyle, crossing behind the ACL, and stops the shin being pushed backward.
ligaments:structures/pcl/issues/0/note: Usually from a blow to the front of the shin with the knee bent, as against a dashboard, or a fall onto the bent knee. Pain at the back of the knee and mild swelling. Most recover with rehabilitation.
ligaments:structures/mcl/summary: A broad, flat band on the inner side of the knee, from the inner femoral epicondyle to the tibia well below the joint. It stops the knee buckling inward and is joined to the inner meniscus.
ligaments:structures/mcl/issues/0/note: Pain and tenderness along the inner knee after a blow to the outside of the knee or a twist. It heals well without surgery, often in a brace, over weeks.
ligaments:structures/lcl/summary: A cord on the outer side of the knee, from the outer femoral epicondyle to the head of the fibula. It stops the knee bowing outward.
ligaments:structures/lcl/issues/0/note: Less common than an MCL sprain: pain on the outer knee after a blow to its inner side. A bad one can stretch the common fibular nerve nearby, causing a weak, dropping foot, which needs prompt assessment.
ligaments:structures/menisci/summary: Two C-shaped wedges of fibrocartilage sitting on the top of the tibia, one on the inner and one on the outer side. They deepen the shallow tibial surface for the rounded femoral condyles, spread the load and absorb shock.
ligaments:structures/menisci/members/0/n: The larger, more C-shaped one on the inner side, joined to the MCL, so it tears more often.
ligaments:structures/menisci/members/1/n: The rounder, more mobile one on the outer side.
ligaments:structures/menisci/issues/0/no: Pain along the joint line, swelling the next day, and catching or locking. From a twist in younger people, or wear in older ones. Most settle with exercise. A knee locked so it can't straighten needs prompt assessment.
ligaments:structures/patellar-tendon/sum: The thick band from the bottom of the kneecap to the bump at the top of the shin (the tibial tuberosity). It is the last link of the quadriceps, which straightens the knee. Tapping it gives the knee-jerk reflex.
ligaments:structures/patellar-tendon/iss: "Jumper's knee": pain just below the kneecap on jumping, squatting or stairs. It improves with gradual loading exercises over weeks to months.
A tender bump below the knee in active growing children, where the tendon pulls on the shin. It settles once growth finishes. Adjust activity to the pain.
ligaments:structures/quadriceps-tendon/s: Where the four quadriceps muscles join into one tendon above the knee and attach to the top of the kneecap.
ligaments:structures/quadriceps-tendon/i: Mostly over 40: a sudden pain above the kneecap on landing or stumbling, and you can't straighten the leg. It needs urgent assessment, because it is repaired surgically.
ligaments:structures/lateral-ankle-ligam: Three bands that fan out from the tip of the fibula (the outer ankle bone) to the talus and calcaneus. The front one, the anterior talofibular ligament, is the most often injured ligament in the body.
Front of the outer ankle. Torn first when the foot rolls inward.
Down from the fibula to the heel bone.
Behind the joint. The strongest of the three.

Rolling the foot inward: pain, swelling and bruising on the outer ankle. Most improve within weeks with early, gradual walking and balance exercises. See a doctor if you can't take four steps or the bone itself is tender.
ligaments:structures/deltoid-ligament/su: A strong triangular fan from the inner ankle bone (the medial malleolus of the tibia) to the talus, calcaneus and navicular. It holds the inner ankle and helps support the arch.
ligaments:structures/deltoid-ligament/is: Uncommon, because the ligament is so strong. Pain on the inner ankle after the foot turns outward, which can come with a fracture of the fibula. See a doctor.
ligaments:structures/achilles-tendon/sum: The thickest, strongest tendon in the body. It joins the gastrocnemius and soleus to the back of the heel bone and lifts the heel for walking, running and jumping.
ligaments:structures/achilles-tendon/iss: Pain and stiffness in the tendon, worst first thing in the morning or at the start of exercise. Calf-strengthening exercises over months are the main treatment.
A sudden snap, as if kicked in the back of the heel, and you can't push off or stand on tiptoe. It needs urgent assessment the same day.
ligaments:structures/plantar-fascia/summ: A thick sheet under the sole, from the underside of the heel bone fanning out to the bases of the toes. Like a bowstring it holds up the arch, and it tightens as the toes bend back when you push off.
ligaments:structures/plantar-fascia/issu: Sharp pain under the heel with the first steps in the morning or after sitting, easing as you walk. Calf and sole stretches, supportive shoes and easing high-impact exercise help. Most settle within months.
ligaments:structures/iliotibial-band/sum: A long, thick strip of fascia down the outside of the thigh, from the iliac crest, where the tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus pull on it, to the outer front of the top of the tibia. It steadies the hip and the outer knee.
ligaments:structures/iliotibial-band/iss: Pain on the outer side of the knee during running or cycling, often coming on at the same distance each time. It improves with reduced mileage and hip-strengthening exercises.
ligaments:structures/inguinal-ligament/s: The rolled-under lower edge of the external oblique, stretched along the groin crease from the front point of the hip bone (the anterior superior iliac spine) to the pubic tubercle. The femoral vessels and nerve pass under it into the thigh, and the inguinal canal runs just above it.
ligaments:structures/inguinal-ligament/i: A soft bulge in the groin just above the ligament, bigger on standing or coughing. See a doctor. A hernia that becomes hard, very painful and won't go back in needs emergency care.
ligaments:structures/rotator-cuff-tendon: The four rotator cuff muscles end in tendons that merge into one hood over the top, front and back of the head of the humerus. They hold the ball centred in the shallow socket. The supraspinatus tendon, running under the acromion, is the one that wears and tears most.
Ache over the outer shoulder, worse lifting the arm out to the side or overhead and lying on it at night. It usually improves with exercises over months.
Weakness lifting the arm, from a fall or gradual wear. See a doctor, sooner if you suddenly can't lift the arm after an injury.
ligaments:structures/common-extensor-ten: The shared tendon of the wrist and finger extensors, attached to the outer bump of the elbow (the lateral epicondyle of the humerus).

Pain on the outer elbow when gripping, lifting or twisting, from overloading this tendon, rarely from tennis. It usually settles within a year. Easing the aggravating grip and strengthening exercises help.
ligaments:structures/common-flexor-tendo: The shared tendon of the wrist and finger flexors, attached to the inner bump of the elbow (the medial epicondyle of the humerus).
Pain on the inner elbow when gripping or bending the wrist, from overloading this tendon. It settles with rest from the aggravating activity and gradual strengthening.
ligaments:structures/flexor-retinaculum/: A strong band across the front of the wrist, bridging the arch of the carpal bones. It roofs the carpal tunnel, through which the median nerve and the finger flexor tendons pass into the hand.

Tingling and numbness in the thumb, index and middle fingers, often waking you at night, from pressure on the median nerve under this band. Wrist splints at night help. See a doctor for constant numbness or a weak thumb.
ligaments:groups/connective-tissue/summa: The tough, white, fibrous straps of the body. Ligaments tie bone to bone and hold joints together, tendons tie muscle to bone and pass on its pull, and sheets of fascia wrap and connect muscles. They have a poor blood supply, so they heal slowly.
ligaments:groups/connective-tissue/issue: A stretched or torn ligament: pain, swelling and bruising around a joint after a twist. Most heal with rest, ice, compression, elevation and then gradual use over weeks. See a doctor if you can't bear weight or the joint feels unstable.
A painful, stiff tendon from more load than it can adapt to, often after a change in training. It improves with gradual strengthening over weeks to months rather than complete rest.
ligaments:groups/knee-ligaments/summary: Four main ligaments hold the knee: the two cruciates cross inside the joint and stop the shin sliding forward or back, and the two collaterals stop it bending sideways. Two menisci cushion the joint, and the quadriceps and patellar tendons straighten it through the kneecap.
ligaments:groups/ankle-foot-ligaments/su: Ligament fans on both sides of the ankle, the Achilles tendon behind it and the plantar fascia under the foot.
ligaments:groups/upper-limb-ligaments/su: The rotator cuff tendons over the shoulder, the shared forearm tendons at the elbow and the band that roofs the carpal tunnel.
ligaments:groups/hip-thigh-ligaments/sum: The inguinal ligament along the groin and the iliotibial band down the outer thigh.
muscles:structures/temporalis/originNote: The temporal fossa on the side of the skull
muscles:structures/temporalis/summary: A fan-shaped chewing muscle filling the temple. You can feel it tighten when you clench your teeth.
muscles:structures/temporalis/issues/0/n: Tight, tender temples from clenching or stress.
muscles:structures/temporalis/issues/1/n: Grinding at night overworks it, causing a morning jaw ache and headache.
muscles:structures/masseter/insertionNot: Outer surface of the ramus and angle of the jaw
muscles:structures/masseter/summary: The main chewing muscle, from the cheekbone to the angle of the jaw. For its size it is one of the strongest muscles in the body.
muscles:structures/masseter/issues/0/not: Aching cheeks and jaw from clenching, grinding or chewing gum; often part of a TMJ disorder.
muscles:structures/pterygoids/listOnly: Not drawn on the map: they lie inside the jaw, behind the ramus of the mandible, so both views hide them.
muscles:structures/pterygoids/originNote: The pterygoid plates of the sphenoid at the back of the nose, and (medial pterygoid) the back of the upper jaw
muscles:structures/pterygoids/insertionN: Lateral: the neck of the jaw's condyle and the disc of the jaw joint. Medial: the inner surface of the angle of the jaw
muscles:structures/pterygoids/nerve: Mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve
muscles:structures/pterygoids/actions/0: Push the jaw forward and open the mouth (lateral pterygoid)
muscles:structures/pterygoids/actions/1: Close the jaw, with the masseter (medial pterygoid)
muscles:structures/pterygoids/actions/2: Grind side to side when chewing, one side at a time
muscles:structures/pterygoids/summary: Two chewing muscles inside the jaw. The lateral pterygoid pulls the jaw's condyle and disc forward as the mouth opens; the medial pterygoid mirrors the masseter on the inside of the jaw, forming a sling around its angle.
muscles:structures/pterygoids/members/0/: Runs back almost horizontally to the condyle and the jaw-joint disc. The only chewing muscle that opens the mouth.
muscles:structures/pterygoids/members/1/: Runs down and back to the inside of the angle of the jaw. Closes the jaw.
muscles:structures/pterygoids/issues/0/n: Tight or overworked pterygoids, often from clenching or grinding, cause aching in front of the ear, clicking and a jaw that deviates on opening.
muscles:structures/pterygoids/issues/1/n: Spasm that stops the mouth opening fully, for example after a wisdom-tooth extraction or a dental injection. A spreading swelling with fever needs urgent care.
muscles:structures/buccinator/originNote: The outer jaw bones beside the molar teeth, and the pterygomandibular raphe behind them
muscles:structures/buccinator/insertionN: Blends into the orbicularis oris at the corner of the mouth
muscles:structures/buccinator/nerve: Buccal branches of the facial nerve
muscles:structures/buccinator/actions/0: Presses the cheek against the teeth, keeping food between them when chewing
muscles:structures/buccinator/actions/1: Blows air out through pursed lips (it is the trumpeter’s muscle)
muscles:structures/buccinator/summary: The muscle of the cheek, a thin sheet deep to the masseter that forms the side wall of the mouth. Although it helps chewing, it is a muscle of facial expression, supplied by the facial nerve.
muscles:structures/buccinator/issues/0/n: With a facial palsy the cheek is slack, so food collects inside it and the cheek is bitten. A sudden one-sided weakness of the face needs emergency care, as it may be a stroke.
muscles:structures/extraocular-muscles/l: Not drawn on the map: they lie inside the eye socket, behind and around the eyeball.
muscles:structures/extraocular-muscles/o: A common tendon ring at the back of the eye socket around the optic canal (the four recti and the superior oblique); the inferior oblique from the floor of the socket at the front
muscles:structures/extraocular-muscles/i: The white of the eye (sclera); the levator into the upper eyelid
muscles:structures/extraocular-muscles/n: Oculomotor nerve (most), trochlear nerve (superior oblique) and abducens nerve (lateral rectus)
muscles:structures/extraocular-muscles/a: Turn the eye up, down, in and out, and rotate it
Keep both eyes pointing at the same thing, so you see one image
Lift the upper eyelid (levator palpebrae superioris)
muscles:structures/extraocular-muscles/s: Six small muscles that aim each eye, plus the muscle that lifts the upper eyelid. They make the fastest movements in the body and keep the two eyes precisely aligned.
muscles:structures/extraocular-muscles/m: Turns the eye in, towards the nose (oculomotor nerve).
Its tendon hooks through a pulley (the trochlea); turns the eye down and in (trochlear nerve).
From the floor of the socket; turns the eye up and out (oculomotor nerve).
muscles:structures/extraocular-muscles/i: Sudden double vision, especially with a droopy eyelid, a headache or weakness, needs emergency care. It can come from a stroke, an aneurysm pressing on a nerve, or a nerve palsy.
The eyes point in different directions. In children it needs early assessment to protect the sight of the weaker eye.
Swollen eye muscles in an overactive thyroid push the eyes forward and limit their movement.
muscles:structures/occipitofrontalis/ori: Back of the skull, above the nuchal line (occipital belly)
muscles:structures/occipitofrontalis/ins: The skin of the eyebrows (frontal belly). The two bellies are joined by a sheet of tendon over the top of the head (galea aponeurotica)
muscles:structures/occipitofrontalis/act: Raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead
muscles:structures/occipitofrontalis/sum: A thin muscle with two bellies, over the forehead and the back of the head, joined by a sheet of tendon across the scalp.
muscles:structures/occipitofrontalis/iss: Tight scalp and forehead muscles can add to a band-like headache.
muscles:structures/orbicularis-oculi/ori: The bone on the inner side of the eye socket
muscles:structures/orbicularis-oculi/ins: Loops round the eye into the skin of the eyelids
muscles:structures/orbicularis-oculi/act: Closes the eyelids: gently to blink, tightly to squeeze
Helps tears drain towards the nose
muscles:structures/orbicularis-oculi/sum: A flat ring of muscle around each eye, in the eyelids.
muscles:structures/orbicularis-oculi/iss: Harmless flickers, often with tiredness, stress or caffeine.
Being unable to close one eye fully, with the face drooping on that side, may be Bell’s palsy or a stroke. Sudden facial weakness needs emergency care.
muscles:structures/orbicularis-oris/orig: Near the midline of the upper and lower jaws, and the other muscles around the mouth
muscles:structures/orbicularis-oris/inse: The skin and lining of the lips
muscles:structures/orbicularis-oris/summ: A ring of muscle inside the lips.
muscles:structures/orbicularis-oris/issu: A sudden one-sided droop needs emergency care, as it may be a stroke (think FAST). Bell’s palsy also weakens it.
muscles:structures/sternocleidomastoid/o: Top of the sternum (sternal head) and inner clavicle (clavicular head)
muscles:structures/sternocleidomastoid/i: Mastoid process behind the ear and the base of the skull
muscles:structures/sternocleidomastoid/a: Turns the head to the opposite side
Tilts the head toward the same shoulder
Bends the neck forward (both sides together)
Helps lift the ribcage in hard breathing
muscles:structures/sternocleidomastoid/s: The prominent diagonal strap at the side of the neck, from behind the ear to the top of the breastbone. It divides the neck into front and back triangles.
muscles:structures/sternocleidomastoid/i: Spasm pulls the head to one side. In babies it can be present from birth.
Pain and stiffness after a jolt or sleeping awkwardly.
muscles:structures/platysma/originNote: The skin and fascia over the upper chest and the front of the shoulder
muscles:structures/platysma/insertionNot: The lower border of the jaw, and the skin and muscles at the corner of the mouth
muscles:structures/platysma/nerve: Cervical branch of the facial nerve
muscles:structures/platysma/actions/0: Tenses the skin of the neck into ridges
muscles:structures/platysma/actions/1: Pulls the corners of the mouth down, as in a grimace or fright
muscles:structures/platysma/actions/2: Helps open the jaw against resistance
muscles:structures/platysma/summary: A broad, paper-thin sheet just under the skin of the front of the neck, from the upper chest up over the jaw. It is a muscle of facial expression, so the facial nerve supplies it.
muscles:structures/platysma/issues/0/not: The front edges of the two sheets can show as vertical cords under the chin. This is harmless.
muscles:structures/platysma/issues/1/not: In Bell’s palsy or a stroke the platysma on one side stops working, along with the other muscles of facial expression. A sudden facial droop needs emergency care.
muscles:structures/suprahyoid/originNote: Inner jaw, chin and the mastoid and styloid processes of the temporal bone
muscles:structures/suprahyoid/actions/0: Lift the hyoid and larynx when you swallow
muscles:structures/suprahyoid/summary: Four small muscles forming the floor of the mouth, slinging the hyoid up toward the jaw and skull.
muscles:structures/suprahyoid/members/0/: Two bellies joined by a tendon that loops through a sling on the hyoid.
muscles:structures/suprahyoid/members/1/: A thin sheet forming the floor of the mouth.
muscles:structures/suprahyoid/members/2/: From the inside of the chin to the hyoid.
muscles:structures/suprahyoid/members/3/: From the styloid process of the temporal bone.
muscles:structures/suprahyoid/issues/0/n: Weakness after a stroke or with nerve conditions can make swallowing unsafe. Coughing or choking on food needs assessment.
muscles:structures/infrahyoid/originNote: Back of the manubrium, and the top edge of the shoulder blade (omohyoid)
muscles:structures/infrahyoid/insertionN: The hyoid, and the thyroid cartilage of the larynx (sternothyroid, thyrohyoid)
muscles:structures/infrahyoid/actions/0: Pull the hyoid and larynx back down after swallowing
muscles:structures/infrahyoid/actions/1: Steady the hyoid so the tongue and jaw can work
muscles:structures/infrahyoid/summary: Thin strap muscles running down the front of the neck from the hyoid to the sternum and shoulder blade, covering the thyroid and windpipe.
muscles:structures/infrahyoid/members/0/: From the sternum to the hyoid.
muscles:structures/infrahyoid/members/1/: From the sternum to the thyroid cartilage.
muscles:structures/infrahyoid/members/2/: From the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid.
muscles:structures/infrahyoid/members/3/: Two bellies; it slips under the sternocleidomastoid to the top of the shoulder blade.
muscles:structures/infrahyoid/issues/0/n: They are parted in thyroid surgery and can feel tight while healing.
muscles:structures/scalenes/insertionNot: The first rib (anterior and middle scalenes) and the second rib (posterior scalene)
muscles:structures/scalenes/nerve: Front (ventral) branches of the cervical nerves, C3–C8
muscles:structures/scalenes/actions/0: Bend the neck to the side
muscles:structures/scalenes/actions/1: Lift the top two ribs in deep or hard breathing
muscles:structures/scalenes/summary: Three muscles at the side of the neck, from the neck vertebrae to the top ribs. The brachial plexus and the subclavian artery pass out between the front and middle scalenes.
muscles:structures/scalenes/members/0/no: C3–C6 to the first rib, in front of the subclavian artery.
muscles:structures/scalenes/members/1/no: C2–C7 to the first rib, behind the brachial plexus.
muscles:structures/scalenes/issues/0/not: Pins and needles, aching or weakness in the arm or hand, worse with the arms raised, from pressure on the nerves or vessels near the first rib.
muscles:structures/scalenes/issues/1/not: Aching at the side of the neck, sometimes spreading to the shoulder or upper chest.
muscles:structures/levator-scapulae/inse: The upper inner corner (superior angle) of the shoulder blade
muscles:structures/levator-scapulae/nerv: Dorsal scapular nerve (C5) and cervical nerves C3–C4
muscles:structures/levator-scapulae/acti: Bends and turns the neck to the same side
muscles:structures/levator-scapulae/summ: A strap-like muscle at the side and back of the neck, under the trapezius, that lifts the shoulder blade.
muscles:structures/levator-scapulae/issu: A knot-like ache where the neck meets the shoulder blade, worse turning the head, often after sleeping awkwardly or long desk work.
muscles:structures/splenius/originNote: The nuchal ligament and the spinous processes of C7–T6
muscles:structures/splenius/insertionNot: The mastoid process and the skull just behind it (capitis), and the transverse processes of C1–C3 (cervicis)
muscles:structures/splenius/nerve: Back (dorsal) branches of the cervical nerves
muscles:structures/splenius/actions/0: Tilts the head back (both sides together)
muscles:structures/splenius/actions/1: Turns the head to the same side
muscles:structures/splenius/summary: A broad, bandage-like muscle at the back of the neck under the trapezius, running up and out from the spine to the skull.
muscles:structures/splenius/members/0/no: C7–T3 to the mastoid process and skull.
muscles:structures/splenius/members/1/no: T3–T6 to the transverse processes of C1–C3.
muscles:structures/splenius/issues/0/not: Aching and stiffness at the back of the neck after a sudden jolt, or after a long time looking down.
muscles:structures/splenius/issues/1/not: Tight neck muscles can send pain up the back of the head.
muscles:structures/trapezius/originNote: Base of the skull, the nuchal ligament and the spinous processes of C7–T12
muscles:structures/trapezius/insertionNo: Outer third of the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula
muscles:structures/trapezius/actions/1: Rotates the shoulder blade so the arm can reach overhead
muscles:structures/trapezius/summary: A large diamond-shaped muscle of the upper back and neck. From the front you only see its upper fibres, which form the slope from neck to shoulder.
muscles:structures/trapezius/issues/0/no: Tight, tender knots between the neck and shoulder, often from desk work and stress.
muscles:structures/trapezius/issues/1/no: A tight trapezius and neck can refer pain to the back of the head.
muscles:structures/deltoid/originNote: Outer third of the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula
muscles:structures/deltoid/insertionNote: Deltoid tuberosity, halfway down the outer humerus
muscles:structures/deltoid/actions/0: Lifts the arm out to the side
muscles:structures/deltoid/actions/1: Front fibres raise the arm forward
muscles:structures/deltoid/summary: The rounded cap of the shoulder, shaped like the Greek letter delta (Δ). A common site for vaccinations.
muscles:structures/deltoid/issues/0/note: Pain on lifting after heavy or repetitive overhead work.
muscles:structures/deltoid/issues/1/note: After a shoulder dislocation: a numb patch on the outer shoulder and weakness lifting the arm.
muscles:structures/rotator-cuff/originNo: Front and back surfaces of the shoulder blade
muscles:structures/rotator-cuff/insertio: Greater and lesser tubercles at the top of the humerus
muscles:structures/rotator-cuff/actions/: Hold the ball of the humerus in its shallow socket
Rotate and help lift the arm
muscles:structures/rotator-cuff/summary: Four muscles from the shoulder blade whose tendons merge into a cuff around the head of the humerus. Most of them lie on the back of the shoulder blade.
muscles:structures/rotator-cuff/members/: Starts lifting the arm out to the side. The most commonly torn.
On the front of the shoulder blade, against the ribs. Turns the arm inward.
muscles:structures/rotator-cuff/issues/0: Pain on the outer shoulder when lifting the arm, worse at night.
muscles:structures/rotator-cuff/issues/1: Weakness lifting the arm after a fall, or gradually with age. It may need imaging.
muscles:structures/rotator-cuff/issues/2: A painful arc when raising the arm, roughly between shoulder height and overhead.
muscles:structures/rhomboids/insertionNo: Inner (medial) border of the shoulder blade
muscles:structures/rhomboids/summary: Two flat muscles between the spine and the shoulder blade, under the trapezius.
muscles:structures/rhomboids/issues/0/no: Aching from posture or a sudden strain. Pain here can also come from the neck, the heart or the gallbladder.
muscles:structures/teres-major/originNot: Back of the lower corner (inferior angle) of the shoulder blade
muscles:structures/teres-major/insertion: Inner lip of the groove at the front of the upper humerus, beside the latissimus dorsi tendon
muscles:structures/teres-major/actions/0: Pulls the raised arm down and back
muscles:structures/teres-major/actions/2: Works with the latissimus dorsi in pull-ups and rowing
muscles:structures/teres-major/summary: A thick, rounded muscle from the lower corner of the shoulder blade to the upper humerus. With the latissimus dorsi it forms the back fold of the armpit. Despite its name it is not part of the rotator cuff.
muscles:structures/teres-major/issues/0/: Pain at the back of the armpit or along the outer edge of the shoulder blade after throwing, rowing or climbing. It usually settles with rest.
muscles:structures/latissimus-dorsi/orig: Lower thoracic spine, the thoracolumbar fascia, the iliac crest and the lowest ribs
muscles:structures/latissimus-dorsi/inse: Floor of the groove at the front of the upper humerus
muscles:structures/latissimus-dorsi/acti: Pulls the arm down and back
muscles:structures/latissimus-dorsi/summ: The broadest muscle of the back, sweeping from the lower spine and pelvis up into the armpit. From the front only its edge shows along the side of the chest.
muscles:structures/latissimus-dorsi/issu: Pain along the side of the back or in the armpit after pulling or throwing.
muscles:structures/pectoralis-major/orig: Inner clavicle, the sternum and the upper six costal cartilages
muscles:structures/pectoralis-major/inse: Outer lip of the groove at the front of the upper humerus
muscles:structures/pectoralis-major/acti: Brings the arm across the chest
muscles:structures/pectoralis-major/summ: The large fan-shaped muscle of the chest, converging on the upper humerus. Its lower edge forms the front fold of the armpit.
muscles:structures/pectoralis-major/issu: Sudden pain and bruising at the front of the armpit during a heavy press.
A sore chest muscle after exertion, tender to press. If unsure, get chest pain checked.
muscles:structures/pectoralis-minor/inse: Coracoid process of the shoulder blade
muscles:structures/pectoralis-minor/acti: Pulls the shoulder blade forward and down
Helps lift the ribs in deep breathing
muscles:structures/pectoralis-minor/summ: A thin triangular muscle hidden under pectoralis major.
muscles:structures/pectoralis-minor/issu: Rounded shoulders. It can squeeze the nerves and vessels going to the arm (thoracic outlet).
muscles:structures/subclavius/originNote: The junction of the first rib and its cartilage
muscles:structures/subclavius/insertionN: A groove on the underside of the middle of the collarbone
muscles:structures/subclavius/nerve: Nerve to subclavius (C5–C6), from the brachial plexus
muscles:structures/subclavius/actions/0: Pulls the collarbone down and in, steadying it against the breastbone
muscles:structures/subclavius/actions/1: Cushions the vessels and nerves beneath a broken collarbone
muscles:structures/subclavius/summary: A small, rounded muscle under the collarbone, deep to the pectoralis major. It lies just above the subclavian vessels and the brachial plexus as they pass under the collarbone to the arm.
muscles:structures/subclavius/issues/0/n: A tight subclavius can narrow the gap between the collarbone and the first rib, pressing on the nerves or vein to the arm: pins and needles or a heavy, swollen arm, worse with the arms raised.
muscles:structures/serratus-anterior/ori: Outer surfaces of ribs 1–8, in saw-tooth slips
muscles:structures/serratus-anterior/ins: The inner border of the shoulder blade (front surface)
muscles:structures/serratus-anterior/act: Pulls the shoulder blade forward around the ribs, as in punching
Holds the shoulder blade flat against the chest wall
Rotates it upward for reaching overhead
muscles:structures/serratus-anterior/sum: Saw-toothed slips on the side of the chest that wrap around to the shoulder blade.
muscles:structures/serratus-anterior/iss: If its nerve is injured, the shoulder blade sticks out when you push against a wall.
muscles:structures/intercostals/originNo: Each rib, to the rib below it
muscles:structures/intercostals/actions/: Lift and lower the ribs during breathing
muscles:structures/intercostals/summary: Three thin layers of muscle filling each space between the ribs.
muscles:structures/intercostals/members/: Lift the ribs as you breathe in.
Pull the ribs down when you breathe out hard.
The deepest layer, with the nerves and vessels running between.
muscles:structures/intercostals/issues/0: Sharp pain between the ribs after coughing fits, twisting or lifting.
muscles:structures/intercostals/issues/1: Burning pain along one rib space. A blistering rash suggests shingles.
muscles:structures/diaphragm/originNote: Xiphoid process, the inner surfaces of the lower six ribs and the lumbar vertebrae (the crura)
muscles:structures/diaphragm/insertionNo: Its own central tendon at the top of the dome
muscles:structures/diaphragm/actions/0: The main muscle of breathing: contracting flattens the dome and draws air in
muscles:structures/diaphragm/actions/1: Helps raise abdominal pressure for coughing, lifting and childbirth
muscles:structures/diaphragm/summary: A dome-shaped sheet separating the chest from the abdomen. The esophagus, aorta and inferior vena cava pass through it.
muscles:structures/diaphragm/issues/0/no: Part of the stomach slides up through the diaphragm, causing reflux.
muscles:structures/diaphragm/issues/1/no: Involuntary spasms. Hiccups lasting more than two days should be checked.
muscles:structures/diaphragm/issues/2/no: Irritation under the diaphragm (blood, infection, gallbladder) is often felt at the tip of the shoulder.
muscles:structures/rectus-abdominis/inse: Xiphoid process and the cartilages of ribs 5–7
muscles:structures/rectus-abdominis/acti: Bends the trunk forward, as in sit-ups
muscles:structures/rectus-abdominis/summ: The paired “six-pack” running down the front of the abdomen, crossed by tendinous bands and joined in the midline by the linea alba.
muscles:structures/rectus-abdominis/issu: The two halves separate along the midline, common after pregnancy: a ridge or bulge appears when sitting up.
Pain on coughing, laughing or sitting up after a sudden twist or overtraining.
muscles:structures/external-oblique/inse: Iliac crest and pubic tubercle, and the linea alba through its broad tendon sheet
muscles:structures/external-oblique/acti: Twists the trunk to the opposite side
muscles:structures/external-oblique/summ: The outermost flat muscle on the side of the abdomen. Its fibres run down and inward like hands in pockets, and its tendon sheet forms the inguinal ligament.
muscles:structures/external-oblique/issu: Pain at the side of the waist after twisting sports.
A weak spot in the groin wall formed by its tendon sheet can let a bulge through.
muscles:structures/deep-abdominals/origi: Iliac crest, the inguinal ligament and the thoracolumbar fascia
muscles:structures/deep-abdominals/inser: The lowest ribs and the linea alba
muscles:structures/deep-abdominals/nerve: Lower intercostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves
muscles:structures/deep-abdominals/summa: The two deeper layers of the abdominal wall, hidden under the external oblique.
muscles:structures/deep-abdominals/membe: Fibres run up and inward, at right angles to the external oblique.
Horizontal fibres that wrap the abdomen like a corset.
muscles:structures/deep-abdominals/issue: Linked with low back pain. Targeted strengthening helps many people.
muscles:structures/pelvic-floor/originNo: Inside of the pubis, the side walls of the pelvis and the ischial spines
muscles:structures/pelvic-floor/insertio: The coccyx and the tissue around the anus and urethra
muscles:structures/pelvic-floor/nerve: Sacral nerves (S3–S4) and the pudendal nerve
muscles:structures/pelvic-floor/actions/: Relax to let you pass urine and stool
muscles:structures/pelvic-floor/summary: A muscular hammock across the bottom of the pelvis.
muscles:structures/pelvic-floor/members/: The main sling: puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus.
A small muscle at the back, to the coccyx.
muscles:structures/pelvic-floor/issues/0: Leaking when coughing, sneezing or jumping. Pelvic floor exercises help.
muscles:structures/pelvic-floor/issues/1: A heavy, dragging feeling or a bulge in the vagina.
muscles:structures/pelvic-floor/issues/2: Pelvic pain, painful sex or difficulty emptying when the muscles can’t relax.
muscles:structures/pelvic-floor/issues/3: Weak pelvic floor after prostate surgery
Leaking urine after prostate surgery is common at first. Pelvic floor exercises help most men regain control.
muscles:structures/erector-spinae/origin: Sacrum, the back of the iliac crest and the lumbar spinous processes
muscles:structures/erector-spinae/insert: Ribs, thoracic and cervical vertebrae, and the mastoid process
muscles:structures/erector-spinae/nerve: Back (dorsal) branches of the spinal nerves
muscles:structures/erector-spinae/summar: Three columns of muscle running either side of the spine from the pelvis to the skull.
muscles:structures/erector-spinae/member: The outer column, to the ribs.
The middle and longest column, reaching the skull.
The inner column, next to the spinous processes.
muscles:structures/erector-spinae/issues: Spasm and pain on bending or lifting. It usually settles within weeks, and staying gently active helps.
Ache from long periods of sitting or standing.
muscles:structures/quadratus-lumborum/in: The 12th rib and the lumbar transverse processes
muscles:structures/quadratus-lumborum/su: A deep, square muscle of the lower back between the pelvis, the lowest rib and the lumbar spine.
muscles:structures/quadratus-lumborum/is: Deep pain on one side, worse turning in bed or standing up from sitting.
muscles:structures/biceps/originNote: Coracoid process (short head) and the bump above the shoulder socket (long head)
muscles:structures/biceps/insertionNote: Radial tuberosity, plus a tendon sheet onto the forearm
muscles:structures/biceps/actions/0: Turns the palm up, its strongest action
muscles:structures/biceps/summary: The two-headed muscle on the front of the upper arm. It crosses both the shoulder and the elbow.
muscles:structures/biceps/issues/0/note: Pain at the front of the shoulder, worse lifting or reaching.
muscles:structures/biceps/issues/1/note: A pop at the elbow when lifting, then bruising and a weak twist (as with a screwdriver). See a doctor within days, because repair works best early.
muscles:structures/biceps/issues/2/note: A “Popeye” bulge in the upper arm, often in older adults. Usually little loss of function.
muscles:structures/brachialis/originNote: Lower half of the front of the humerus
muscles:structures/brachialis/insertionN: Coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna
muscles:structures/brachialis/actions/0: The main elbow bender, whichever way the palm faces
muscles:structures/brachialis/summary: It lies under the biceps and does most of the work of bending the elbow.
muscles:structures/brachialis/issues/0/n: A deep ache at the front of the elbow after heavy lifting or climbing.
muscles:structures/triceps/originNote: Just below the shoulder socket (long head) and the back of the humerus (lateral and medial heads)
muscles:structures/triceps/insertionNote: Olecranon, the point of the elbow
muscles:structures/triceps/actions/1: Helps pull the arm back (long head)
muscles:structures/triceps/summary: The three-headed muscle on the back of the upper arm. From the front only its inner edge shows.
muscles:structures/triceps/issues/0/note: Pain at the back of the elbow with pushing exercises.
muscles:structures/coracobrachialis/orig: Tip of the coracoid process, shared with the short head of biceps
muscles:structures/coracobrachialis/inse: Inner side of the humerus, halfway down the shaft
muscles:structures/coracobrachialis/nerv: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C7), which passes through it
muscles:structures/coracobrachialis/acti: Draws the arm forward and in towards the body
Helps hold the head of the humerus in the shoulder socket
muscles:structures/coracobrachialis/summ: A slim muscle high on the inner side of the upper arm, from the coracoid process of the shoulder blade to the middle of the humerus, beside the short head of biceps.
muscles:structures/coracobrachialis/issu: Pain at the front of the shoulder and the inner upper arm after throwing, bench-pressing or push-ups. It usually settles with rest.
Rare: weakness bending the elbow and numbness along the outer forearm, from the nerve being squeezed where it passes through the muscle, sometimes after heavy weight training.
muscles:structures/brachioradialis/origi: Outer ridge of the humerus just above the elbow
muscles:structures/brachioradialis/inser: Styloid process of the radius at the wrist
muscles:structures/brachioradialis/actio: Bends the elbow, especially with the thumb pointing up (hammer grip)
muscles:structures/brachioradialis/summa: The muscle forming the outer edge of the forearm, from just above the elbow to the wrist.
muscles:structures/brachioradialis/issue: Ache along the outer forearm after repetitive lifting with a hammer grip.
muscles:structures/forearm-flexors/origi: Inner elbow (medial epicondyle) and the front of the radius and ulna
muscles:structures/forearm-flexors/inser: Wrist, palm and finger bones; pronator teres to the middle of the radius
muscles:structures/forearm-flexors/summa: The muscles on the palm side of the forearm, mostly starting from the inner elbow. Their tendons pass through the carpal tunnel.
muscles:structures/forearm-flexors/membe: Turns the palm down; runs to the middle of the radius.
Bends the wrist toward the thumb side.
A thin tendon at the centre of the wrist; absent in roughly 1 in 7 people.
Bends the wrist toward the little-finger side.
Bends the middle joints of the fingers.
Bends the tip of the thumb.
muscles:structures/forearm-flexors/issue: Pain at the inner elbow with gripping and lifting.
A flexor tendon catches in its sheath, making a finger lock.
Swollen flexor tendon sheaths can squeeze the median nerve at the wrist.
muscles:structures/forearm-extensors/ori: Outer elbow (lateral epicondyle) and the back of the radius and ulna
muscles:structures/forearm-extensors/ins: Backs of the hand and finger bones
muscles:structures/forearm-extensors/act: Straighten and cock back the wrist and fingers
Steady the wrist so you can grip
muscles:structures/forearm-extensors/sum: The muscles on the back of the forearm, mostly starting from the outer elbow. In the front view only their outer edge shows.
muscles:structures/forearm-extensors/mem: Cock the wrist back. ECRB is the usual source of tennis elbow.
Cocks the wrist toward the little-finger side.
Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis longus & brevis move the thumb out and back.
Straightens the index finger for pointing.
muscles:structures/forearm-extensors/iss: Pain on the outer elbow when gripping, lifting a kettle or turning a handle.
Pain on the thumb side of the wrist from two thumb tendons in this group.
muscles:structures/thenar/originNote: Scaphoid, trapezium and the ligament roofing the carpal tunnel
muscles:structures/thenar/insertionNote: First metacarpal and the base of the thumb
muscles:structures/thenar/actions/0: Bring the thumb across the palm to touch the fingertips (opposition)
muscles:structures/thenar/summary: The fleshy mound at the base of the thumb.
muscles:structures/thenar/members/0/note: Moves the thumb away from the palm.
muscles:structures/thenar/members/2/note: Rolls the thumb across to meet the fingers.
muscles:structures/thenar/members/3/note: Deep; pulls the thumb in, as in pinch grip.
muscles:structures/thenar/issues/0/note: A flattened thumb mound with a clumsy pinch can be a sign of advanced carpal tunnel syndrome.
muscles:structures/hypothenar/insertionN: Fifth metacarpal and the base of the little finger
muscles:structures/hypothenar/actions/0: Move and cup the little finger
muscles:structures/hypothenar/summary: The mound on the little-finger side of the palm.
muscles:structures/hypothenar/issues/0/n: Numbness of the little and ring fingers with weak hand muscles, from pressure at the elbow or the wrist (for example in cyclists).
muscles:structures/hand-lumbricals/origi: Tendons of the deep finger flexor (flexor digitorum profundus) in the palm
muscles:structures/hand-lumbricals/inser: Thumb-side edge of the extensor expansions on the backs of the four fingers
muscles:structures/hand-lumbricals/nerve: Median nerve (first and second), ulnar nerve (third and fourth)
muscles:structures/hand-lumbricals/actio: Bend the knuckles while straightening the finger joints, as when holding a card or a pen
muscles:structures/hand-lumbricals/summa: Four small worm-shaped muscles in the palm. They start on the long finger-bending tendons and join the tendons on the backs of the fingers, linking bending and straightening for precise movements.
muscles:structures/hand-lumbricals/issue: Pain in the palm when one finger is held straight while the others bend, typically in climbers. It usually heals with rest.
muscles:structures/hand-interossei/origi: Sides of the metacarpals, filling the spaces between them
muscles:structures/hand-interossei/inser: Bases of the first finger bones and the extensor expansions
muscles:structures/hand-interossei/actio: Spread the fingers apart (dorsal) and bring them together (palmar)
With the lumbricals, bend the knuckles while straightening the fingers
muscles:structures/hand-interossei/summa: Small muscles between the metacarpals. The four dorsal ones fill the spaces on the back of the hand, the largest forming the fleshy web between the thumb and the index finger. The three palmar ones lie deeper, on the palm side.
muscles:structures/hand-interossei/membe: Spread the fingers away from the middle finger.
Bring the fingers together towards the middle finger.
muscles:structures/hand-interossei/issue: Hollows between the metacarpals on the back of the hand, with weak finger-spreading and a clumsy grip, can be a sign of ulnar nerve compression at the elbow or the wrist.
muscles:structures/iliopsoas/originNote: Lumbar vertebrae (psoas) and the inside of the pelvic wing (iliacus)
muscles:structures/iliopsoas/nerve: Lumbar plexus (L1–L3) and the femoral nerve
muscles:structures/iliopsoas/actions/0: The strongest hip flexor: lifts the thigh
muscles:structures/iliopsoas/actions/1: Bends the trunk forward when the legs are fixed, as in sitting up
muscles:structures/iliopsoas/summary: A deep muscle running from the spine and inner pelvis over the front of the hip to the femur. It is the main muscular link between the spine and the legs.
muscles:structures/iliopsoas/members/1/n: From the inside of the pelvic wing.
muscles:structures/iliopsoas/members/2/n: Small, absent in about half of people.
muscles:structures/iliopsoas/issues/0/no: Deep groin pain when lifting the knee, after sprinting or kicking.
muscles:structures/iliopsoas/issues/1/no: A clunk at the front of the hip as the tendon flicks over the pelvis.
muscles:structures/iliopsoas/issues/2/no: Rare: infection here causes fever, back or groin pain and a limp. It needs urgent care.
muscles:structures/gluteus-maximus/origi: Back of the ilium, the sacrum and the coccyx
muscles:structures/gluteus-maximus/inser: The gluteal tuberosity of the femur and, through the IT band, the tibia
muscles:structures/gluteus-maximus/actio: Extends the hip: standing up, climbing, running
muscles:structures/gluteus-maximus/summa: The largest muscle in the body, forming the buttock.
muscles:structures/gluteus-maximus/issue: Often referred from the lower back or the sacroiliac joint; a true muscle strain is less common.
muscles:structures/gluteus-medius/action: Lifts the leg out to the side
Keeps the pelvis level when you stand on one leg
muscles:structures/gluteus-medius/summar: A fan-shaped hip muscle, mostly hidden behind gluteus maximus, that is vital for walking without a limp.
muscles:structures/gluteus-medius/issues: Pain on the outer hip, worse lying on that side, on stairs or standing on one leg. Common in women over 40.
If it is weak, the pelvis drops on the opposite side with each step (Trendelenburg gait).
muscles:structures/gluteus-minimus/origi: Outer surface of the ilium, below gluteus medius
muscles:structures/gluteus-minimus/actio: Lifts the leg out to the side, with gluteus medius
Keeps the pelvis level when you stand on one leg
Its front fibres turn the thigh inwards
muscles:structures/gluteus-minimus/summa: The smallest and deepest of the three gluteal muscles, a fan under gluteus medius. The two work as a pair, and their tendons share the outer hip.
muscles:structures/gluteus-minimus/issue: Pain on the outer hip, worse lying on that side or climbing stairs. The gluteus minimus and medius tendons are usually involved together.
muscles:structures/piriformis/nerve: Nerve to piriformis (S1–S2), from the sacral plexus
muscles:structures/piriformis/actions/1: Steadies the head of the femur in the hip socket
muscles:structures/piriformis/summary: A pear-shaped muscle deep in the buttock under gluteus maximus. The sciatic nerve usually passes out just below it.
muscles:structures/piriformis/issues/0/n: A deep buttock ache, worse sitting or climbing stairs, sometimes with sciatica-like pain down the back of the leg.
muscles:structures/gemelli/originNote: The ischial spine (superior gemellus) and the top of the ischial tuberosity (inferior gemellus)
muscles:structures/gemelli/insertionNote: With the obturator internus tendon, on the inner side of the greater trochanter
muscles:structures/gemelli/nerve: Nerve to obturator internus (superior) and nerve to quadratus femoris (inferior), from the sacral plexus
muscles:structures/gemelli/actions/1: Hold the head of the femur in the hip socket
muscles:structures/gemelli/summary: Two small ‘twin’ muscles in the deep buttock, one above and one below the obturator internus tendon, which they join. Together with the piriformis and the quadratus femoris they form the deep hip rotators under the gluteus maximus.
muscles:structures/gemelli/members/0/not: From the ischial spine, along the top of the obturator internus tendon.
muscles:structures/gemelli/members/1/not: From the ischial tuberosity, along the bottom of the obturator internus tendon.
muscles:structures/gemelli/issues/0/note: A deep buttock ache, worse sitting, sometimes with sciatica-like pain, when the sciatic nerve is irritated among the deep rotators.
muscles:structures/obturator-internus/or: The inner surface of the pelvis around the obturator foramen, and the membrane that closes it
muscles:structures/obturator-internus/in: The inner side of the greater trochanter, above the trochanteric fossa
muscles:structures/obturator-internus/ne: Nerve to obturator internus (L5–S2), from the sacral plexus
muscles:structures/obturator-internus/ac: Lifts the bent thigh out to the side
Steadies the head of the femur in its socket
muscles:structures/obturator-internus/su: A fan of muscle lining the side wall of the pelvis. Its tendon turns a right angle around the lesser sciatic notch, out into the buttock between the gemelli. Only that tendon and the gemelli show from behind; the belly lies inside the pelvis.
muscles:structures/obturator-internus/is: A deep ache in the buttock, pelvis or pelvic floor, worse sitting. It is often linked with pelvic floor tension.
muscles:structures/quadratus-femoris/ori: The outer edge of the ischial tuberosity
muscles:structures/quadratus-femoris/ins: The quadrate tubercle on the back of the femur, between the trochanters
muscles:structures/quadratus-femoris/ner: Nerve to quadratus femoris (L4–S1), from the sacral plexus
muscles:structures/quadratus-femoris/act: Turns the thigh outwards (the strongest of the deep rotators)
Holds the head of the femur in its socket
muscles:structures/quadratus-femoris/sum: A flat, square muscle at the bottom of the deep hip rotators, between the sitting bone and the back of the femur, just below the inferior gemellus.
muscles:structures/quadratus-femoris/iss: The muscle is pinched between the sitting bone and the femur, causing deep buttock or groin pain on long strides or when the thigh is turned in.
muscles:structures/obturator-externus/or: The outer surface of the bone around the obturator foramen, and its membrane
muscles:structures/obturator-externus/in: The trochanteric fossa, under the neck of the femur
muscles:structures/obturator-externus/ac: Steadies the head of the femur in its socket
muscles:structures/obturator-externus/su: A flat, triangular muscle over the front of the obturator foramen, deep under the pectineus and the adductors. Its tendon runs back under the neck of the femur to the trochanteric fossa.
muscles:structures/obturator-externus/is: Deep groin pain in kicking and twisting sports, easily mistaken for an adductor strain or a hip problem.
muscles:structures/tensor-fasciae-latae/: Anterior superior iliac spine, the front point of the hip bone
Through the iliotibial (IT) band onto the outer tibia
Helps flex the hip and lift it outward
Tightens the IT band to steady the knee
A short hip muscle that tightens the iliotibial band, the tough strip running down the outside of the thigh to the knee.
Sharp pain on the outer knee in runners and cyclists, worse going downhill.
muscles:structures/sartorius/actions/0: Flexes the hip, turns it outward and bends the knee: the cross-legged “tailor” position
muscles:structures/sartorius/summary: The longest muscle in the body: a strap crossing the thigh diagonally from the hip to the inner knee.
muscles:structures/sartorius/issues/0/no: Pain on the inner knee just below the joint, common with knee arthritis and in runners.
muscles:structures/adductors/insertionNo: Back of the femur and, for gracilis, the upper inner tibia
muscles:structures/adductors/actions/2: Help flex and rotate the hip
muscles:structures/adductors/summary: The muscles of the inner thigh, fanning from the pubic bone to the femur.
muscles:structures/adductors/members/0/n: The highest, next to the hip flexors.
muscles:structures/adductors/members/3/n: The largest, reaching down to the knee.
muscles:structures/adductors/members/4/n: A long strap down to the inner knee.
muscles:structures/adductors/issues/0/no: Sudden inner-thigh pain during kicking, sprinting or changing direction.
muscles:structures/adductors/issues/1/no: Persistent pain where the adductors attach to the pubis, common in football and hockey.
muscles:structures/rectus-femoris/origin: Anterior inferior iliac spine and just above the hip socket
muscles:structures/rectus-femoris/insert: The patella through the quadriceps tendon, then the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament
muscles:structures/rectus-femoris/action: Flexes the hip (the only quadriceps muscle that crosses it)
muscles:structures/rectus-femoris/summar: The middle muscle of the quadriceps, running straight down the front of the thigh.
muscles:structures/rectus-femoris/issues: Sudden pain at the front of the thigh when sprinting or kicking.
Pain just below the kneecap with jumping and squatting (patellar tendinopathy).
muscles:structures/vastus-lateralis/orig: Greater trochanter and the outer back ridge of the femur
muscles:structures/vastus-lateralis/summ: The largest quadriceps muscle, forming the outer thigh.
muscles:structures/vastus-lateralis/issu: A hard knock causes painful bruising in the thigh. Heavy, worsening swelling needs checking.
muscles:structures/vastus-medialis/origi: Inner back ridge of the femur
muscles:structures/vastus-medialis/actio: Its lowest fibres help the kneecap track straight
muscles:structures/vastus-medialis/summa: The teardrop-shaped quadriceps muscle just above the inner knee.
muscles:structures/vastus-medialis/issue: Weakness here is linked with pain around the kneecap.
muscles:structures/vastus-intermedius/or: Front and outer surface of the femoral shaft
muscles:structures/vastus-intermedius/su: The deep quadriceps muscle, lying on the femur under rectus femoris.
muscles:structures/hamstrings/originNote: Ischial tuberosity (the sitting bone); the short head of biceps from the femur
muscles:structures/hamstrings/insertionN: Head of the fibula and the upper inner tibia
muscles:structures/hamstrings/actions/1: Straighten the hip, swinging the leg back
muscles:structures/hamstrings/summary: Three muscles on the back of the thigh, from the sitting bone to just below the knee.
muscles:structures/hamstrings/members/0/: The outer hamstring, with long and short heads.
muscles:structures/hamstrings/members/1/: The inner, with a long cord-like tendon.
muscles:structures/hamstrings/issues/0/n: Sudden pain at the back of the thigh while sprinting; bruising may follow.
muscles:structures/hamstrings/issues/1/n: Deep pain at the sitting bone, worse sitting or running uphill.
muscles:structures/tibialis-anterior/ori: Outer surface of the upper two-thirds of the tibia
muscles:structures/tibialis-anterior/ins: Medial cuneiform and the base of the first metatarsal
muscles:structures/tibialis-anterior/sum: The muscle just outside the shinbone. You can feel its tendon at the front of the ankle when you lift your toes.
muscles:structures/tibialis-anterior/iss: Pain along the front-outer shin, worse at the start of a run.
If its nerve is damaged, the foot slaps or the toes catch when walking.
Severe, rising pain and tightness in the front of the shin after an injury or hard exercise. It is urgent.
muscles:structures/toe-extensors/originN: Outer tibial condyle and the front of the fibula
muscles:structures/toe-extensors/summary: Long muscles on the front of the leg whose tendons fan out over the top of the foot to the toes.
muscles:structures/toe-extensors/members: A small slip that lifts the outer foot.
muscles:structures/toe-extensors/issues/: Pain on the top of the foot, often from tight laces or a sudden increase in running.
muscles:structures/fibularis/insertionNo: Bases of the first and fifth metatarsals and the medial cuneiform
muscles:structures/fibularis/summary: Muscles along the outside of the leg whose tendons run behind the outer ankle bone.
muscles:structures/fibularis/members/0/n: Its tendon crosses under the foot to the first metatarsal.
muscles:structures/fibularis/issues/0/no: Pain and swelling behind the outer ankle, often after sprains.
muscles:structures/fibularis/issues/1/no: Rolling the ankle can make fibularis brevis pull off a piece of bone.
muscles:structures/gastrocnemius/originN: Both femoral condyles, just above the knee
muscles:structures/gastrocnemius/inserti: The heel bone (calcaneus), through the Achilles tendon
muscles:structures/gastrocnemius/actions: Points the foot: rising on tiptoe and pushing off
muscles:structures/gastrocnemius/summary: The two-headed muscle forming the bulk of the calf. From the front only its inner edge shows.
muscles:structures/gastrocnemius/issues/: Sudden pain in the upper calf, as if kicked, during a push-off.
Pain and stiffness above the heel, worst in the morning.
muscles:structures/soleus/originNote: Back of the upper tibia and fibula
muscles:structures/soleus/insertionNote: The heel bone (calcaneus), through the Achilles tendon
muscles:structures/soleus/actions/0: Points the foot, especially with the knee bent
muscles:structures/soleus/actions/1: Pumps blood back up from the legs while walking
muscles:structures/soleus/summary: A broad, flat calf muscle under gastrocnemius. Together they form the triceps surae.
muscles:structures/soleus/issues/0/note: Gradually tightening lower-calf pain in runners.
muscles:structures/soleus/issues/1/note: Pain along the inner edge of the shin where soleus and the deep calf muscles attach.
muscles:structures/popliteus/originNote: Outer side of the lateral femoral condyle, and the lateral meniscus
muscles:structures/popliteus/insertionNo: Back of the tibia, above the soleal line
muscles:structures/popliteus/actions/0: Unlocks the straightened knee by turning the tibia inwards
muscles:structures/popliteus/actions/1: Draws the lateral meniscus back as the knee bends
muscles:structures/popliteus/summary: A small, flat, triangular muscle across the back of the knee, deep under gastrocnemius.
muscles:structures/popliteus/issues/0/no: Pain at the back and outer side of the knee, worse running downhill.
muscles:structures/tibialis-posterior/or: Back of the tibia, the fibula and the membrane between them
muscles:structures/tibialis-posterior/in: Mainly the navicular, with slips to the other tarsals and metatarsals 2–4
muscles:structures/tibialis-posterior/ac: Points the foot and turns the sole inwards
Holds up the arch of the foot
muscles:structures/tibialis-posterior/su: The deepest calf muscle. Its tendon runs behind the inner ankle bone to support the arch.
muscles:structures/tibialis-posterior/is: Pain and swelling behind the inner ankle, and an arch that gradually flattens.
Pain along the inner edge of the shin.
muscles:structures/toe-flexors/originNot: Back of the tibia (flexor digitorum longus) and the lower back of the fibula (flexor hallucis longus)
muscles:structures/toe-flexors/insertion: Undersides of the last toe bones
muscles:structures/toe-flexors/actions/0: Bend the toes, gripping the ground
muscles:structures/toe-flexors/actions/1: Help point the foot and support the arch
muscles:structures/toe-flexors/actions/2: Give the final push-off from the big toe in walking and running
muscles:structures/toe-flexors/summary: Two deep calf muscles on either side of tibialis posterior. Their tendons pass behind the inner ankle bone and run under the sole to the toes.
muscles:structures/toe-flexors/members/1: Bends the big toe, the strongest push-off of the toes.
muscles:structures/toe-flexors/issues/0/: Pain behind the inner ankle or under the big toe, worse on tiptoe. Common in ballet dancers and runners.
muscles:structures/toe-flexors/issues/1/: Flexor digitorum longus pulls on the inner edge of the shin together with tibialis posterior and soleus.
muscles:structures/extensor-digitorum-br: Upper outer surface of the heel bone (calcaneus)
Base of the big toe, and the long extensor tendons of the second to fourth toes
The only muscle on the top of the foot: a soft, fleshy pad in front of the outer ankle bone with four slim tendons to the toes. Its bulge is normal and is sometimes mistaken for swelling.
Lifts the second to fourth toes.
Its innermost slip; lifts the big toe.
Aching on the top of the foot from tight laces or a sudden increase in running, often together with the long extensor tendons.
muscles:structures/foot-interossei/inser: Bases of the first bones of the second to fifth toes
muscles:structures/foot-interossei/nerve: Lateral plantar nerve, from the tibial nerve
muscles:structures/foot-interossei/actio: Spread the toes (dorsal) and bring them together (plantar)
Steady the toes and the front of the foot during push-off
muscles:structures/foot-interossei/summa: Small muscles in the spaces between the metatarsals. The four dorsal ones can be felt between the bones on the top of the foot; the three plantar ones lie under them, on the sole side.
muscles:structures/foot-interossei/membe: Spread the toes away from the second toe.
Bring the third to fifth toes towards the second.
muscles:structures/foot-interossei/issue: Aching between the metatarsals after a rise in walking or running. One very tender spot on a bone could be a stress fracture, which needs checking.
muscles:structures/sole-muscles/listOnly: Not drawn on the map: they lie under the sole, which faces the ground in both the front and the back views.
muscles:structures/sole-muscles/originNo: Heel bone, the other tarsals, the bases of the metatarsals and the plantar fascia
muscles:structures/sole-muscles/insertio: The toe bones, and the long toe-flexor tendons
muscles:structures/sole-muscles/nerve: Medial and lateral plantar nerves, from the tibial nerve
muscles:structures/sole-muscles/actions/: Bend, spread and steady the toes
Hold up the arches of the foot when standing and pushing off
muscles:structures/sole-muscles/summary: Four layers of small muscles under the sole, between the plantar fascia and the bones. Together they brace the arches and keep the toes pressed to the ground.
muscles:structures/sole-muscles/members/: Along the inner edge of the foot; moves the big toe away from the others and supports the inner arch.
In the middle of the sole, on the plantar fascia; bends the four small toes.
Along the outer edge; moves the little toe.
Pulls on the long toe-flexor tendons to straighten their line of pull.
Bend the toes at the base while straightening the toe joints.
Bends the big toe; its tendons hold the two small sesamoid bones under the big-toe joint.
Pulls the big toe towards the others and braces the arch across the forefoot.
muscles:structures/sole-muscles/issues/0: Aching under the arch after long standing, a new sport or a change of shoes. It usually settles with rest and supportive footwear.
muscles:structures/sole-muscles/issues/1: Pain under the ball of the foot behind the big toe, common in dancers and runners.
muscles:groups/head-muscles/summary: The chewing muscles that close and grind the jaw, and the muscles of facial expression around the eyes, mouth and forehead.
muscles:groups/neck-muscles/summary: Muscles that turn and steady the head and move the hyoid and larynx for swallowing.
muscles:groups/shoulder-muscles/summary: Muscles that move the shoulder blade and the arm at the shoulder.
muscles:groups/chest-muscles/summary: Muscles on and between the ribs, plus the diaphragm, the main muscle of breathing.
muscles:groups/abdomen-muscles/summary: The layered abdominal wall and pelvic floor that brace the trunk and support the organs.
muscles:groups/back-muscles/summary: Deep muscles that hold the spine upright. They lie behind the spine, so they are drawn in the back view.
muscles:groups/arm-muscles/summary: Muscles that bend and straighten the elbow, and the coracobrachialis, which draws the arm forward at the shoulder.
muscles:groups/forearm-muscles/summary: Muscles that move the wrist, fingers and thumb.
muscles:groups/hip-muscles/summary: Muscles that flex, extend and steady the hip.
muscles:groups/thigh-muscles/summary: The quadriceps in front, the adductors on the inside and the hamstrings behind.
muscles:groups/quadriceps/summary: Four muscles on the front of the thigh joining in one tendon over the kneecap. They are the only muscles that straighten the knee.
muscles:groups/quadriceps/issues/0/note: Sudden pain at the front of the thigh when sprinting or kicking.
muscles:groups/quadriceps/issues/1/note: Usually an older adult falling with the knee bent, then unable to straighten the leg. It is urgent.
muscles:groups/leg-muscles/summary: Muscles that lift, point and tilt the foot and move the toes.
muscles:groups/foot-muscles/summary: Small muscles inside the foot that move the toes and hold up the arches. Most lie in layers under the sole.
vessels:structures/aorta/summary: The body’s main artery, about as wide as a garden hose. It rises from the left ventricle, arches over the heart, runs down beside the spine through the chest and the diaphragm, and divides into the two iliac arteries in front of the fourth lumbar vertebra.
vessels:structures/aorta/suppliesNote: Directly, through small paired branches along its length: the bronchial, oesophageal, intercostal, lumbar, phrenic and middle suprarenal arteries. Its big named branches have their own pages.
vessels:structures/aorta/members/0/note: Rises from the heart. The coronary arteries leave its root.
vessels:structures/aorta/members/1/note: Curves over the heart and gives off the arteries to the head and arms.
vessels:structures/aorta/members/2/note: Runs down beside the spine through the chest.
vessels:structures/aorta/members/3/note: From the diaphragm to its split at the fourth lumbar vertebra.
vessels:structures/aorta/issues/0/note: A bulge in the abdominal aorta, most common in older men who smoke. It is usually silent and found by screening. Sudden severe belly or back pain with collapse can mean it has burst. Call emergency services.
vessels:structures/aorta/issues/1/note: A tear in the aortic wall: sudden, severe, tearing pain in the chest or back. Call emergency services.
vessels:structures/pulmonary-trunk/summa: Leaves the right ventricle and splits under the aortic arch into the right and left pulmonary arteries. They are the only arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood, which goes to the lungs to pick up oxygen.
vessels:structures/pulmonary-trunk/suppl: Carries blood through the lungs to be oxygenated. The lung tissue itself is fed by small bronchial arteries from the aorta.
vessels:structures/pulmonary-trunk/membe: Passes behind the aorta and superior vena cava to the right lung.
vessels:structures/pulmonary-trunk/issue: A clot, usually from a leg vein, lodges in the lung arteries: sudden breathlessness, sharp chest pain that is worse on breathing in, sometimes coughing up blood. Call emergency services.
High pressure in the lung arteries causes breathlessness on exertion and tiredness. It needs specialist assessment.
vessels:structures/coronary-arteries/sum: The heart’s own blood supply: two arteries that leave the very start of the aorta and run in the grooves on the heart’s surface. The left one splits early into the front (LAD) and circumflex branches.
vessels:structures/coronary-arteries/mem: The right side of the heart, and in most people the heart’s natural pacemaker.
The front of the heart and the wall between the ventricles.
The left side and back of the heart.
vessels:structures/coronary-arteries/iss: Narrowing by fatty plaques causes angina: chest tightness on exertion that eases with rest. It needs medical assessment.
A clot blocks a coronary artery: crushing chest pain, possibly spreading to the arm, jaw or back, with sweating or breathlessness. Call emergency services.
vessels:structures/brachiocephalic-trunk: The first and largest branch of the aortic arch. It runs up and to the right behind the breastbone and divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. There is no left one: on the left, those two arteries come straight off the arch.
vessels:structures/common-carotid-artery: Side of the neck, beside the windpipe

Runs up the neck beside the windpipe, under the front edge of the sternocleidomastoid, and divides at the level of the top of the voice box. The internal carotid enters the skull to feed the brain and eye; the external carotid feeds the face, scalp, jaw and thyroid.
The brain, eye, eye muscles and pituitary through the internal carotid (its upper part drawn faint, behind the jaw). The face, scalp, thyroid and jaw through the external carotid.
Into the skull, to the front and middle of the brain and the eye.
