Narrowing at the fork can shed clots to the brain. A mini-stroke (TIA), with brief weakness, numbness, loss of speech or loss of vision in one eye, is a warning: get seen urgently the same day.
A drooping face, arm weakness or trouble speaking: call emergency services straight away.
vessels:structures/external-carotid-arte: The branch of the common carotid that feeds everything in the head outside the skull: the thyroid, tongue, face, jaw and scalp. It rises behind the angle of the jaw, inside the parotid gland, and ends just in front of the ear by splitting into the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries.
To the thyroid and the voice box.
Deep in the face: the jaws, teeth, chewing muscles and the lining of the skull (middle meningeal artery).
To the back of the scalp.
vessels:structures/facial-artery/pulse: Lower edge of the jaw, just in front of the masseter muscle
vessels:structures/facial-artery/summary: Hooks over the lower edge of the jaw just in front of the masseter, where you can feel its pulse, then winds up past the corner of the mouth and the side of the nose to the inner corner of the eye. It feeds the lips, cheek and nose, and is why face cuts bleed so freely.
vessels:structures/facial-artery/supplie: The submandibular gland, the nose, the lips and the muscles of facial expression.
vessels:structures/superficial-temporal-: Just in front of the ear, above the jaw joint

The end of the external carotid. It climbs just in front of the ear, where its pulse is easy to feel, and branches over the temple and scalp. Its winding branches often show under the skin of the temple in older people.
The front of the ear, the forehead and the skin of the temple and scalp.

Inflamed temple arteries, almost only over 50: a new headache, a tender scalp or temple, and jaw pain on chewing. See a doctor the same day, because it can damage sight. Any loss or blurring of vision is an emergency.
vessels:structures/vertebral-artery/summ: Rises from the subclavian artery and climbs through holes in the side processes of the neck vertebrae into the skull. The two join at the base of the brain into the basilar artery, which feeds the brainstem, the cerebellum and the back of the brain. Drawn faint because it runs inside the vertebrae.
vessels:structures/vertebral-artery/issu: A tear in the wall, sometimes after neck injury or a sudden neck movement: neck pain or headache followed by dizziness, unsteadiness, double vision or slurred speech. Call emergency services.
vessels:structures/subclavian-artery/sum: Arches over the first rib just above the collarbone, carrying blood to the arm. On the right it comes from the brachiocephalic trunk, on the left straight from the aortic arch. At the outer edge of the first rib it becomes the axillary artery.
vessels:structures/subclavian-artery/sup: Through the thyrocervical trunk (thyroid, neck and shoulder muscles), the dorsal scapular artery, and the internal thoracic artery, which runs down inside the front of the chest beside the breastbone and also feeds the inner part of the breast.
vessels:structures/subclavian-artery/mem: The lower thyroid and the neck and shoulder muscles.
Runs down beside the breastbone to the chest wall and the rectus abdominis. Surgeons often use it for heart bypasses.
The rhomboids and the muscles over the shoulder blade.
vessels:structures/subclavian-artery/iss: A narrowed subclavian artery can make the arm ache with use and cause dizziness. A big difference in blood pressure between the two arms needs checking.
vessels:structures/axillary-artery/summa: The artery of the armpit, from the first rib to the lower edge of the teres major, where it becomes the brachial artery. It runs behind the pectoralis minor with the cords of the brachial plexus around it.
vessels:structures/axillary-artery/suppl: Through the thoracoacromial, lateral thoracic, subscapular and circumflex humeral arteries. The lateral thoracic artery also feeds the outer part of the breast.
vessels:structures/axillary-artery/membe: The pectoral muscles, the deltoid and the top of the shoulder.
The serratus anterior and the side of the chest wall.
The shoulder-blade muscles and the latissimus dorsi.
Wrap around the neck of the humerus to the deltoid and the shoulder joint.
vessels:structures/brachial-artery/pulse: Inside of the elbow crease, where blood pressure is measured
vessels:structures/brachial-artery/summa: The main artery of the upper arm. It runs down the inner side of the biceps into the elbow crease, where a blood-pressure cuff listens to it, and divides just below the elbow into the radial and ulnar arteries.
vessels:structures/brachial-artery/suppl: The triceps and the humerus through its deep branch (profunda brachii).
vessels:structures/brachial-artery/membe: Runs with the radial nerve around the back of the humerus.
vessels:structures/brachial-artery/issue: A badly displaced elbow fracture, especially in children, can pinch it. A cold, pale hand or severe forearm pain after an elbow injury needs emergency care.
vessels:structures/radial-artery/pulse: Wrist, at the base of the thumb
vessels:structures/radial-artery/summary: Runs down the thumb side of the forearm under the brachioradialis. At the wrist it lies just under the skin, where you take a pulse, then turns around the base of the thumb into the hand and forms the deep palmar arch.
vessels:structures/radial-artery/supplie: Its branches reach the scaphoid mainly from the far end, which is why a break through the middle of the scaphoid can cut off the blood to the near half.
vessels:structures/ulnar-artery/summary: The larger of the two forearm arteries. It runs down the little-finger side of the forearm beside the ulnar nerve and enters the palm next to the pisiform bone, where it forms the superficial palmar arch.
vessels:structures/ulnar-artery/supplies: The back of the forearm through its interosseous branches.
vessels:structures/palmar-arches/summary: Two loops of artery across the palm that join the radial and ulnar arteries, so the hand has two supplies. The superficial arch lies under the skin of the palm, the deep arch against the bones. Together they send an artery along each side of every finger.
vessels:structures/palmar-arches/members: Run along both sides of each finger.
vessels:structures/palmar-arches/issues/: In the cold, the fingers turn white, then blue, then red as they warm up, as the small arteries clamp down. Keep the hands warm. See a doctor if it affects one side only, is severe, or causes sores.
vessels:structures/celiac-trunk/summary: A short, wide artery leaving the front of the aorta just below the diaphragm. Within a centimetre it splits three ways to feed the organs of the upper abdomen: the stomach, liver, gallbladder, spleen and pancreas.
vessels:structures/celiac-trunk/supplies: Through its three branches. The lowest part of the oesophagus is fed by the left gastric artery.
vessels:structures/celiac-trunk/members/: The top of the stomach and the lower oesophagus.
Winds along the top of the pancreas to the spleen.
The liver, the gallbladder (through the cystic artery) and the first part of the small intestine.
vessels:structures/superior-mesenteric-a: Leaves the front of the aorta just below the coeliac trunk and runs down into the mesentery, the fan of tissue that holds the small intestine. It feeds the whole small intestine, the appendix and the large intestine about two-thirds of the way across.
A fan of 15 or more branches to the small intestine.
The end of the small intestine, the caecum and the appendix.
A blocked gut artery: sudden, severe belly pain that seems out of proportion to what a doctor finds, often in older people with an irregular heartbeat. Call emergency services.
vessels:structures/inferior-mesenteric-a: The smallest of the three gut arteries, leaving the aorta low in the abdomen. It runs down and to the left to feed the last third of the large intestine and the rectum.
Reduced blood flow to the left side of the colon: sudden cramping pain on the left with bloody diarrhoea. See a doctor urgently.
vessels:structures/renal-artery/summary: Leaves the side of the aorta just below the superior mesenteric artery and enters the kidney at its notch (the hilum). The right one is longer and passes behind the inferior vena cava. Together they carry about a fifth of all the blood the heart pumps.
vessels:structures/renal-artery/issues/0: A narrowed kidney artery can cause high blood pressure that is hard to control, and slowly reduce kidney function. It needs specialist assessment.
vessels:structures/iliac-artery/summary: The aorta ends by splitting into the two common iliac arteries. Each divides in front of the sacroiliac joint: the internal iliac goes down into the pelvis, and the external iliac runs along the rim of the pelvis to the groin, where it becomes the femoral artery.
vessels:structures/iliac-artery/supplies: The pelvic organs, reproductive organs, buttock and pelvic floor through the internal iliac (the gluteal, obturator, uterine, vesical and pudendal arteries). The lower belly wall through the inferior epigastric artery, from the external iliac.
vessels:structures/iliac-artery/members/: From the end of the aorta to the sacroiliac joint.
The bladder, the pelvic floor, the buttock and the reproductive organs.
Along the rim of the pelvis to the groin.
Runs up behind the rectus abdominis.
Runs across the floor of the pelvis to the side of the uterus and up along it, also feeding the cervix, the vagina and the uterine tube.
Leaves the pelvis with the pudendal nerve to the perineum, the external genitals and the lower end of the bowel.
vessels:structures/ovarian-artery/summar: A long, thin artery from the front of the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries. It runs down on the psoas muscle, crosses the iliac vessels at the rim of the pelvis and reaches the ovary in a fold of tissue. The ovaries form high in the abdomen, which is why their arteries start so high.
vessels:structures/ovarian-artery/suppli: It joins the uterine artery beside the uterus, so the ovary and the tube are fed from both.
vessels:structures/testicular-artery/sum: A long, thin artery from the front of the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries. It runs down on the psoas muscle and through the groin (the inguinal canal) in the spermatic cord to the testis. The testes form high in the abdomen and descend before birth, which is why their arteries start so high.
vessels:structures/femoral-artery/pulse: Groin, halfway between the bony point of the hip and the pubic bone
vessels:structures/femoral-artery/summar: The main artery of the thigh. It enters under the inguinal ligament in the middle of the groin, where its pulse is easy to feel, runs down the inner front of the thigh under the sartorius, and passes through a gap in the adductors to the back of the knee.
vessels:structures/femoral-artery/suppli: Most of the thigh through its deep branch (profunda femoris, drawn faint), whose circumflex branches also feed the head of the femur. A broken femoral neck can tear them.
vessels:structures/femoral-artery/member: The main supply of the thigh muscles, running deep near the femur.
The outer thigh muscles and the hip.
The main supply of the head of the femur.
vessels:structures/popliteal-artery/puls: Deep behind the knee (hard to feel)
vessels:structures/popliteal-artery/summ: Continues the femoral artery behind the knee, deep in the hollow there. It sends branches around the knee joint and divides below it into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries. Drawn faint in the front view, where it lies behind the knee.
vessels:structures/popliteal-artery/supp: The knee through the genicular arteries, and the calf muscles through the sural arteries.
vessels:structures/popliteal-artery/issu: A widening of the artery behind the knee, often on both sides. It can form clots that block the blood to the lower leg. A pulsing lump behind the knee needs checking.
vessels:structures/anterior-tibial-arter: Passes forward between the tibia and fibula and runs down the front of the leg with the deep fibular nerve. In front of the ankle it becomes the dorsalis pedis artery, whose pulse you can feel on the top of the foot.
vessels:structures/dorsalis-pedis-artery: Top of the foot, just beside the tendon of the big toe

The continuation of the anterior tibial artery past the front of the ankle. It runs over the top of the foot toward the gap between the first two toes, where it dives into the sole to join the plantar arch. Doctors feel its pulse to check the blood supply to the foot.
And the skin on the top of the foot.
Common with peripheral arterial disease and diabetes, though in a few healthy people it is simply hard to find. A cold, pale, painful foot needs emergency care.
vessels:structures/posterior-tibial-arte: The larger branch of the popliteal artery. It runs deep in the calf, then behind the inner ankle bone into the sole, where it divides into the plantar arteries. Its fibular branch feeds the outer side of the leg. Drawn faint in the front view, where it lies behind the bones.
Runs down behind the fibula to the outer leg and ankle.
The sole of the foot and the toes.
vessels:structures/superior-vena-cava/su: A short, wide vein that collects all the blood from the head, neck and arms and empties it into the right atrium. It forms behind the right side of the breastbone, where the two brachiocephalic veins meet.
vessels:structures/superior-vena-cava/is: A blockage, usually from a tumour or a clot, makes the face, neck and arms swell, with breathlessness. It needs urgent medical care.
vessels:structures/pulmonary-veins/carri: Oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the heart
vessels:structures/pulmonary-veins/summa: Two veins from each lung that bring freshly oxygenated blood into the left atrium. They are the only veins that carry oxygen-rich blood. Drawn faint in the front view, because they enter the back of the heart.
vessels:structures/pulmonary-veins/issue: The most common irregular heartbeat often starts in the muscle around the openings of the pulmonary veins. Palpitations or an irregular pulse need a doctor. With chest pain or fainting, get urgent care.
vessels:structures/brachiocephalic-vein/: Formed on each side behind the inner end of the collarbone, where the internal jugular and subclavian veins meet. The left one is about twice as long and crosses in front of the branches of the aortic arch. The two join to form the superior vena cava.
vessels:structures/internal-jugular-vein: Drains the brain, face and neck. It leaves the skull through the jugular foramen (its top drawn faint, behind the jaw) and runs down the neck in a sheath with the carotid artery and vagus nerve, deep to the sternocleidomastoid.
Visibly swollen neck veins when sitting upright can be a sign of heart failure. A doctor checks for it as part of an examination.
vessels:structures/external-jugular-vein: A surface vein that runs from behind the angle of the jaw down across the sternocleidomastoid to just above the middle of the collarbone. You can often see it stand out when someone strains, sings or shouts.
vessels:structures/subclavian-vein/summa: Continues the axillary vein over the first rib, just behind the collarbone and in front of the subclavian artery. It joins the internal jugular vein to form the brachiocephalic vein, and is a common site for central lines.
vessels:structures/subclavian-vein/issue: A clot after repeated heavy arm use, where the vein is squeezed between the collarbone and the first rib: a swollen, heavy, bluish arm. It needs urgent assessment.
vessels:structures/axillary-vein/summary: The vein of the armpit, formed where the basilic vein meets the deep veins of the arm. It runs beside the axillary artery and becomes the subclavian vein at the outer edge of the first rib.
vessels:structures/cephalic-vein/summary: A surface vein that runs from the thumb side of the back of the hand up the outer forearm and arm, then in the groove between the deltoid and pectoralis major to the axillary vein. It is often used for drips.
vessels:structures/basilic-vein/summary: A surface vein that runs from the little-finger side of the back of the hand up the inner forearm. Halfway up the arm it dives deep and joins the brachial veins to become the axillary vein.
vessels:structures/median-cubital-vein/s: A short surface vein crossing the front of the elbow from the cephalic to the basilic vein. It is the usual vein for blood tests, because it is wide, close to the skin and held steady.
vessels:structures/median-cubital-vein/i: Common and harmless. Press firmly for a few minutes afterwards. A hard, hot, red area that spreads, or a fever, needs a doctor.
vessels:structures/inferior-vena-cava/su: The largest vein in the body. It forms in front of the fifth lumbar vertebra from the two iliac veins, rises on the right of the aorta, collects the veins of the kidneys and liver, and passes through the diaphragm into the right atrium.
vessels:structures/inferior-vena-cava/is: Lying flat on the back late in pregnancy can squash it and cause dizziness or faintness. Lying on the left side relieves it.
vessels:structures/hepatic-portal-vein/c: Nutrient-rich blood from the gut to the liver
vessels:structures/hepatic-portal-vein/s: Formed behind the neck of the pancreas where the splenic and superior mesenteric veins meet. It carries blood from the stomach, intestines, spleen and pancreas to the liver, which processes nutrients and clears toxins before the blood reaches the rest of the body.
vessels:structures/hepatic-portal-vein/m: From the spleen, along the back of the pancreas.
From the small intestine and the right half of the colon.
From the left colon and rectum, into the splenic vein.
vessels:structures/hepatic-portal-vein/i: Scarring of the liver (cirrhosis) raises the pressure in the portal vein, causing fluid in the belly, a large spleen and swollen veins in the oesophagus that can bleed. Vomiting blood or passing black stools needs emergency care.
vessels:structures/renal-vein/summary: Carries filtered blood from each kidney to the inferior vena cava. The left one is longer and crosses in front of the aorta, just below the superior mesenteric artery.
vessels:structures/iliac-vein/summary: The external iliac vein continues the femoral vein from the groin along the rim of the pelvis, and the internal iliac vein drains the pelvis. They join into the common iliac vein, and the two common iliac veins form the inferior vena cava. The left one passes behind the right common iliac artery.
vessels:structures/iliac-vein/members/0/: From the sacroiliac joint to the inferior vena cava.
vessels:structures/iliac-vein/members/1/: The bladder, pelvic floor, buttock and reproductive organs.
vessels:structures/iliac-vein/members/2/: From the groin along the rim of the pelvis.
vessels:structures/ovarian-vein/summary: Drains the ovary and the uterine tube, starting as a web of veins beside the ovary. The right one empties into the inferior vena cava, the left one into the left renal vein.
vessels:structures/ovarian-vein/issues/0: Widened ovarian veins can cause a dull, dragging pelvic ache that is worse after standing. See a doctor about pelvic pain that lasts.
vessels:structures/testicular-vein/summa: Starts as a web of veins around the testicular artery in the spermatic cord (the pampiniform plexus), which cools the blood flowing in, then joins into one vein in the abdomen. The right one empties into the inferior vena cava, the left one into the left renal vein.
vessels:structures/testicular-vein/issue: Swollen veins above the testicle that feel like a bag of worms, much more often on the left because of the way its vein drains. Usually harmless, but have any swelling checked.
vessels:structures/femoral-vein/summary: The main deep vein of the thigh. It continues the popliteal vein and runs up beside the femoral artery, on its inner side at the groin, where it receives the great saphenous vein.
vessels:structures/popliteal-vein/summar: Formed below the knee by the deep veins of the calf, which run in pairs beside the arteries. It runs up behind the knee and becomes the femoral vein. Each squeeze of the calf muscles pumps blood up through these veins. Drawn faint in the front view, where it lies behind the bones.
vessels:structures/popliteal-vein/member: From the sole and the back of the calf.
From the outer side of the calf.
From the front of the leg and the top of the foot.
vessels:structures/popliteal-vein/issues: Most leg clots start in these deep calf veins, after long journeys, surgery, bed rest, pregnancy or with some medicines. A swollen, painful calf needs urgent assessment the same day.
vessels:structures/great-saphenous-vein/: The longest vein in the body. It starts at the inner end of the arch of veins on the top of the foot, passes in front of the inner ankle bone and runs up the inner leg and thigh, just under the skin, to join the femoral vein below the groin.
Leaky valves let blood pool, so the vein and its branches swell and twist. Mostly harmless. Walking and raising the legs help. See a doctor for skin changes, ulcers or bleeding.
A tender, red, hard cord along the vein. It usually settles, but see a doctor, because it can extend into the deep veins.
vessels:structures/small-saphenous-vein/: The surface vein of the back of the leg. It starts at the outer end of the arch of veins on the top of the foot, passes behind the outer ankle bone and runs up the middle of the calf, just under the skin, to join the popliteal vein behind the knee.
Swollen, twisting veins on the back of the calf when its valves leak. Mostly harmless. Walking and raising the legs help. See a doctor for skin changes, ulcers or bleeding.
vessels:groups/arteries/summary: Vessels that carry blood away from the heart under pressure. Their walls are thick and muscular, and you can feel a pulse wherever one runs close to the surface over bone.
vessels:groups/arteries/issues/0/note: Fatty plaques narrow and stiffen arteries over many years. Smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and diabetes speed it up. It underlies most heart attacks and strokes.
vessels:groups/arteries/issues/1/note: A limb that suddenly turns cold, pale, painful or numb, or signs of a stroke or heart attack, need emergency care.
vessels:groups/arteries-chest/summary: The aorta, the arteries of the heart and lungs, and the first branches of the aortic arch.
vessels:groups/arteries-head-arm/summary: The carotid and vertebral arteries to the head, and the chain of arteries that runs down each arm to the hand.
vessels:groups/arteries-abdomen/summary: The branches of the abdominal aorta to the gut, kidneys and pelvis.
vessels:groups/arteries-leg/summary: The femoral artery and its continuations down to the foot.
vessels:groups/arteries-leg/issues/0/not: Narrowed leg arteries cause cramping pain in the calf, thigh or buttock when walking, easing within minutes of rest (claudication). Stopping smoking and regular walking help. See a doctor.
vessels:groups/arteries-leg/issues/1/not: A leg that suddenly turns cold, pale, painful or numb needs emergency care.
vessels:groups/veins/summary: Vessels that bring blood back to the heart at low pressure. Many have one-way valves, and in the legs the squeeze of the calf muscles pumps the blood upward.
vessels:groups/veins/issues/0/note: A clot blocking a vein makes the area it drains swollen, painful and sometimes discoloured. A swollen, painful limb needs urgent assessment.
vessels:groups/veins-chest/summary: The veins that empty into the heart.
vessels:groups/veins-head-arm/summary: The jugular veins from the head and neck, and the deep and surface veins of the arm.
vessels:groups/veins-head-arm/issues/0/n: Less common than in the legs. It can follow a drip or central line, or heavy repeated arm use. A swollen, painful or bluish arm needs prompt assessment.
vessels:groups/veins-head-arm/issues/1/n: An inflamed surface vein, often after a drip: a tender, red cord under the skin. It usually settles. See a doctor if it spreads or you have a fever.
vessels:groups/veins-abdomen/summary: The inferior vena cava, the veins of the kidneys and pelvis, and the portal vein that takes blood from the gut to the liver.
vessels:groups/veins-leg/summary: The deep veins that run with the arteries, and the great saphenous vein just under the skin.
vessels:groups/veins-leg/issues/0/note: A clot in a deep leg vein: a swollen, painful, warm calf or thigh. It needs urgent assessment the same day. Sudden breathlessness or chest pain can mean a clot has moved to the lungs. Call emergency services.
vessels:groups/veins-leg/issues/1/note: Leaky valves let blood pool, so surface veins swell and twist. Mostly harmless. Walking and raising the legs help. See a doctor for skin changes, ulcers or bleeding.
lymphatics:structures/thoracic-duct/summ: The body's main lymph vessel. It rises from the cisterna chyli in the upper abdomen, runs up in front of the spine between the aorta and the azygos vein, crosses to the left in the upper chest and empties into the veins at the base of the left side of the neck. It carries lymph from both legs, the abdomen and the left half of the chest, head and arm: about three quarters of the body.
lymphatics:structures/thoracic-duct/drai: at the left venous angle, where the left internal jugular vein joins the subclavian vein
lymphatics:structures/thoracic-duct/issu: Rarely, injury or surgery in the chest damages the duct and milky lymph collects around the lung, causing breathlessness. It needs hospital treatment.
lymphatics:structures/cisterna-chyli/sum: A small sac in front of the first and second lumbar vertebrae where the lymph trunks of the legs, pelvis and gut meet. Its lymph is milky after a fatty meal (chyle) because it carries fat absorbed from the intestine. It is the start of the thoracic duct.
lymphatics:structures/right-lymphatic-du: A short duct, about a centimetre long, at the base of the right side of the neck. It returns lymph from the right half of the head, neck and chest and the right arm: about a quarter of the body.
at the right venous angle, where the right internal jugular vein joins the subclavian vein
lymphatics:structures/arm-lymphatics/sum: Fine vessels that start as a mesh in the skin of the fingers and palm and run up the forearm and arm, mostly along the surface veins, to the lymph nodes of the armpit.
lymphatics:structures/arm-lymphatics/iss: Red streaks running up from an infected cut or bite mean the infection is spreading along lymph vessels. See a doctor the same day.
Swelling of the arm after the armpit nodes are removed or treated, most often for breast cancer. Compression, exercise and skin care help.
lymphatics:structures/leg-lymphatics/sum: Fine vessels from the skin of the foot that run up the inner leg with the great saphenous vein to the inguinal nodes in the groin. Lymph from the outer foot and back of the calf goes first to the popliteal nodes behind the knee.
lymphatics:structures/leg-lymphatics/iss: Persistent swelling of the foot and leg, either from birth or after surgery, radiotherapy or infection in the groin. Skin care matters, because swollen legs get cellulitis easily.
Red streaks running up the leg from an infected cut or bite need a doctor the same day.
lymphatics:structures/cervical-lymph-nod: Chains of nodes under the jaw and along the internal jugular vein, under the sternocleidomastoid. They filter lymph from the scalp, face, mouth, throat and thyroid. The ones just below the angle of the jaw are the "glands" that swell with a sore throat.
Common with colds, sore throats and dental infections, and they settle as the infection clears. See a doctor if one keeps growing, feels hard or fixed, or lasts more than three weeks.
Large, tender neck nodes with a severe sore throat, fever and tiredness, mostly in teenagers and young adults. It settles over weeks. Avoid contact sports until a doctor says the spleen is safe.
lymphatics:structures/axillary-lymph-nod: About 20 to 30 nodes in the fat of the armpit, around the axillary vein. They filter lymph from the arm, the chest wall and most of the breast, which is why they are checked in breast cancer.
Often from an infection in the hand or arm, a recent vaccination or shaving rash. See a doctor for a lump that lasts more than three weeks, or any lump with a change in the breast.
lymphatics:structures/mediastinal-lymph-: Nodes in the middle of the chest, around the trachea, its split into the two bronchi and the roots of the lungs. They filter lymph from the lungs, heart and oesophagus. They can't be felt, but show on chest scans.
Found on scans in infections such as tuberculosis, in sarcoidosis and in some cancers. Doctors decide on tests depending on the cause.
lymphatics:structures/para-aortic-lymph-: A chain of nodes on either side of the abdominal aorta, at the back of the abdomen. They collect lymph from the kidneys, the testes or ovaries and, through the iliac nodes, from the pelvis and legs, and pass it to the cisterna chyli.
lymphatics:structures/mesenteric-lymph-n: Hundreds of small nodes in the mesentery, the fan of tissue that holds the intestines to the back of the abdomen. They filter lymph and absorbed fat from the gut on its way to the cisterna chyli.
Inflamed abdominal nodes after a viral infection, mostly in children. The pain can mimic appendicitis and usually settles in a few days. Worsening pain in the lower right abdomen needs a doctor.
lymphatics:structures/iliac-lymph-nodes/: Nodes along the iliac arteries and veins in the pelvis. They filter lymph from the bladder, the pelvic organs and, through the inguinal nodes, the leg, and pass it up to the para-aortic nodes.
lymphatics:structures/inguinal-lymph-nod: Nodes in the groin, a row just below the crease and a vertical group around the top of the great saphenous vein. They filter lymph from the leg, the buttock, the lower abdominal wall and the genitals, and pass it to the iliac nodes.

Usually from an infection of the foot, leg or skin, and it settles. A groin lump that comes and goes with coughing or standing is more likely a hernia. See a doctor for a lump that lasts more than three weeks.
lymphatics:structures/popliteal-lymph-no: A few small nodes deep in the hollow behind the knee, beside the popliteal vessels. They filter lymph from the outer foot and the back of the calf, along the small saphenous vein, and pass it to the inguinal nodes.
lymphatics:structures/thymus/summary: A two-lobed organ behind the top of the breastbone, in front of the heart and great vessels. T cells, the white blood cells that recognise germs, mature here. It is largest in childhood and is slowly replaced by fat after puberty.
lymphatics:structures/tonsils/summary: Two lumps of lymphoid tissue at the back of the throat, one on each side. Together with the adenoid and the tissue at the back of the tongue they form a ring that meets germs entering through the mouth and nose.
lymphatics:structures/tonsils/issues/0/n: Sore throat, painful swallowing, fever and red, swollen tonsils, usually from a virus. Rest, fluids and pain relief help. See a doctor if it lasts more than a week or keeps coming back.
lymphatics:structures/tonsils/issues/1/n: An abscess beside a tonsil: a severe one-sided sore throat, trouble opening the mouth and a muffled voice. It needs urgent treatment.
lymphatics:groups/lymphatic-system/summa: A second network of vessels that collects the fluid leaking out of the blood into the tissues (lymph), filters it through lymph nodes, where immune cells check it for germs and abnormal cells, and returns it to the veins at the base of the neck. It also carries fat absorbed from the gut.
lymphatics:groups/lymphatic-system/issue: Tender, swollen nodes near an infection (a sore throat, an infected cut) are the immune system at work and usually settle within two or three weeks. See a doctor for nodes that keep growing, feel hard or fixed, last more than three weeks, or come with night sweats, fever or weight loss.

Persistent swelling of a limb when lymph can't drain away, most often after lymph nodes are removed or treated for cancer. Early treatment (compression, skin care, exercise) helps. See a doctor for a newly swollen limb.
lymphatics:groups/lymph-nodes/summary: Bean-shaped filters, usually a few millimetres long, clustered where lymph vessels from a region converge: the neck, armpit, groin, chest and abdomen. There are about 600 in the body.
lymphatics:groups/lymph-vessels/summary: Thin-walled vessels with one-way valves. Muscle movement and breathing push lymph along them, from the tissues through the nodes to the two ducts that empty into the veins of the neck.
lymphatics:groups/lymphoid-organs/summar: Organs where immune cells mature or meet germs: the thymus, the tonsils and the spleen.
nerves:structures/spinal-cord/carries: Messages between the brain and the body
nerves:structures/spinal-cord/summary: A finger-thick cable of nerve tissue running down the canal inside the spine, from the base of the skull to about the first lumbar vertebra. Below that, its nerve roots carry on down the canal as the cauda equina. Drawn faint in the front view, where it lies behind the vertebral bodies.
nerves:structures/spinal-cord/members/0/: Thicker in the neck, where the nerves to the arms leave.
nerves:structures/spinal-cord/members/1/: Thicker again low in the back, where the nerves to the legs leave.
nerves:structures/spinal-cord/members/2/: The tapered end, at about the L1–L2 level.
nerves:structures/spinal-cord/members/3/: The “horse’s tail”: the bundle of lower nerve roots that runs on down the canal to the sacrum.
nerves:structures/spinal-cord/issues/0/n: Damage from a fall, crash or diving accident can cause weakness or loss of feeling below the injured level. Don’t move someone with a suspected neck or back injury. Call emergency services.
nerves:structures/spinal-cord/issues/1/n: Squashed nerve roots at the bottom of the spine cause numbness around the bottom or genitals, new trouble passing urine or controlling the bowel, or weakness in both legs. It needs emergency care.
nerves:structures/spinal-cord/issues/2/n: Narrowing of the canal, usually with age, can cause leg pain, numbness or heaviness on walking that eases on sitting or bending forward.
nerves:structures/spinal-nerves/summary: Thirty-one pairs of nerves, one pair leaving the spine at each level through the gap between two vertebrae. Each soon splits into a back branch for the muscles and skin of the back, and a front branch that joins a plexus or runs around the body wall.
nerves:structures/spinal-nerves/innervat: Through their back (dorsal) branches. Their front branches form the plexuses and the intercostal nerves.
nerves:structures/spinal-nerves/members/: 8 pairs, C1–C8: neck, shoulders and arms.
12 pairs, T1–T12: chest and belly wall.
5 pairs, L1–L5: lower belly wall and legs.
5 pairs, S1–S5: buttocks, legs, pelvic floor, bladder and bowel.
1 pair: the skin around the tailbone.
nerves:structures/spinal-nerves/issues/0: A bulging disc or bony narrowing presses on a nerve as it leaves the spine, causing pain, tingling or weakness along that nerve’s path. Most cases settle within weeks.
nerves:structures/spinal-nerves/issues/1: The chickenpox virus wakes up in one nerve root and causes a painful, blistering rash in a band on one side of the body. See a doctor early, as treatment works best in the first three days.
nerves:structures/olfactory-nerve/summar: Twenty or so bundles of very fine fibres that pass up from the roof of the nose through the sieve-like plate of the ethmoid bone to the olfactory bulb under the front of the brain. They carry smell, which is also most of what we call flavour.
nerves:structures/olfactory-nerve/issues: Most often after a cold, flu or COVID-19, or with nasal polyps, and it often recovers over weeks to months. Smell training can help. See a doctor if it lasts or comes with other new symptoms.
nerves:structures/olfactory-nerve/innerv: Smell, from the roof of the nasal cavity.
nerves:structures/optic-nerve/summary: Carries everything the eye sees from the retina back through the orbit to the optic chiasm under the brain, where the fibres from the inner half of each retina cross to the other side. It is really an outgrowth of the brain, wrapped in the same membranes.
nerves:structures/optic-nerve/issues/0/n: Inflammation of the nerve: blurred or dim vision in one eye over days, with pain on moving the eye. See a doctor urgently. Any sudden loss of vision is an emergency.
nerves:structures/optic-nerve/innervates: Carries sight from the retina to the brain.
nerves:structures/oculomotor-nerve/carri: Eye movement, eyelid lift, pupil size and focusing
nerves:structures/oculomotor-nerve/summa: Moves the eye up, down and inward through four of the six eye muscles, lifts the upper eyelid, and through its parasympathetic fibres narrows the pupil and focuses the lens for near vision.
nerves:structures/oculomotor-nerve/issue: A drooping eyelid with the eye turned down and out, double vision and sometimes a large pupil. A sudden one with a large pupil or a severe headache is an emergency, because it can come from an aneurysm pressing on the nerve.
nerves:structures/oculomotor-nerve/inner: Four of the six eye muscles and the eyelid lifter, plus the muscles that narrow the pupil and focus the lens.
nerves:structures/trochlear-nerve/summar: The thinnest cranial nerve, and the only one that leaves the back of the brainstem. It supplies a single eye muscle, the superior oblique, which turns the eye down and in, the movement used to look down stairs or read.
nerves:structures/trochlear-nerve/issues: Vertical double vision, worse looking down, often with the head tilted to compensate. Usually after a head injury. See a doctor for any new double vision.
nerves:structures/trochlear-nerve/innerv: The superior oblique muscle, which turns the eye down and in.
nerves:structures/abducens-nerve/summary: Supplies the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward. Its long path along the base of the skull makes it easily affected by raised pressure inside the head.
nerves:structures/abducens-nerve/issues/: Horizontal double vision, worse looking toward the affected side, because the eye can't turn outward. New double vision needs a doctor promptly, and urgently with headache.
nerves:structures/abducens-nerve/innerva: The lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outwards.
nerves:structures/trigeminal-nerve/carri: Feeling in the face, and chewing
nerves:structures/trigeminal-nerve/summa: The main nerve of feeling for the face, scalp, eyes, teeth and inside of the mouth. Its three divisions come out through small holes above the eye, below the eye and on the chin, and the third division also works the chewing muscles.
nerves:structures/trigeminal-nerve/inner: Through the mandibular division (V3): the chewing muscles, and the mylohyoid and front of the digastric above the hyoid.
nerves:structures/trigeminal-nerve/membe: Forehead, scalp, upper eyelid, eye and nose.
Cheek, lower eyelid, upper lip, upper teeth and gums.
Lower lip, chin, lower teeth, jaw and the chewing muscles.
nerves:structures/trigeminal-nerve/issue: Sudden, severe, electric-shock pains in the face, set off by touch, chewing or brushing the teeth. A doctor can confirm it, and treatment usually helps.
A painful rash on the forehead or near the eye needs a doctor the same day, because it can affect the eye.
nerves:structures/facial-nerve/summary: Moves the muscles of facial expression. It leaves the skull just below the ear, passes through the parotid gland and fans out into five branches across the face. It also carries taste from the front of the tongue and runs the tear and saliva glands.
nerves:structures/facial-nerve/innervate: All the muscles of facial expression (occipitofrontalis, the rings around the eyes and mouth, the buccinator and the platysma are drawn), and the back of the digastric and the stylohyoid above the hyoid.
nerves:structures/facial-nerve/members/4: The thin platysma muscle in the neck.
nerves:structures/facial-nerve/issues/0/: Weakness of one whole side of the face, including the forehead, coming on over a day or two. Get seen the same day: sudden facial weakness can also be a stroke.
nerves:structures/facial-nerve/issues/1/: Shingles of the facial nerve: facial weakness with a painful rash in or around the ear. See a doctor promptly.
nerves:structures/vestibulocochlear-nerv: Runs a short distance from the inner ear, through the internal acoustic canal in the temporal bone, to the brainstem. Its cochlear part carries hearing and its vestibular part carries the sense of head position and movement.

Sudden severe spinning dizziness lasting days, with nausea but no hearing loss, usually after a virus. It settles over weeks. Dizziness with slurred speech, weakness, a drooping face or trouble walking is an emergency.
Hearing loss in one ear over hours or a few days needs to be seen within a day or two, because early treatment improves recovery.
Hearing from the cochlea and balance from the vestibule and semicircular canals.
nerves:structures/glossopharyngeal-nerve: Taste and feeling at the back of the tongue and throat, and swallowing

Leaves the skull with the vagus and runs down to the back of the tongue and throat. It carries taste and touch from the back third of the tongue and the throat (the gag reflex), supplies one swallowing muscle and the parotid salivary gland, and reports blood pressure from the carotid sinus.
Taste and feeling from the back of the tongue and the throat, one swallowing muscle (stylopharyngeus), and the parotid gland.
nerves:structures/vagus-nerve/summary: The longest cranial nerve. It runs down the neck beside the carotid artery and on into the chest and abdomen. It slows the heart, narrows the airways and drives digestion, and its branches work the throat and voice box.
nerves:structures/vagus-nerve/innervates: The “rest and digest” (parasympathetic) supply to the organs of the chest and most of the gut, as far as the middle of the large intestine.
nerves:structures/vagus-nerve/members/0/: Hooks under the aortic arch on the left and under the subclavian artery on the right, then climbs back up beside the trachea to the voice box.
nerves:structures/vagus-nerve/members/1/: The swallowing muscles of the throat.
nerves:structures/vagus-nerve/members/3/: Pass through the diaphragm with the oesophagus to the stomach and gut.
nerves:structures/vagus-nerve/issues/0/n: A surge of vagal activity, set off by pain, standing for a long time or the sight of blood, slows the heart and drops the blood pressure. Lie down with the legs raised. See a doctor if it happens during exercise or without warning.
nerves:structures/vagus-nerve/issues/1/n: Damage to the recurrent laryngeal branch, for example after thyroid surgery, can weaken the voice. Hoarseness lasting more than three weeks needs checking.
nerves:structures/accessory-nerve/summar: Starts in the top of the spinal cord, climbs into the skull and leaves it again beside the vagus. It runs through the sternocleidomastoid and across the side of the neck, just under the skin, to the trapezius.
nerves:structures/accessory-nerve/issues: Because it lies so close to the surface, surgery or a wound in the side of the neck can damage it. This leaves a drooping shoulder and trouble lifting the arm above shoulder height.
nerves:structures/hypoglossal-nerve/summ: Leaves the skull just above the top of the spine, curves forward below the jaw, past the carotid arteries, and enters the tongue from below. It supplies all of the tongue muscles but one, for speaking, chewing and swallowing.
nerves:structures/hypoglossal-nerve/issu: The tongue points toward the weak side when stuck out, with slurred speech. A new one needs a doctor, and sudden speech or swallowing problems are an emergency.
nerves:structures/cervical-plexus/carrie: Feeling in the neck, and movement
nerves:structures/cervical-plexus/summar: A network formed by the top four neck nerves, deep to the sternocleidomastoid. Its skin branches fan out from the middle of that muscle’s back edge to the ear, the neck and the collarbone. Its muscle branches include a loop for the strap muscles (the ansa cervicalis) and the phrenic nerve.
nerves:structures/cervical-plexus/innerv: The strap muscles below the hyoid through the ansa cervicalis, the geniohyoid above it through C1 fibres, and direct branches to levator scapulae and the scalenes.
nerves:structures/cervical-plexus/member: Skin over the ear and the angle of the jaw.
Skin at the front of the neck.
Skin over the collarbone and the top of the shoulder.
A loop in front of the carotid artery that supplies the strap muscles.
nerves:structures/phrenic-nerve/summary: The nerve of the diaphragm, from the neck nerves C3 to C5 (“C3, 4 and 5 keep the diaphragm alive”). It runs down the front of the neck muscles into the chest, along the sides of the heart, to the diaphragm, the main muscle of breathing.
nerves:structures/phrenic-nerve/innervat: Its only muscle. It also carries feeling from the coverings of the heart and the centre of the diaphragm.
nerves:structures/phrenic-nerve/issues/0: Irritation under the diaphragm, from the gallbladder, liver or blood in the abdomen, is felt in the tip of the shoulder, because the phrenic nerve and the shoulder skin share the same spinal levels. Shoulder-tip pain with belly pain needs a doctor.
nerves:structures/phrenic-nerve/issues/1: Damage to one phrenic nerve, from surgery, a tumour or a neck injury, weakens one side of the diaphragm. It can cause breathlessness, especially when lying flat.
nerves:structures/intercostal-nerves/sum: The front branches of the twelve thoracic nerves. Each runs around the body in the groove under its rib, supplying the muscles between the ribs, the belly wall and a band of skin. The twelfth, below the last rib, is called the subcostal nerve.
nerves:structures/intercostal-nerves/inn: The upper six stay on the chest wall; the lower six carry on into the muscles of the belly wall. The subcostal nerve also reaches the quadratus lumborum.
nerves:structures/intercostal-nerves/iss: A painful, blistering rash in a band around one side of the chest or belly, along one intercostal nerve. See a doctor early, as treatment works best in the first three days.

Burning or stabbing pain in a band around the chest, for example after shingles or chest surgery. Chest pain with breathlessness or sweating, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw, needs emergency care instead.
nerves:structures/brachial-plexus/summar: The network that supplies the whole arm. Its five roots leave the neck between the scalene muscles, merge and divide again behind the collarbone, and regroup in the armpit into the five nerves of the arm. On the way it sends branches to the chest and shoulder-blade muscles.
nerves:structures/brachial-plexus/innerv: Through short branches that leave before the plexus ends: the pectoral, long thoracic, thoracodorsal, suprascapular, subscapular and dorsal scapular nerves.
nerves:structures/brachial-plexus/member: Runs down the side of the chest to the serratus anterior. Damage gives a “winged” shoulder blade.
Supraspinatus and infraspinatus of the rotator cuff.
nerves:structures/brachial-plexus/issues: A hard knock to the head and shoulder in contact sport stretches the plexus: burning pain and tingling down one arm for seconds to minutes. Repeated episodes, or weakness that lasts, need assessment.
Pressure on the plexus between the collarbone and the first rib causes aching, tingling or weakness in the arm, often worse with the arm raised.
A violent pull on the arm or neck, as in a motorbike fall, can tear the roots and leave the arm weak and numb. It needs specialist assessment.
nerves:structures/axillary-nerve/summary: Leaves the back of the armpit and wraps around the neck of the humerus to reach the deltoid and teres minor. It also gives feeling to a patch of skin over the outside of the shoulder.
nerves:structures/axillary-nerve/innerva: The deltoid, and teres minor in the rotator cuff.
nerves:structures/axillary-nerve/issues/: A dislocated shoulder or a broken top of the humerus can stretch it, leaving a numb patch on the outer shoulder and a weak deltoid. Doctors check for this when treating these injuries.
nerves:structures/musculocutaneous-nerve: Runs down the front of the arm between the biceps and the brachialis and supplies both. Below the elbow it becomes the skin nerve of the outer forearm.
It passes through the coracobrachialis on its way down the arm.
nerves:structures/median-nerve/summary: Runs down the arm beside the brachial artery, through the middle of the forearm and under the band across the wrist (the carpal tunnel) into the palm. It works most forearm flexors and the ball of the thumb, and gives feeling to the thumb, index, middle and half of the ring finger.
nerves:structures/median-nerve/innervate: All the forearm flexors except the flexor carpi ulnaris and half of the deep finger flexor, most of the thenar muscles and the first two lumbricals.
nerves:structures/median-nerve/issues/0/: Pressure in the carpal tunnel causes tingling, numbness and pain in the thumb and first fingers, often at night. Wrist splints and avoiding long bent-wrist positions help. Constant numbness or a weak thumb needs a doctor.
nerves:structures/ulnar-nerve/summary: Runs down the inner side of the arm and passes behind the bony bump on the inside of the elbow, the “funny bone”, just under the skin. It carries on down the inner forearm to the little-finger side of the hand, where it works most of the small hand muscles.
nerves:structures/ulnar-nerve/innervates: In the forearm, the flexor carpi ulnaris and half of the deep finger flexor. In the hand, the hypothenar muscles, the interossei, the third and fourth lumbricals and the adductor of the thumb.
nerves:structures/ulnar-nerve/issues/0/n: A knock on the inner elbow presses the nerve against bone: a brief electric tingle into the little and ring fingers.
nerves:structures/ulnar-nerve/issues/1/n: Pressure at the elbow, often from leaning on it or sleeping with it bent, numbs the little and ring fingers and can later weaken the grip. See a doctor if it persists.
nerves:structures/radial-nerve/summary: The largest branch of the brachial plexus. It spirals around the back of the humerus in a groove (drawn faint in the front view), comes forward at the outer elbow and splits: a deep branch to the muscles on the back of the forearm and a skin branch to the back of the hand on the thumb side. It straightens the elbow, wrist and fingers.
nerves:structures/radial-nerve/issues/0/: Pressure in the spiral groove, from a broken humerus or sleeping with an arm hung over a chair back (“Saturday night palsy”), leaves the wrist and fingers unable to lift. Get it checked. Most pressure palsies recover over weeks.
nerves:structures/lumbar-plexus/summary: A network formed inside the psoas muscle from the upper lumbar nerves. Its small branches run around the belly wall to the groin and down the outer thigh. Its two big branches, the femoral and obturator nerves, go to the front and inner thigh.
nerves:structures/lumbar-plexus/innervat: Directly to the psoas and quadratus lumborum, and to the lowest belly-wall muscles through the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.
nerves:structures/lumbar-plexus/members/: L1: the lowest belly wall and the skin above the pubic bone.
L1: the groin and the skin of the genitals. It can be irritated after hernia repair.
L1–L2: the groin and the cremaster muscle.
L2–L3: skin of the outer thigh. It passes just inside the bony point at the front of the hip.
nerves:structures/lumbar-plexus/issues/0: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is pinched where it passes under the inguinal ligament, causing burning, tingling or numbness over the outer thigh. Tight belts, weight gain and pregnancy are common causes. It isn’t dangerous and usually settles.
nerves:structures/femoral-nerve/summary: The largest branch of the lumbar plexus. It runs down in the groove between psoas and iliacus, passes under the inguinal ligament on the outer side of the femoral artery, and splits into branches for the front of the thigh. Its longest branch, the saphenous nerve, gives feeling down the inner leg to the foot.
nerves:structures/femoral-nerve/members/: To the quadriceps, sartorius and iliacus.
Skin over the front of the thigh.
Skin of the inner knee, leg and foot, alongside the great saphenous vein.
nerves:structures/femoral-nerve/issues/0: Bleeding into the groin or pelvis, or hip surgery, can weaken knee straightening so the knee buckles, with numbness over the front of the thigh. See a doctor.
nerves:structures/obturator-nerve/summar: Runs down the side wall of the pelvis and through the obturator foramen, the large hole in the hip bone, into the inner thigh. It supplies the adductors that pull the legs together, and a patch of skin on the inner thigh.
nerves:structures/sacral-plexus/summary: A network on the back wall of the pelvis, in front of the sacrum, made from the last two lumbar and the first four sacral nerves. It supplies the buttock and the pelvic floor and ends as the sciatic nerve.
nerves:structures/sacral-plexus/innervat: Through the superior and inferior gluteal nerves (drawn faint in the front view, behind the hip bone), short direct branches (piriformis and the deep hip rotators), and the pudendal nerve, which has its own page.
nerves:structures/sacral-plexus/members/: Gluteus medius and minimus, and tensor fasciae latae.
Skin of the back of the thigh.
nerves:structures/pudendal-nerve/summary: Leaves the pelvis below the piriformis, hooks around the ischial spine and runs forward in a canal along the side wall of the pelvic outlet to the perineum. It works the pelvic floor and the sphincters that keep urine and stool in, and gives feeling to the genitals and the skin around the anus. Drawn in the back view.
nerves:structures/pudendal-nerve/innerva: The external anal and urethral sphincters, the pelvic floor, and the skin and erectile tissue of the genitals.
nerves:structures/pudendal-nerve/members: The external anal sphincter and the skin around the anus.
The muscles of the perineum, the urethral sphincter and the skin of the scrotum or labia.
Dorsal nerve of the penis or clitoris
Feeling in the penis or the clitoris.
nerves:structures/pudendal-nerve/issues/: Burning or stabbing pain in the genitals, the perineum or around the anus, worse sitting and eased by standing or lying down. Long cycling and childbirth can set it off. See a doctor.
New numbness around the genitals or bottom with bladder or bowel trouble can mean cauda equina syndrome. Get emergency care.
nerves:structures/sciatic-nerve/summary: The thickest and longest nerve in the body, about as wide as a thumb. It leaves the pelvis below the piriformis, runs down the back of the thigh and splits above the knee into the tibial and common fibular nerves. Drawn faint in the front view, where it lies behind the femur.
nerves:structures/sciatic-nerve/innervat: The hamstrings and the hamstring part of adductor magnus. Through its two branches it also runs every muscle below the knee.
nerves:structures/sciatic-nerve/issues/0: Pain spreading from the lower back or buttock down the back of the leg, often with tingling, usually from a disc pressing on a nerve root. Most cases settle within six weeks with staying active and simple pain relief.
nerves:structures/sciatic-nerve/issues/1: Numbness around the bottom or genitals, new trouble with the bladder or bowel, or weakness in both legs can mean cauda equina syndrome. Get emergency care.
nerves:structures/tibial-nerve/summary: The larger branch of the sciatic nerve. It runs down the middle of the back of the knee and deep in the calf, then curves behind the inner ankle bone into the sole, where it splits into the medial and lateral plantar nerves. Drawn faint in the front view, where it lies behind the bones.
nerves:structures/tibial-nerve/innervate: Every muscle in the back of the calf, and through the plantar nerves the small muscles of the sole.
nerves:structures/tibial-nerve/members/0: The inner sole and the big toe side.
nerves:structures/tibial-nerve/members/1: The outer sole and most of the small foot muscles.
nerves:structures/tibial-nerve/members/2: Skin of the outer ankle and foot, joined by a branch of the common fibular nerve.
nerves:structures/tibial-nerve/issues/0/: Pressure behind the inner ankle bone causes burning, tingling or numbness in the sole. See a doctor if it persists.
nerves:structures/tibial-nerve/issues/1/: A thickened toe nerve, usually between the third and fourth toes, causing burning pain in the ball of the foot, like standing on a pebble. Wider shoes help.
nerves:structures/common-fibular-nerve/s: The smaller branch of the sciatic nerve. It follows the outer hamstring tendon behind the knee (drawn faint in the front view), winds around the neck of the fibula just under the skin below the outer knee, and splits into the deep and superficial fibular nerves.
nerves:structures/common-fibular-nerve/i: Only the short head of biceps femoris above the knee. Everything below it goes through its two branches.

Pressure where it crosses the fibula, from crossing the legs for a long time, a tight cast or a knee injury, makes it hard to lift the foot and toes, so the toes catch when walking. See a doctor promptly.
nerves:structures/deep-fibular-nerve/sum: Runs down the front of the leg beside the anterior tibial artery to the top of the foot. It lifts the foot and toes, and gives feeling to the small web of skin between the big and second toes.
nerves:structures/superficial-fibular-ne: Runs down the outer side of the leg among the fibularis muscles, comes to the surface above the ankle and spreads over the top of the foot. It turns the sole outward and gives feeling to most of the top of the foot.
nerves:groups/spinal/summary: The cord inside the spine and the 31 pairs of nerves that leave it, one pair at each level.
nerves:groups/cranial-nerves/summary: Twelve pairs of nerves that leave the brain and brainstem directly, through openings in the skull, numbered I to XII from front to back. They carry smell, sight, eye movement, feeling and movement in the face, hearing and balance, taste, swallowing and speech, and the vagus reaches down to the chest and gut. Most run inside the head, so they are drawn faint.
nerves:groups/trunk-nerves/summary: Nerves of the neck, the diaphragm, and the chest and belly wall.
nerves:groups/trunk-nerves/issues/0/note: The chickenpox virus wakes up in one nerve root and causes a painful, blistering rash in a band on one side of the body. See a doctor early, as treatment works best in the first three days.
nerves:groups/arm-nerves/summary: The brachial plexus and the five nerves it ends in, which run the whole arm and hand.
nerves:groups/arm-nerves/issues/0/note: Pressure on a nerve causes tingling, numbness or weakness in the area it supplies. Most cases settle once the pressure is taken off. Weakness that persists or gets worse needs a doctor.
nerves:groups/leg-nerves/summary: The lumbar and sacral plexuses and the nerves they send into the leg, including the sciatic nerve, the largest in the body.
nerves:groups/leg-nerves/issues/0/note: Pressure on a nerve causes tingling, numbness or weakness in the area it supplies. Most cases settle once the pressure is taken off. Weakness that persists or gets worse needs a doctor.
regions:disclaimer: Corpus is an educational map, not a diagnosis. It can’t examine you or know your history. If you are worried about a symptom, talk to a doctor or pharmacist.
regions:emergency: In an emergency call your local emergency number: 112 (EU), 999 (UK), 911 (US).
regions:redFlags/0: Chest pain or pressure, especially with breathlessness, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to the arm, neck or jaw
regions:redFlags/1: Signs of stroke: face drooping, arm weakness, slurred speech
regions:redFlags/2: A sudden, severe headache, or a headache with fever, stiff neck or rash
regions:redFlags/3: Difficulty breathing, choking, or blue lips
regions:redFlags/4: Heavy bleeding, vomiting blood, or black tarry stools
regions:redFlags/5: Severe abdominal pain with a rigid belly or fainting, or abdominal pain in pregnancy
regions:redFlags/7: Sudden, severe pain in a testicle
regions:redFlags/8: Heavy bleeding, or severe pain, in pregnancy
regions:regions/head/causes/0/signs: Band-like pressure on both sides, often with stress, poor sleep, dehydration or long screen time.
regions:regions/head/causes/1/signs: Throbbing, often one-sided, with nausea and sensitivity to light or sound; sometimes a visual aura first.
regions:regions/head/causes/2/signs: Pressure over the forehead or cheeks with a blocked nose after a cold, worse bending forward.
regions:regions/head/causes/3/signs: Headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion after a knock to the head.
regions:regions/head/causes/4/signs: Near-daily headaches in someone taking painkillers on most days.
regions:regions/head/redFlags/0: A sudden “thunderclap” headache, the worst you’ve ever had
regions:regions/head/redFlags/1: Headache with fever, a stiff neck, a rash or confusion
regions:regions/head/redFlags/2: Headache after a head injury with vomiting, drowsiness or worsening pain
regions:regions/head/redFlags/3: Headache with weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking or seeing
regions:regions/head/redFlags/4: A new headache after 50 with scalp tenderness or jaw pain when chewing
regions:regions/face/causes/0/signs: Pressure in the cheeks or forehead, blocked nose, thick discharge.
regions:regions/face/causes/1/signs: Brief electric-shock pains in the face set off by touch, eating or wind.
regions:regions/face/causes/2/signs: One side of the face droops or won’t move, including the forehead, coming on over a day or two, sometimes with pain behind the ear. Sudden facial weakness can also be a stroke, so get seen the same day.
regions:regions/face/causes/3/signs: After a blow: swelling, numbness, a bite that doesn’t meet, or double vision.
regions:regions/face/causes/4/signs: Bleeding from one nostril, often after picking, a cold or dry air. Sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for 10 to 15 minutes.
regions:regions/face/causes/5/signs: A burning pain, then a blistering rash on one side of the forehead or face. See a doctor within 3 days, and the same day if it is near the eye.
regions:regions/face/redFlags/0: Sudden drooping of one side of the face (possible stroke)
regions:regions/face/redFlags/1: Facial swelling that is spreading fast, or swelling with difficulty swallowing or breathing
regions:regions/face/redFlags/2: A hot, red, swollen area around the eye or nose with fever
regions:regions/eye/causes/0/signs: A red, gritty or itchy eye with watery or sticky discharge, often in both eyes, while your sight stays normal. It usually clears in one to two weeks.
regions:regions/eye/causes/1/signs: Burning, gritty or tired eyes, worse with screens, heating, air conditioning or wind.
regions:regions/eye/causes/2/signs: A tender red lump on the edge of the eyelid that usually settles in a week or two with warm compresses.
regions:regions/eye/causes/3/title: Scratch or something in the eye
regions:regions/eye/causes/3/signs: Sharp pain, watering and a feeling that something is there, after dust, a fingernail or a contact lens. If it isn’t better within a day, see a pharmacist, optician or doctor.
regions:regions/eye/causes/4/signs: A red, sore or gritty eye. Pain with blurred vision or light sensitivity, or after an injury, needs same-day care.
regions:regions/eye/causes/5/signs: Pain on moving one eye, with blurring or faded colours in that eye coming on over a few days.
regions:regions/eye/causes/6/signs: Sudden, severe pain in one eye with redness, blurred vision, haloes around lights, headache and sometimes vomiting.
regions:regions/eye/causes/7/signs: Seeing two of things, side by side or one above the other. If it starts suddenly, especially with a droopy eyelid, a headache, or weakness or numbness elsewhere, get emergency care. Double vision that comes and goes over weeks, worse when tired, also needs a doctor.
regions:regions/eye/redFlags/0: Sudden loss of sight, or a curtain or shadow across part of your vision
regions:regions/eye/redFlags/1: New flashes of light or a shower of new floaters
regions:regions/eye/redFlags/2: A chemical splash (rinse with plenty of clean water first), or an injury from something sharp or fast-moving
regions:regions/eye/redFlags/3: A painful red eye with blurred vision
regions:regions/eye/redFlags/4: Sudden double vision, especially with a droopy eyelid or a headache
regions:regions/ear/causes/0/signs: Earache with a cold, sometimes with muffled hearing or a fever. Common in children, and most settle within 3 days.
regions:regions/ear/causes/1/signs: An itchy, painful ear canal, worse when the ear is pulled, often after swimming. A pharmacist can help.
regions:regions/ear/causes/2/signs: A blocked, full feeling with muffled hearing, sometimes with ringing.
regions:regions/ear/causes/3/title: Jaw joint pain felt in the ear
regions:regions/ear/causes/3/signs: Aching in front of the ear, worse when chewing or yawning, often with clicking. The ear itself is healthy.
regions:regions/ear/causes/4/title: Pain from the throat or teeth
regions:regions/ear/causes/4/signs: Tonsillitis, a bad tooth or a sore throat can be felt as earache, because they share nerves with the ear.
regions:regions/ear/causes/5/signs: Brief spells of spinning when you move your head (often from loose crystals in the inner ear), or constant dizziness after a cold (inner ear inflammation).
regions:regions/ear/causes/6/signs: Hearing drops in one ear over hours to a few days, without a cold or earwax. Get seen within a day, because early treatment helps.
regions:regions/ear/redFlags/0: A red, tender swelling behind the ear that pushes it forward, with a fever
regions:regions/ear/redFlags/1: Sudden hearing loss in one ear
regions:regions/ear/redFlags/2: Earache with a drooping face, or blisters in or around the ear
regions:regions/ear/redFlags/3: Dizziness with a severe headache, double vision, slurred speech or weakness (possible stroke)
regions:regions/jaw-teeth/causes/0/signs: Aching in front of the ear, clicking, pain when chewing, often with clenching or grinding.
regions:regions/jaw-teeth/causes/1/signs: Toothache, sensitivity to hot or cold, or a swollen gum or cheek. Swelling or fever needs a dentist promptly.
regions:regions/jaw-teeth/causes/2/signs: An aching jaw, tired face muscles or a headache on waking, sometimes with worn or chipped teeth.
regions:regions/jaw-teeth/causes/3/signs: Pain and swelling at the back of the jaw, sometimes with a bad taste or trouble opening the mouth.
regions:regions/jaw-teeth/causes/4/signs: Small, painful sores inside the mouth that heal within 2 weeks. One that lasts longer than 3 weeks needs checking.
regions:regions/jaw-teeth/causes/5/signs: A painful swelling under the jaw or in front of the ear that comes on when you eat.
regions:regions/jaw-teeth/causes/6/title: Pain on chewing with a new headache
regions:regions/jaw-teeth/causes/6/signs: Jaw tiredness when chewing, with a new headache or a tender scalp, in someone over 50, can be inflamed arteries (giant cell arteritis) and needs treatment the same day to protect your sight.
regions:regions/jaw-teeth/causes/7/signs: An ache in the jaw or neck brought on by effort, or with chest tightness, breathlessness or sweating, can be angina or a heart attack.
regions:regions/jaw-teeth/causes/8/signs: After a blow: the teeth don’t meet properly, it hurts to open the mouth, or the lower lip is numb.
regions:regions/jaw-teeth/redFlags/0: Jaw pain with chest pain, breathlessness or sweating: call emergency services
regions:regions/jaw-teeth/redFlags/1: Swelling in the face, jaw or floor of the mouth that is spreading, or makes it hard to swallow, breathe or open the mouth
regions:regions/jaw-teeth/redFlags/2: A mouth ulcer, lump or white or red patch that hasn’t healed after 3 weeks
regions:regions/jaw-teeth/redFlags/3: A new headache with jaw pain on chewing after 50
regions:regions/neck/causes/0/signs: Stiffness and pain after sleeping awkwardly, long desk work or a jolt.
regions:regions/neck/causes/1/signs: Neck pain shooting into the arm with tingling, numbness or weakness.
regions:regions/neck/causes/2/signs: Waking with the head stuck turned to one side, painful to straighten. It usually eases within a few days to a week.
regions:regions/neck/causes/3/signs: Stiffness and aching that come and go with age, sometimes with grinding when you turn your head. Gentle movement helps.
regions:regions/neck/causes/4/signs: Neck pain and stiffness coming on in the hours after a sudden jolt, such as a car being hit from behind.
regions:regions/neck/redFlags/0: Neck pain after a significant injury such as a fall or car crash: keep still and get help
regions:regions/neck/redFlags/1: Fever with a stiff neck, headache or rash
regions:regions/neck/redFlags/2: Neck pain with arm weakness or clumsy hands
regions:regions/neck/redFlags/3: A lump in the side of the neck that is growing or hasn’t gone after 3 weeks
regions:regions/throat/causes/0/signs: Pain on swallowing, sometimes with white patches on the tonsils and tender glands under the jaw, during a cold. Most get better within a week.
regions:regions/throat/causes/1/signs: A hoarse, weak or lost voice after a cold or a lot of talking or shouting. See a doctor if it lasts more than 3 weeks.
regions:regions/throat/causes/2/signs: Burning in the throat and a sour taste, worse lying down.
regions:regions/throat/causes/3/signs: A feeling of something stuck in the throat between meals, while food and drink go down normally. It is common, harmless and often linked to reflux or stress.
regions:regions/throat/causes/4/signs: A lump at the front of the neck that moves when you swallow.
regions:regions/throat/causes/5/signs: Food sticking on the way down, or swallowing that is getting harder over weeks.
regions:regions/throat/causes/6/signs: A severe sore throat on one side, getting worse, with difficulty swallowing or opening the mouth, a muffled voice and fever.
regions:regions/throat/causes/7/signs: A feeling of food stuck after swallowing, with drooling or being unable to swallow your own saliva.
regions:regions/throat/redFlags/0: Difficulty breathing, noisy breathing, drooling or being unable to swallow saliva
regions:regions/throat/redFlags/1: Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat with a rash or breathlessness (possible severe allergic reaction): call emergency services
regions:regions/throat/redFlags/2: A hoarse voice for more than 3 weeks, especially if you smoke
regions:regions/throat/redFlags/3: Swallowing that keeps getting harder, or weight loss you can’t explain
regions:regions/shoulder/causes/0/signs: Pain on the outer shoulder when lifting the arm, and pain at night lying on it.
regions:regions/shoulder/causes/1/signs: Gradually increasing pain and stiffness in every direction.
regions:regions/shoulder/causes/2/signs: Pain at the top of the shoulder after falling onto it; a bump may appear.
regions:regions/shoulder/causes/3/signs: After a fall: deformity and unable to move the arm.
regions:regions/shoulder/causes/4/signs: Shoulder pain can come from the neck, or from the diaphragm, gallbladder or heart irritating shared nerves.
regions:regions/shoulder/redFlags/0: Shoulder or arm pain with chest pressure, breathlessness or sweating: call emergency services
regions:regions/shoulder/redFlags/1: Deformity after an injury, or a cold, numb arm
regions:regions/shoulder/redFlags/2: Shoulder-tip pain after a blow to the abdomen (possible internal bleeding)
regions:regions/armpit/causes/0/signs: A tender lump after an infection in the hand or arm, a recent vaccination or a shaving rash. It usually settles within two or three weeks.
regions:regions/armpit/causes/1/signs: A red, hot, tender lump in the skin, sometimes with a yellow head, often after shaving. Warm compresses help. See a doctor if it spreads, grows or you feel unwell.
regions:regions/armpit/causes/2/signs: Painful lumps and abscesses that keep coming back in the armpits or groin, healing with scars. It is treatable, so see a doctor.
regions:regions/armpit/causes/3/signs: Pain at the front or back fold of the armpit after lifting, throwing or pushing, worse using the arm.
regions:regions/armpit/causes/4/signs: Breast tissue extends into the armpit, and breast cancer can spread to these nodes. Any new lump with a change in the breast needs a doctor.
regions:regions/armpit/causes/5/signs: A swollen, heavy, aching or bluish arm, sometimes after heavy repeated arm use or a drip.
regions:regions/armpit/redFlags/0: A hard, fixed or growing lump, especially with a change in the breast
regions:regions/armpit/redFlags/1: A swollen, discoloured or heavy arm: same-day assessment (possible blood clot)
regions:regions/armpit/redFlags/2: Spreading redness or red streaks up the arm with fever
regions:regions/chest-center/causes/0/si: Pressure, tightness or heaviness that may spread to the arm, neck, jaw or back, with breathlessness, sweating or nausea.
regions:regions/chest-center/causes/1/si: Burning behind the breastbone after meals or lying down, with a sour taste.
regions:regions/chest-center/causes/2/si: Sharp pain where the ribs meet the breastbone, tender to press and worse with movement.
regions:regions/chest-center/causes/3/si: Sharp central pain, worse lying flat and better leaning forward, often after a viral illness.
regions:regions/chest-center/causes/4/si: Chest tightness with a racing heart, fast breathing and tingling. Get chest pain checked before assuming this.
regions:regions/chest-center/redFlags/0: Chest pain that lasts more than a few minutes, or comes with breathlessness, sweating, nausea or fainting: call emergency services now
regions:regions/chest-center/redFlags/1: Sudden tearing pain going through to the back
regions:regions/chest-right/causes/0/sig: Pain on twisting, coughing or pressing one spot, often after exertion or a fall.
regions:regions/chest-right/causes/1/sig: Sharp pain on breathing in, with fever and cough.
regions:regions/chest-right/causes/2/sig: Sudden sharp pain and breathlessness, maybe with a swollen calf or coughing blood.
regions:regions/chest-right/causes/3/sig: Sudden one-sided chest pain and breathlessness.
regions:regions/chest-right/causes/4/sig: A burning band of pain on one side, followed by a blistering rash. Early treatment helps.
regions:regions/chest-right/causes/5/sig: Pain under the lower right ribs after fatty meals, sometimes felt in the back.
regions:regions/chest-left/causes/0/sign: Pressure or tightness that may spread to the left arm, neck or jaw, with breathlessness or sweating.
regions:regions/chest-left/causes/1/sign: Pain on twisting, coughing or pressing one spot.
regions:regions/chest-left/causes/2/sign: Sharp pain on breathing in, with fever and cough.
regions:regions/chest-left/causes/3/sign: Sudden sharp pain and breathlessness, maybe with a swollen calf or coughing blood.
regions:regions/chest-left/causes/4/sign: Sudden one-sided chest pain and breathlessness.
regions:regions/chest-left/causes/5/sign: A burning band of pain on one side, followed by a blistering rash.
regions:regions/upper-arm/causes/0/signs: Ache after lifting or unaccustomed exercise, easing over days.
regions:regions/upper-arm/causes/1/signs: Pain at the front of the shoulder or upper arm. A sudden snap followed by a bulge in the arm suggests a rupture.
regions:regions/upper-arm/causes/2/signs: After a fall: severe pain, swelling, unable to use the arm.
regions:regions/upper-arm/causes/3/signs: Arm pain with tingling that follows a strip of skin, often with neck stiffness.
regions:regions/upper-arm/redFlags/0: Left arm pain with chest discomfort, breathlessness or sweating: call emergency services
regions:regions/elbow/causes/0/signs: Pain on the outer elbow when gripping, lifting or turning a handle.
regions:regions/elbow/causes/1/signs: Pain on the inner elbow with gripping.
regions:regions/elbow/causes/2/signs: A soft swelling on the point of the elbow. A red, hot one may be infected.
regions:regions/elbow/causes/3/signs: Tingling in the ring and little fingers, worse with the elbow bent.
regions:regions/elbow/causes/4/signs: After a fall: deformity, swelling, can’t bend or straighten the elbow.
regions:regions/forearm/causes/0/signs: Aching along the forearm after repetitive gripping, typing or tools.
regions:regions/forearm/causes/1/signs: After a fall: pain, swelling, a bend in the forearm.
regions:regions/forearm/causes/2/signs: Severe, increasing pain after a crush or fracture, worse when moving the fingers.
regions:regions/wrist/causes/0/signs: Pain and swelling after a twist, improving over days.
regions:regions/wrist/causes/1/signs: A smooth, rubbery lump on the back or front of the wrist, often painless, that can grow and shrink. Many go away on their own.
regions:regions/wrist/causes/2/signs: Pain on the thumb side of the wrist when gripping, lifting or turning the wrist, often in new parents.
regions:regions/wrist/causes/3/signs: Tingling or numbness in the thumb, index and middle fingers, often at night.
regions:regions/wrist/causes/4/signs: Aching at the base of the thumb when pinching or opening jars.
regions:regions/wrist/causes/5/signs: Pain at the base of the thumb after a fall on an outstretched hand, even if it seems only sprained. Needs an X-ray.
regions:regions/wrist/causes/6/signs: Pain, swelling or a bent shape just above the wrist after a fall on an outstretched hand.
regions:regions/wrist/redFlags/0: A wrist that looks bent or out of shape after a fall
regions:regions/wrist/redFlags/1: A hand that is cold, pale or numb after an injury
regions:regions/wrist/redFlags/2: A red, hot, swollen joint with fever
regions:regions/hand/causes/0/signs: Aching and swelling after a knock or a lot of gripping, easing over days.
regions:regions/hand/causes/1/signs: Tingling or numbness in the ring and little fingers, sometimes with a weak grip, often from leaning on the elbow or long bike rides.
regions:regions/hand/causes/2/signs: Firm lumps and cords in the palm that slowly pull one or more fingers, usually the ring and little fingers, into a bend.
regions:regions/hand/causes/3/signs: Swollen, stiff, tender knuckles on both hands, worse in the morning and lasting more than half an hour.
regions:regions/hand/causes/4/signs: Pain, swelling and a sunken knuckle after punching something or a fall.
regions:regions/hand/causes/5/signs: A red, hot, swollen, throbbing hand after a cut, bite or splinter. Bites, especially human or animal bites, need checking the same day.
regions:regions/hand/redFlags/0: Redness spreading quickly from a bite or wound, or a red streak up the arm
regions:regions/hand/redFlags/1: A deep cut with loss of movement or feeling
regions:regions/hand/redFlags/2: A hand that is cold, pale or numb after an injury
regions:regions/fingers/causes/0/signs: A swollen, painful finger joint after a ball hits the tip. A finger that looks crooked or won’t bend or straighten needs checking.
regions:regions/fingers/causes/1/signs: Knobbly, stiff, aching joints near the fingertips or at the base of the thumb, usually from middle age.
regions:regions/fingers/causes/2/signs: A red, swollen, painful fold of skin beside a nail, sometimes with pus. Warm soaks help; see a doctor if it spreads.
